8|⚪ T3 ROS2 Core|Architecture & Communic.what_it_is: ROS2 is the ground-up successor to ROS1, a robotics middleware framework rebuilt on top of DDS (Data Distribution Service) for inter-process communication instead of ROS1's custom TCPROS protocol and central roscore master.
8|⚪ T3 ROS2 Core|Architecture & Communic.why_it_exists: ROS1 had a single point of failure (roscore), no real-time guarantees, no built-in security, no native Windows/RTOS support, and could not cleanly support multi-robot fleets. Commercial and industrial robotics (autonomous vehicles, warehouse fleets, drones) needed decentralized discovery, configurable delivery guarantees, and security that ROS1's architecture could not retrofit without major hacks.
8|⚪ T3 ROS2 Core|Architecture & Communic.how_it_works: ROS2 nodes discover each other peer-to-peer via DDS's decentralized discovery protocol (multicast by default) -- there is no central registry to query or restart. Topics, services, and actions all map onto DDS publish-subscribe entities carrying Quality-of-Service (QoS) policies. The client libraries (rclcpp, rclpy) sit on top of an rmw (ROS middleware) abstraction layer that can plug in different DDS vendors (Fast DDS, Cyclone DDS, RTI Connext) or non-DDS transports (Zenoh).
8|⚪ T3 ROS2 Core|Architecture & Communic.use_when: Starting any new robotics project today -- ROS1 Noetic was the final ROS1 release and is end-of-life; building systems that need multi-robot communication, real-time control loops, embedded/microcontroller nodes via micro-ROS, or DDS-Security for sensitive deployments.
8|⚪ T3 ROS2 Core|Architecture & Communic.avoid_when: Maintaining a large legacy ROS1 codebase where the porting cost of the existing package ecosystem outweighs near-term benefits -- though this is increasingly rare given ROS1's EOL; extremely resource-constrained microcontrollers where even the lightest DDS implementation is too heavy (use micro-ROS or raw embedded protocols instead).
8|⚪ T3 ROS2 Core|Architecture & Communic.what_goes_wrong: Engineers coming from ROS1 expect a roscore-equivalent and get confused when nodes 'can't find each other' -- it's almost always a QoS incompatibility (e.g. a best-effort publisher and a reliable-only subscriber never connect, with no error). Multicast discovery also commonly fails across Docker containers or VLAN-segmented networks without extra configuration (Discovery Server or unicast peer lists).
8|⚪ T3 ROS2 Core|Architecture & Communic.real_example: A team porting a ROS1 navigation stack to ROS2 finds that nodes which subscribe late to '/tf_static' never receive the static transforms, because the ROS1-style default QoS (volatile durability) doesn't replay history to late joiners -- switching that topic to transient-local durability fixes it.

8|⚪ T3 ROS2 Core|Architecture & Communic.what_it_is: DDS is an OMG (Object Management Group) standard for data-centric, real-time publish-subscribe middleware, originally built for defense and aerospace systems, that ROS2 adopted as its default transport via the RTPS (Real-Time Publish-Subscribe) wire protocol.
8|⚪ T3 ROS2 Core|Architecture & Communic.why_it_exists: Rather than reinvent decentralized discovery, QoS-driven delivery guarantees, real-time determinism, and security, ROS2 adopted an existing open standard so it could swap vendor implementations (Fast DDS, Cyclone DDS, Connext, or Zenoh-based rmw layers) without changing any application code -- DDS had already solved these hard distributed-systems problems over two decades of use.
8|⚪ T3 ROS2 Core|Architecture & Communic.how_it_works: DDS implements a 'Global Data Space' abstraction: a DataWriter publishes typed data under a topic name, and any DataReader anywhere on the network matching that topic and type automatically receives it via RTPS over UDP (multicast or unicast), with no broker in between. Discovery is peer-to-peer using SPDP (participant discovery) and SEDP (endpoint discovery). Every DataWriter/DataReader carries a QoS profile, and communication only happens if writer and reader QoS are 'compatible'.
8|⚪ T3 ROS2 Core|Architecture & Communic.use_when: Any ROS2 system, since DDS is the default rmw layer -- especially when fine-grained per-topic delivery guarantees matter (reliable+transient-local for '/tf_static', best-effort+volatile for high-rate '/scan'), and for multi-robot or multi-machine deployments.
8|⚪ T3 ROS2 Core|Architecture & Communic.avoid_when: Extremely constrained microcontrollers, where even micro-ROS's lightweight client-server DDS (eProsima Micro XRCE-DDS) is too heavy -- drop to raw serial/CAN; WAN deployments where multicast-based discovery doesn't traverse routers well, where a Discovery Server or a Zenoh-based rmw is a better fit.
8|⚪ T3 ROS2 Core|Architecture & Communic.what_goes_wrong: Different DDS vendor implementations are nominally RTPS-compatible but in practice mixing Fast DDS and Cyclone DDS nodes on one network can cause intermittent discovery failures due to vendor-specific extensions and differing default buffer sizes. DDS's default multicast discovery also generates O(n^2) announcement traffic across all participants, which becomes a scalability bottleneck in large fleets.
8|⚪ T3 ROS2 Core|Architecture & Communic.real_example: A factory floor with 50 AMRs on the same ROS_DOMAIN_ID sees random connection drops once the fleet network is saturated with discovery announcements; the fix is deploying a Fast DDS Discovery Server as a central (but data-plane-optional) discovery broker, configuring each robot with unicast discovery against it, and splitting the fleet across multiple domain IDs by zone.

8|⚪ T3 ROS2 Core|Architecture & Communic.what_it_is: QoS policies are settings attached to ROS2 publishers and subscribers that control how messages are delivered: reliability (best-effort vs. reliable), durability (volatile vs. transient-local for late joiners), history depth, deadline, and liveliness.
8|⚪ T3 ROS2 Core|Architecture & Communic.why_it_exists: Different data streams have fundamentally different delivery requirements: a 30Hz LiDAR scan can tolerate dropped samples (best-effort, shallow queue), but a one-shot '/map' or '/tf_static' message must reach nodes that start up later (transient-local durability). ROS1 had no such concept -- every topic used the same TCP-based delivery, wasteful for high-rate sensors and insufficient for guaranteed delivery of critical data.
8|⚪ T3 ROS2 Core|Architecture & Communic.how_it_works: A publisher 'offers' a QoS profile and a subscriber 'requests' one; DDS only forms a connection if the subscriber's request is satisfiable by the publisher's offer (e.g. a RELIABLE subscriber cannot connect to a BEST_EFFORT publisher). rclcpp/rclpy provide ready-made profiles -- SensorDataQoS (best-effort, volatile, shallow queue, for sensor streams) and SystemDefaultsQoS (reliable, volatile) -- plus the ability to define custom profiles for topics like '/tf_static' (reliable, transient-local, keep-all).
8|⚪ T3 ROS2 Core|Architecture & Communic.use_when: Tuning a topic's communication to match its actual semantics -- sensor streams (camera, LiDAR, IMU) on best-effort/volatile to avoid back-pressure; commands, state, and static configuration (maps, transforms, parameters) on reliable/transient-local so late subscribers get the last value.
8|⚪ T3 ROS2 Core|Architecture & Communic.avoid_when: Don't default everything to reliable + keep-all history -- on high-frequency topics this causes unbounded memory growth and back-pressure stalls when a subscriber is slow; don't assume a QoS mismatch between publisher and subscriber will raise an error -- DDS simply never forms the connection, silently.
8|⚪ T3 ROS2 Core|Architecture & Communic.what_goes_wrong: The single most common ROS2 beginner bug is 'my subscriber callback never fires' with zero error output, caused by incompatible QoS (e.g. a publisher using best-effort while the subscriber defaults to reliable). A second common bug: setting transient-local durability on a high-rate topic exhausts memory because every historical sample is retained for hypothetical late joiners.
8|⚪ T3 ROS2 Core|Architecture & Communic.real_example: RViz2 shows nothing for '/camera/image_raw' even though 'ros2 topic hz' confirms it's publishing at 30Hz. Running 'ros2 topic info /camera/image_raw --verbose' reveals the publisher uses BEST_EFFORT (typical for image transport) while RViz2's image display subscribes RELIABLE by default -- overriding the display's QoS to best-effort fixes it immediately.

8|⚪ T3 ROS2 Core|Architecture & Communic.what_it_is: A ROS2 node is a single-purpose process (or, for composable nodes, a component loaded into a shared process) that performs one logical function -- e.g. a camera driver, an object detector, or a path planner -- and communicates with other nodes via topics, services, actions, and parameters.
8|⚪ T3 ROS2 Core|Architecture & Communic.why_it_exists: Decomposing a robot's software into many small, independently startable and restartable nodes gives modularity (swap a planner without touching perception), fault isolation, and language interoperability -- a Python perception node and a C++ controller node communicate transparently over the same middleware.
8|⚪ T3 ROS2 Core|Architecture & Communic.how_it_works: A node is created by instantiating rclcpp::Node (C++) or rclpy.node.Node (Python) with a unique name and optional namespace, then registering publishers, subscribers, service servers/clients, action servers/clients, parameters, and timers. An executor 'spins' the node, dispatching callbacks as messages, timers, and requests arrive. Nodes run standalone via 'ros2 run', or are composed into one process for zero-copy intra-process communication.
8|⚪ T3 ROS2 Core|Architecture & Communic.use_when: Structuring any ROS2 application around one node per logical responsibility (driver, filter, planner, controller); using namespaces to run multiple instances of the same node type for multi-robot systems (e.g. '/robot1/camera', '/robot2/camera').
8|⚪ T3 ROS2 Core|Architecture & Communic.avoid_when: Don't build a single monolithic 'god node' that does everything -- it defeats modularity, complicates testing, and becomes a single point of failure; conversely, don't over-decompose a tightly-coupled, high-rate pipeline into many tiny nodes communicating over standard topics, where serialization and IPC overhead dominates -- use composable nodes with intra-process communication instead.
8|⚪ T3 ROS2 Core|Architecture & Communic.what_goes_wrong: Forgetting to call rclcpp::spin() or rclpy.spin() means the node never processes callbacks -- subscriptions, timers, and services are registered but never fire, and the process appears to 'run' while doing nothing, with no error raised. Duplicate node names on the same domain also cause undefined behavior in discovery and confuse 'ros2' CLI introspection.
8|⚪ T3 ROS2 Core|Architecture & Communic.real_example: A student's subscriber node compiles and runs without error but never prints incoming messages. 'ros2 node info /my_node' shows the subscription exists, but 'ros2 node list' shows the node disappears almost immediately -- the process exits right after setup because spin() was never called, so no callback ever has a chance to run.

8|⚪ T3 ROS2 Core|Architecture & Communic.what_it_is: Topics are ROS2's asynchronous, many-to-many publish-subscribe communication channel: a publisher node sends typed messages on a named topic, and any number of subscriber nodes receive a copy, with no direct coupling between them.
8|⚪ T3 ROS2 Core|Architecture & Communic.why_it_exists: Most robot data is continuous streams -- sensor readings, state estimates, control commands -- where producers and consumers don't need to know about each other, may come and go dynamically, and may have multiple consumers (e.g. a camera feed consumed by both a perception node and a logging node). Topics decouple producers from consumers entirely.
8|⚪ T3 ROS2 Core|Architecture & Communic.how_it_works: A node creates a publisher with 'create_publisher<MsgType>(topic_name, qos)' and calls 'publish(msg)' whenever new data is ready; subscribers create a subscription with a callback that the executor invokes whenever a message arrives. Under the hood this maps directly onto a DDS DataWriter/DataReader pair on the matching topic name and type, with delivery governed by QoS. Topic names form a hierarchical namespace (e.g. '/robot1/camera/image_raw').
8|⚪ T3 ROS2 Core|Architecture & Communic.use_when: Any continuous or event stream where the publisher doesn't need a response and there can be zero, one, or many subscribers -- sensor data, odometry, velocity commands, state/status broadcasts, visualization data.
8|⚪ T3 ROS2 Core|Architecture & Communic.avoid_when: Don't use topics when you need a guaranteed one-to-one request/response with a return value (use a service) or a long-running task with progress feedback and cancellation (use an action) -- topics provide no acknowledgment that a message was received or processed.
8|⚪ T3 ROS2 Core|Architecture & Communic.what_goes_wrong: Type or name mismatches are silent: 'ros2 topic list' might show '/cmd_vel' from two different packages using different message types (Twist vs. TwistStamped), and they simply never connect, with nothing in the logs. High publish rates without QoS tuning (e.g. publishing full-resolution point clouds at 30Hz with reliable QoS and no queue limit) can also overwhelm subscribers and cause memory growth.
8|⚪ T3 ROS2 Core|Architecture & Communic.real_example: A teleop node publishes '/cmd_vel' as geometry_msgs/Twist, but the robot's base controller, recently migrated to ROS2, subscribes to geometry_msgs/TwistStamped on the same topic name -- 'ros2 topic info /cmd_vel' shows mismatched types, the robot simply never moves, and there's no runtime error pointing at the cause.

8|⚪ T3 ROS2 Core|Architecture & Communic.what_it_is: Services provide ROS2's synchronous (from the client's perspective) request-response communication pattern: a client sends a request message and blocks (or registers a callback) until the server returns exactly one response.
8|⚪ T3 ROS2 Core|Architecture & Communic.why_it_exists: Some operations are inherently one-shot, transactional queries or commands that need a direct answer -- 'what is the current battery level', 'reset this counter', 'compute inverse kinematics for this pose' -- where polling a topic for the answer would be wasteful and awkward, and where the caller needs to know the request was actually handled.
8|⚪ T3 ROS2 Core|Architecture & Communic.how_it_works: A '.srv' file defines a request type and a response type separated by '---'. A server node calls 'create_service(srv_type, name, callback)'; the callback receives the request and returns the response. A client calls 'create_client(srv_type, name)' and sends requests asynchronously (returning a future) or via a blocking spin-until-complete call. Internally this is implemented as a pair of DDS topics (request and response) correlated by a request ID.
8|⚪ T3 ROS2 Core|Architecture & Communic.use_when: Short, one-shot operations with a clear request/response contract and no need for progress feedback -- toggling a mode, querying a parameter or state snapshot, triggering a calibration routine, computing a one-off transform.
8|⚪ T3 ROS2 Core|Architecture & Communic.avoid_when: Don't use services for long-running operations (path planning that takes 30 seconds, navigation to a goal) -- a blocking service call with no feedback or cancellation will hang the client and there's no standard way to abort it; use an action instead. Also avoid services for continuous data -- that's what topics are for.
8|⚪ T3 ROS2 Core|Architecture & Communic.what_goes_wrong: Calling a service synchronously from within a node's main executor thread (e.g. calling another service from inside a subscription callback) can deadlock if the callee is on the same executor and single-threaded -- the call never returns because the executor can't process the response while blocked waiting. Service servers that are slow or down also cause clients to hang indefinitely without a timeout.
8|⚪ T3 ROS2 Core|Architecture & Communic.real_example: A node's timer callback calls '/get_robot_state' synchronously using 'rclpy.spin_until_future_complete' from inside an already-spinning single-threaded executor -- the call hangs forever because the executor is busy waiting on the future and can never process the response callback; switching to a MultiThreadedExecutor or using async/await resolves it.

8|⚪ T3 ROS2 Core|Architecture & Communic.what_it_is: Actions are ROS2's pattern for long-running, asynchronous tasks that report periodic feedback during execution and support cancellation -- think 'navigate to this pose' or 'follow this trajectory', as opposed to the instant request/response of a service.
8|⚪ T3 ROS2 Core|Architecture & Communic.why_it_exists: Many robot tasks take seconds to minutes (navigation, manipulation, charging), need to report progress (percentage complete, current waypoint), and must be cancellable mid-execution (user aborts a nav goal). Neither topics (no request/response semantics) nor services (no feedback, no cancel, blocking) fit this need.
8|⚪ T3 ROS2 Core|Architecture & Communic.how_it_works: An '.action' file defines Goal, Result, and Feedback message types. Internally an action server is built from services (goal submission, cancellation) plus topics (feedback, status) -- a client sends a goal, receives a goal handle, can poll/subscribe to feedback messages as the server executes, and can send a cancel request; the server eventually returns a Result with a terminal status (succeeded, aborted, canceled).
8|⚪ T3 ROS2 Core|Architecture & Communic.use_when: Any task with a meaningful duration, intermediate progress, and a legitimate cancel path -- Nav2's 'navigate_to_pose', MoveIt motion execution, a gripper close-with-force-feedback, a multi-step calibration sequence.
8|⚪ T3 ROS2 Core|Architecture & Communic.avoid_when: Don't use actions for instantaneous queries (overkill compared to a service) or for continuous streaming data with no concept of 'goal completion' (use topics). The added complexity (goal handles, feedback callbacks, cancellation state machine) isn't worth it for simple operations.
8|⚪ T3 ROS2 Core|Architecture & Communic.what_goes_wrong: Forgetting to handle the cancel callback means a client's cancel request is accepted but the server keeps running the goal to completion anyway -- the robot keeps moving toward a goal the operator thought they cancelled. Also, action servers that don't properly transition goal state (accepted -> executing -> succeeded/canceled/aborted) can leave clients waiting on a result that never arrives.
8|⚪ T3 ROS2 Core|Architecture & Communic.real_example: An operator sends a Nav2 'navigate_to_pose' goal, then immediately cancels it via 'ros2 action send_goal ... --feedback' interrupted with Ctrl-C -- but the underlying controller server doesn't check for cancellation inside its control loop, so the robot continues driving toward the original goal for several more seconds despite the action reporting 'canceling'.

8|⚪ T3 ROS2 Core|Architecture & Communic.what_it_is: Parameters are named, typed configuration values (int, double, string, bool, arrays) owned by individual nodes, settable at launch time via YAML files or command-line overrides, and readable/settable at runtime via service calls.
8|⚪ T3 ROS2 Core|Architecture & Communic.why_it_exists: Hardcoding constants (PID gains, topic names, thresholds, frame IDs) into source code means recompiling for every tuning change or deployment variant. Parameters let the same compiled node be configured differently per robot, per environment, and tuned live during development without restarting.
8|⚪ T3 ROS2 Core|Architecture & Communic.how_it_works: A node declares parameters with 'declare_parameter(name, default_value)' (ROS2 requires explicit declaration, unlike ROS1's dynamic parameter server), optionally with constraints/descriptors. Parameters can be set at launch from a YAML file passed to a Node action in a launch file, overridden with '--ros-args -p name:=value', read with 'get_parameter()', and changed at runtime via the '/node_name/set_parameters' service, with an optional callback to react to changes.
8|⚪ T3 ROS2 Core|Architecture & Communic.use_when: Any value that legitimately differs between deployments, robots, or tuning sessions -- controller gains, sensor topic remappings, frame names, thresholds, feature toggles, file paths.
8|⚪ T3 ROS2 Core|Architecture & Communic.avoid_when: Don't use parameters for values that change at high frequency or represent live sensor/state data -- that's what topics are for; parameters are meant for relatively static configuration, not a substitute for pub-sub. Also avoid using parameters to pass large data blobs (maps, point clouds) -- they're meant for scalars and small arrays/strings.
8|⚪ T3 ROS2 Core|Architecture & Communic.what_goes_wrong: Forgetting to call 'declare_parameter' before 'get_parameter' raises an exception at runtime in ROS2 (unlike ROS1's lenient parameter server) -- a common porting bug. Another common issue: a YAML parameter file's node name or namespace doesn't exactly match the running node, so the parameters are silently ignored and the node falls back to defaults with no warning.
8|⚪ T3 ROS2 Core|Architecture & Communic.real_example: A launch file loads 'controller_params.yaml' with parameters under the key 'my_controller:', but the node is actually launched in namespace '/robot1' so its fully-qualified name is '/robot1/my_controller' -- the YAML's top-level key doesn't match, the parameters aren't applied, and the controller silently runs with default (wrong) gains.

8|⚪ T3 ROS2 Core|Architecture & Communic.what_it_is: ros2 bag is ROS2's tool for recording the messages published on a set of topics to disk (in an SQLite3 or MCAP-backed container format) and later replaying them at original or adjusted speed, as if the original nodes were running.
8|⚪ T3 ROS2 Core|Architecture & Communic.why_it_exists: Robotics development needs reproducibility: a perception bug seen during a real test run can't be reliably re-triggered on a live robot, but a recorded bag of the exact sensor data lets developers replay it offline indefinitely, run new algorithms against historical data, and build regression test datasets.
8|⚪ T3 ROS2 Core|Architecture & Communic.how_it_works: 'ros2 bag record /topic1 /topic2 ...' (or '-a' for all topics) subscribes to the specified topics and serializes every message with its timestamp to a bag file (default storage is SQLite3, with MCAP as an increasingly common alternative for performance and tooling like Foxglove). 'ros2 bag play <bag>' republishes the recorded messages on their original topics with original timing (or a '--rate' multiplier), letting any other node consume them exactly as if live.
8|⚪ T3 ROS2 Core|Architecture & Communic.use_when: Capturing real sensor/robot data for offline algorithm development, debugging field issues after the fact, building datasets for SLAM/perception evaluation, and creating repeatable regression tests for perception or planning pipelines.
8|⚪ T3 ROS2 Core|Architecture & Communic.avoid_when: Don't record at full fidelity ('-a' with raw images/point clouds) for long durations without considering disk space -- raw camera and LiDAR topics can generate gigabytes per minute; for long-duration logging, record only the topics you need or use compressed/down-sampled versions. Bags also aren't a substitute for unit tests -- they verify behavior on specific recorded scenarios, not general correctness.
8|⚪ T3 ROS2 Core|Architecture & Communic.what_goes_wrong: Replaying a bag with '/tf' and '/tf_static' both recorded can produce duplicate or conflicting static transforms if static transforms were published more than once during recording, confusing tf2 lookups during replay. Also, clock handling: nodes using 'use_sim_time' must be set consistently, or replayed timestamps won't align with the nodes' notion of 'now', breaking time-based logic like message filters or TF lookups.
8|⚪ T3 ROS2 Core|Architecture & Communic.real_example: A team replays a bag to debug a navigation issue, but their costmap node uses wall-clock time for some internal timers while consuming '/clock' from the bag for everything else -- the mismatch causes the costmap to behave inconsistently during replay versus the original run, until they set 'use_sim_time:=true' uniformly across all nodes.

8|⚪ T3 ROS2 Core|Architecture & Communic.what_it_is: rqt is a Qt-based extensible GUI framework for ROS2 that hosts a collection of plugin tools -- rqt_graph (node/topic connection graphs), rqt_plot (live plotting of numeric topic data), rqt_console (log message viewer), rqt_reconfigure (parameter tuning UI), and more -- all dockable in one window.
8|⚪ T3 ROS2 Core|Architecture & Communic.why_it_exists: Command-line introspection ('ros2 topic', 'ros2 node', etc.) is precise but doesn't show the big picture -- how nodes and topics interconnect, how a numeric value evolves over time, or which nodes are logging warnings. rqt provides visual, real-time views of exactly this system-level information without writing custom code.
8|⚪ T3 ROS2 Core|Architecture & Communic.how_it_works: Launch with 'rqt' for an empty dockable window and add plugins from the Plugins menu, or launch a specific plugin directly (e.g. 'ros2 run rqt_graph rqt_graph'). Each plugin subscribes to the relevant ROS2 introspection topics/services (e.g. rqt_graph queries the node/topic graph via the ROS graph API; rqt_plot subscribes to a numeric topic field and plots it live; rqt_reconfigure exposes a node's parameters with live sliders that call the set_parameters service).
8|⚪ T3 ROS2 Core|Architecture & Communic.use_when: Getting a quick visual overview of a running system's node/topic graph (rqt_graph) when debugging connectivity; live-plotting a sensor value or controller error term (rqt_plot) while tuning; live-tuning parameters with sliders (rqt_reconfigure) during PID gain tuning.
8|⚪ T3 ROS2 Core|Architecture & Communic.avoid_when: Don't rely on rqt_graph as your primary architecture documentation -- it reflects only what's currently running and can be visually overwhelming for large systems; for headless/CI/production environments, GUI tools aren't appropriate -- use 'ros2 topic'/'ros2 node' CLI or logging instead.
8|⚪ T3 ROS2 Core|Architecture & Communic.what_goes_wrong: rqt_plot subscribing to a high-frequency topic (e.g. raw IMU at 200Hz) over a remote connection can itself add enough network/CPU load to perturb the very system being debugged ('observer effect'). Also, rqt_graph's default view hides 'debug' topics and dead-sinks by default, which can mislead users into thinking a topic connection doesn't exist when it's just filtered from the view.
8|⚪ T3 ROS2 Core|Architecture & Communic.real_example: A developer can't figure out why their controller isn't receiving '/joint_states' -- opening rqt_graph with 'Hidden' topics shown reveals two separate nodes both named 'joint_state_publisher' in different namespaces, one of which nobody is subscribing to, immediately explaining the disconnect that 'ros2 topic list' alone didn't make obvious.

8|⚪ T3 ROS2 Core|Architecture & Communic.what_it_is: RViz2 is ROS2's primary 3D visualization tool, rendering robot models (via URDF/TF), sensor data (point clouds, laser scans, images, costmaps), and planning artifacts (paths, markers, goals) in a live, interactive 3D scene synced to the robot's actual coordinate frames.
8|⚪ T3 ROS2 Core|Architecture & Communic.why_it_exists: Robot software reasons about coordinate frames, point clouds, occupancy grids, and trajectories that are nearly impossible to debug by reading raw message dumps -- RViz2 lets developers literally see what the robot 'thinks' the world looks like (its TF tree, sensor data, costmaps, planned paths) overlaid in 3D, which is essential for diagnosing perception, localization, and planning bugs.
8|⚪ T3 ROS2 Core|Architecture & Communic.how_it_works: RViz2 subscribes to topics via 'Display' plugins -- e.g. a 'LaserScan' display subscribes to a sensor_msgs/LaserScan topic and renders points relative to a chosen TF frame, a 'RobotModel' display loads the URDF and renders links positioned via the live TF tree, a 'Map' display shows an occupancy grid, and a 'Path'/'MarkerArray' display shows planner output. Everything is rendered relative to a user-selected 'Fixed Frame' (commonly 'map' or 'odom'), and TF transforms position each display's data correctly relative to that frame.
8|⚪ T3 ROS2 Core|Architecture & Communic.use_when: Visually verifying sensor data alignment (does the LiDAR scan line up with the robot model?), debugging TF tree issues, watching Nav2 costmaps and planned paths update live, and visualizing SLAM map-building progress.
8|⚪ T3 ROS2 Core|Architecture & Communic.avoid_when: Don't run RViz2 on the robot's onboard low-power compute -- it's GPU/CPU-intensive and competes with actual robot software for resources; run it on a workstation connected over the network instead. Also don't treat RViz2 as a functional test -- 'it looks right in RViz2' doesn't guarantee the underlying data or logic is correct (e.g. a costmap can visually look fine while still containing subtly wrong inflation values).
8|⚪ T3 ROS2 Core|Architecture & Communic.what_goes_wrong: If the selected 'Fixed Frame' doesn't exist or there's a broken TF chain to it, displays silently show nothing or throw a 'Transform error' in the display status, which is easy to miss -- the scene just looks empty rather than erroring loudly. Also, displays subscribing with the wrong QoS (e.g. RViz2 default reliable vs. a best-effort sensor publisher) silently show no data, the same QoS pitfall as elsewhere in ROS2.
8|⚪ T3 ROS2 Core|Architecture & Communic.real_example: A robot's point cloud display shows nothing in RViz2 even though 'ros2 topic hz /points' confirms data is flowing -- the Fixed Frame is set to 'map', but the TF tree has no path from 'map' to the LiDAR's frame because the localization node hasn't started yet, so RViz2 can't transform the points into the fixed frame and silently drops them, with the error visible only in small red text in the Displays panel.

8|⚪ T3 ROS2 Core|Architecture & Communic.what_it_is: The 'ros2' command-line tool is the unified entry point for introspecting and interacting with a running ROS2 system -- subcommands like 'ros2 topic', 'ros2 node', 'ros2 service', 'ros2 param', 'ros2 action', 'ros2 interface', and 'ros2 run'/'launch' cover discovery, inspection, manual publishing/calling, and process management.
8|⚪ T3 ROS2 Core|Architecture & Communic.why_it_exists: Replacing ROS1's separate binaries (rostopic, rosnode, rosservice, rosparam, ...) with subcommands of a single 'ros2' tool gives a consistent, discoverable interface (tab completion, consistent flags) for the everyday debugging tasks every ROS2 developer does dozens of times a day: 'what topics exist, what's publishing on this one, what type is it, what's the current value of this parameter'.
8|⚪ T3 ROS2 Core|Architecture & Communic.how_it_works: Each subcommand queries the ROS graph (via the same rcl/rmw discovery mechanisms nodes use) or directly interacts with topics/services: 'ros2 topic list/info/hz/echo/pub', 'ros2 node list/info', 'ros2 service list/call/type', 'ros2 param list/get/set/dump', 'ros2 action list/send_goal', 'ros2 interface show <type>' (prints a message/service/action definition), and 'ros2 run <pkg> <executable>' / 'ros2 launch <pkg> <file>' to start nodes.
8|⚪ T3 ROS2 Core|Architecture & Communic.use_when: Day-to-day debugging and manual testing -- checking whether a topic is publishing and at what rate ('ros2 topic hz'), inspecting a message's exact fields ('ros2 topic echo'), manually triggering a service or action to test a node in isolation, dumping/loading parameter sets, and checking message/service/action definitions without searching source code ('ros2 interface show').
8|⚪ T3 ROS2 Core|Architecture & Communic.avoid_when: Don't build production automation around parsing 'ros2 CLI' text output -- it's meant for humans; use the underlying client library APIs (rclpy/rclcpp) or ROS2 services directly for programmatic access. Also, 'ros2 topic pub' for continuous high-rate publishing is a debugging convenience, not a substitute for a real publisher node.
8|⚪ T3 ROS2 Core|Architecture & Communic.what_goes_wrong: 'ros2 topic echo' on a high-rate topic (e.g. a 30Hz point cloud) can flood the terminal and consume significant CPU/network just for the echo subscription itself, again the 'observer effect'. Also, 'ros2 param set' changes a running node's parameter value but does NOT persist it -- restarting the node reverts to the launch-time/default value unless the change is saved back into a YAML file with 'ros2 param dump'.
8|⚪ T3 ROS2 Core|Architecture & Communic.real_example: After tuning a controller's PID gains live with 'ros2 param set /controller kp 1.5', the values seem perfect -- but on the next robot restart the controller is back to its old, poorly-tuned gains, because the live 'ros2 param set' only changed the in-memory value; the developer needed to 'ros2 param dump /controller > controller_params.yaml' and update the launch file to persist it.

8|⚪ T3 ROS2 Core|Development|ROS2 worksp.what_it_is: A ROS2 workspace is a directory tree with a conventional layout -- 'src/' for source packages, 'build/' for intermediate build artifacts, 'install/' for the final built/installable packages, and 'log/' for build and runtime logs -- managed end-to-end by the 'colcon' build tool.
8|⚪ T3 ROS2 Core|Development|ROS2 worksp.why_it_exists: ROS2 systems are composed of many small packages (often dozens to hundreds) with interdependencies, each potentially in C++, Python, or mixed. A standard workspace layout lets colcon discover, order, and build all of them consistently, and lets every developer's machine, CI runner, and Docker image share the exact same structure and 'source install/setup.bash' workflow.
8|⚪ T3 ROS2 Core|Development|ROS2 worksp.how_it_works: You clone or write packages into 'src/', then run 'colcon build' from the workspace root; colcon topologically sorts packages by their package.xml dependencies, builds each (CMake for C++/ament_cmake, setup.py for Python/ament_python) into 'build/', and installs the results into 'install/'. Sourcing 'install/setup.bash' (or .zsh/.ps1) adds the workspace's packages to your environment (CMAKE_PREFIX_PATH, PYTHONPATH, AMENT_PREFIX_PATH, etc.), 'overlaying' it on top of the underlying ROS2 install.
8|⚪ T3 ROS2 Core|Development|ROS2 worksp.use_when: Any time you're developing, modifying, or building ROS2 packages from source -- whether your own packages or third-party packages not available as binary apt packages for your distro/architecture (e.g. on Jetson or for bleeding-edge versions).
8|⚪ T3 ROS2 Core|Development|ROS2 worksp.avoid_when: Don't build packages from source in a workspace if a maintained binary apt package ('ros-<distro>-<package>') exists and meets your needs -- source builds are slower, and you take on responsibility for rebuilding on every dependency update; for simple scripts/nodes that don't need ROS2 package machinery, a plain Python script with rclpy installed can suffice without a full workspace.
8|⚪ T3 ROS2 Core|Development|ROS2 worksp.what_goes_wrong: Forgetting to re-source 'install/setup.bash' after a rebuild means your shell still points at stale binaries/libraries from before the change -- 'ros2 run' executes the old code and the fix 'doesn't seem to apply'. Another classic: 'underlay/overlay' confusion -- sourcing the workspace overlay before the base ROS2 underlay (or in the wrong order across multiple nested workspaces) causes package resolution to pick up the wrong versions, with cryptic symbol or import errors.
8|⚪ T3 ROS2 Core|Development|ROS2 worksp.real_example: A developer edits a C++ node, runs 'colcon build', and re-runs 'ros2 run my_pkg my_node' in the same terminal -- but the behavior is unchanged. The terminal was opened before the build and never re-sourced 'install/setup.bash', so 'ros2 run' is still resolving the executable from a stale CMAKE_PREFIX_PATH pointing at the previous build's install tree.

8|⚪ T3 ROS2 Core|Development|colcon buil.what_it_is: colcon ('collective construction') is the command-line build tool for ROS2 workspaces, replacing ROS1's catkin_make/catkin tools -- it builds all packages in 'src/' respecting their declared dependencies, supporting mixed C++ (ament_cmake) and Python (ament_python) packages in one invocation.
8|⚪ T3 ROS2 Core|Development|colcon buil.why_it_exists: ROS1's catkin build system was ROS-specific and had well-known issues with mixed-language workspaces and incremental builds. colcon is a general-purpose, extensible meta-build tool (not ROS-specific) that wraps per-package build systems (CMake, setuptools, etc.), giving ROS2 a cleaner, more standard, and more parallelizable build experience.
8|⚪ T3 ROS2 Core|Development|colcon buil.how_it_works: 'colcon build' scans 'src/' for packages (identified by package.xml), builds a dependency graph, and builds packages in topological order (in parallel where possible) using each package's build type. Useful flags: '--packages-select <pkg>' to build only specific packages, '--packages-up-to <pkg>' to build a package and its dependencies, '--symlink-install' (for Python packages, symlinks installed files back to 'src/' so edits to Python files take effect without rebuilding), and '--cmake-args -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release' for build configuration.
8|⚪ T3 ROS2 Core|Development|colcon buil.use_when: Building or rebuilding any ROS2 workspace; using '--packages-select' during iterative development to avoid rebuilding the entire workspace; using '--symlink-install' when actively editing Python nodes to skip the rebuild step entirely.
8|⚪ T3 ROS2 Core|Development|colcon buil.avoid_when: Don't run a full 'colcon build' with no package selection on a large workspace after every tiny change -- it's slow even with caching; scope builds with '--packages-select'/'--packages-up-to'. Also avoid mixing 'Release' and 'Debug' builds across packages in the same workspace without understanding ABI implications for C++ packages that share types across package boundaries.
8|⚪ T3 ROS2 Core|Development|colcon buil.what_goes_wrong: A C++ build failure deep in the dependency graph can produce a wall of cascading errors in dependent packages that are actually just 'package X failed to build, so Y couldn't find its headers' -- developers waste time debugging Y when the real error is in X, found only by scrolling up or checking 'colcon build' summary which lists which packages failed vs. were skipped. Also, without '--symlink-install', editing a Python file and re-running 'ros2 run' without rebuilding silently runs the old installed copy.
8|⚪ T3 ROS2 Core|Development|colcon buil.real_example: After adding a new custom message type to a package, 'colcon build' fails in three downstream packages with 'fatal error: my_pkg/msg/MyMsg.hpp: No such file or directory'. The actual problem is that the message-defining package itself failed to build (a typo in the .msg file) -- but because colcon still attempted the dependents, their errors appear first and are misleading until 'colcon build' summary's 'Failed' list is checked.

8|⚪ T3 ROS2 Core|Development|Python vs C.what_it_is: ROS2 provides first-class client libraries for both C++ (rclcpp) and Python (rclpy), and a single system can freely mix nodes written in either language -- they communicate identically over DDS regardless of implementation language.
8|⚪ T3 ROS2 Core|Development|Python vs C.why_it_exists: Different parts of a robotics stack have very different requirements: low-latency control loops and performance-critical perception need C++'s speed and determinism, while rapid prototyping, scripting, ML integration (most ML frameworks are Python-first), and high-level mission logic benefit from Python's iteration speed and ecosystem.
8|⚪ T3 ROS2 Core|Development|Python vs C.how_it_works: Both rclcpp and rclpy implement the same ROS2 client library API surface on top of the common 'rcl' (ROS client library, written in C) and rmw layers, so a publisher in Python and a subscriber in C++ are wire-compatible with no special handling. Message types are code-generated for both languages from the same .msg/.srv/.action definitions via rosidl.
8|⚪ T3 ROS2 Core|Development|Python vs C.use_when: C++ for hard real-time control loops, high-frequency sensor processing (point cloud filtering, image processing at high FPS), and performance-critical nodes where Python's GIL or interpreter overhead matters; Python for rapid prototyping, mission/behavior logic, calling into ML frameworks (PyTorch/TensorFlow inference), test scripts, and tools/utilities where development speed matters more than raw throughput.
8|⚪ T3 ROS2 Core|Development|Python vs C.avoid_when: Avoid Python for tight control loops running at high rates (e.g. >100Hz joint-level control) where GIL contention and interpreter overhead introduce jitter; avoid C++ for quick exploratory scripts or one-off tools where the compile cycle and verbosity slow you down with no runtime benefit.
8|⚪ T3 ROS2 Core|Development|Python vs C.what_goes_wrong: Mixing languages naively can create hidden performance bottlenecks -- e.g. a Python node republishing a high-rate point cloud topic after light processing can become the bottleneck of an otherwise all-C++ pipeline, because (de)serialization and GIL overhead dominate. Another pitfall: assuming custom message definitions 'just work' in both languages without realizing both the C++ and Python bindings need to be generated and the workspace rebuilt for a new package.
8|⚪ T3 ROS2 Core|Development|Python vs C.real_example: A perception pipeline runs LiDAR processing in C++ at 20Hz, but a Python node in the middle does a small filtering step on the point cloud before passing it on -- profiling shows this single Python node adds 40ms of latency per message (mostly deserialization/reserialization overhead), more than the entire C++ portion of the pipeline combined, prompting a rewrite of that node in C++.

8|⚪ T3 ROS2 Core|Development|Launch file.what_it_is: ROS2 launch files (typically Python, though XML and YAML are also supported) declaratively describe how to start a set of nodes together -- with their parameters, remappings, namespaces, conditional logic, and composition into a single launch description.
8|⚪ T3 ROS2 Core|Development|Launch file.why_it_exists: Real robot systems involve starting dozens of nodes with specific parameter files, topic remappings, and namespaces -- doing this manually with many 'ros2 run' invocations in separate terminals doesn't scale and isn't reproducible. Launch files capture the entire system's startup configuration as code that can be version-controlled, parameterized, and reused across robots/environments.
8|⚪ T3 ROS2 Core|Development|Launch file.how_it_works: A launch file defines a 'generate_launch_description()' function returning a 'LaunchDescription' containing 'Node' actions (specifying package, executable, name, namespace, parameters, remappings), 'IncludeLaunchDescription' (to compose other launch files), 'DeclareLaunchArgument' (CLI-overridable arguments), and conditionals ('IfCondition'/'UnlessCondition') for things like 'only launch RViz if a use_rviz argument is true'. Run with 'ros2 launch <package> <file>.launch.py [arg:=value ...]'.
8|⚪ T3 ROS2 Core|Development|Launch file.use_when: Starting any multi-node system (which is essentially always, for real robots); parameterizing deployments across robots/environments (simulation vs. real hardware, different sensor configs) via launch arguments; composing a large system from smaller, reusable sub-launch files (e.g. a 'sensors.launch.py' included by both a 'real_robot.launch.py' and a 'simulation.launch.py').
8|⚪ T3 ROS2 Core|Development|Launch file.avoid_when: Don't put complex business logic inside launch files -- they're for orchestration/configuration, not application logic; deeply nested conditional launch logic becomes hard to debug ('why didn't this node start?'). For very simple single-node testing, plain 'ros2 run' is faster than writing a launch file.
8|⚪ T3 ROS2 Core|Development|Launch file.what_goes_wrong: Remapping mistakes are common and silent -- e.g. remapping '/cmd_vel' to '/robot1/cmd_vel' for one node but forgetting the corresponding subscriber, so the command never reaches the controller, with both nodes running 'fine' individually. Launch files that include other launch files with overlapping namespace declarations can also produce nodes in unexpected namespaces, breaking topic connectivity in ways that only 'ros2 node list'/'ros2 topic list' reveal.
8|⚪ T3 ROS2 Core|Development|Launch file.real_example: A simulation launch file includes both 'robot_state_publisher.launch.py' and a custom 'spawn_robot.launch.py', each of which independently sets the namespace to 'robot1' via a DeclareLaunchArgument default -- but only one of them receives the launch argument override to 'robot2' when launching a second robot, so robot2's TF tree ends up published under '/robot1/tf', causing both robots' transforms to collide.

8|⚪ T3 ROS2 Core|Development|Composable.what_it_is: Composable nodes are ROS2 nodes packaged as shared-library 'components' that can be loaded into a shared process (a 'component container') at runtime, enabling zero-copy intra-process communication between them instead of going through the full DDS serialization/IPC path.
8|⚪ T3 ROS2 Core|Development|Composable.why_it_exists: For high-throughput pipelines (e.g. image -> rectify -> detect -> track), sending large messages like images or point clouds between separate processes via DDS incurs serialization, memory copies, and IPC overhead at every hop. Loading the relevant nodes into one process lets ROS2 pass messages by pointer/reference when both publisher and subscriber are in the same process, dramatically cutting latency and CPU.
8|⚪ T3 ROS2 Core|Development|Composable.how_it_works: A node is written as a 'rclcpp_components' plugin (registered via a macro and exported as a shared library) rather than (or in addition to) a standalone executable. A 'component_container' (or 'component_container_mt' for multi-threaded) process loads one or more components dynamically via 'ros2 component load', or a launch file uses 'ComposableNodeContainer' with a list of 'ComposableNode' entries. When a publisher and subscriber component are co-located in the same container and use compatible QoS, rclcpp can deliver messages via intra-process communication, skipping the DDS network stack.
8|⚪ T3 ROS2 Core|Development|Composable.use_when: High-bandwidth perception pipelines (camera -> image processing -> detection) where multiple stages run on the same machine and message copying dominates CPU/latency; reducing the number of OS processes for resource-constrained embedded deployments.
8|⚪ T3 ROS2 Core|Development|Composable.avoid_when: Don't compose nodes that benefit from process isolation -- e.g. a node prone to crashing or with experimental code shouldn't share a process with critical safety nodes, since a crash takes down the whole container. Also, intra-process comms only help when messages are large and frequent; for small, low-rate topics the gain is negligible and the added build/deployment complexity may not be worth it.
8|⚪ T3 ROS2 Core|Development|Composable.what_goes_wrong: Intra-process communication only kicks in if QoS is compatible AND both nodes are in the same container AND (for some message types) the message is not modified after publishing -- developers often expect speedups that don't materialize because one of these conditions silently isn't met, with no error, just no improvement. Also, composing nodes that weren't designed as components (e.g. relying on global state or assuming a dedicated process) can introduce subtle bugs from shared address space.
8|⚪ T3 ROS2 Core|Development|Composable.real_example: A perception pipeline composes a camera driver and an image-rectification node into the same container expecting a large latency improvement, but measurements show no change -- the camera driver publishes with 'reliable' QoS while the rectification node's default subscription uses 'sensor data' (best-effort) QoS, which are intra-process-compatible in this case but the image message type used a non-trivial copy constructor, so rclcpp fell back to a full copy anyway; switching to a loaned-message-compatible type closed the gap.

8|⚪ T3 ROS2 Core|Development|Node lifecy.what_it_is: Lifecycle nodes (rclcpp_lifecycle / LifecycleNode) are ROS2 nodes that implement a managed state machine -- Unconfigured, Inactive, Active, Finalized, with transitions like configure(), activate(), deactivate(), cleanup(), and shutdown() -- instead of being 'on' the instant the process starts.
8|⚪ T3 ROS2 Core|Development|Node lifecy.why_it_exists: In real systems, starting a process and being 'ready to operate' are different things -- a sensor driver needs to open hardware and allocate buffers (configure) before it should start publishing (activate), and a system-wide coordinator may need to bring up dozens of nodes in a specific order, or pause/resume subsystems (e.g. deactivate a planner during teleop) without killing processes.
8|⚪ T3 ROS2 Core|Development|Node lifecy.how_it_works: A node extends 'rclcpp_lifecycle::LifecycleNode' and overrides callbacks for each transition (on_configure, on_activate, on_deactivate, on_cleanup, on_shutdown, on_error), each returning a CallbackReturn (SUCCESS/FAILURE/ERROR). Publishers created via the lifecycle node are 'LifecyclePublisher's that only actually publish when the node is Active. An external lifecycle manager (a separate node, or Nav2's 'lifecycle_manager') calls the transition services ('/node/change_state') in the desired order, often tied to a bringup/shutdown sequence.
8|⚪ T3 ROS2 Core|Development|Node lifecy.use_when: Systems needing coordinated, ordered startup/shutdown of many nodes (Nav2 uses lifecycle nodes extensively, managed by lifecycle_manager); hardware drivers that need explicit configure-before-activate semantics (open device, allocate buffers, then start streaming); systems needing to pause/resume subsystems cleanly (e.g. deactivate navigation during manual teleop without restarting the process).
8|⚪ T3 ROS2 Core|Development|Node lifecy.avoid_when: Don't make every node a lifecycle node -- for simple utility/logging nodes the extra state machine and external management add complexity with no benefit; lifecycle nodes are most valuable for nodes that own hardware resources or need coordinated startup ordering.
8|⚪ T3 ROS2 Core|Development|Node lifecy.what_goes_wrong: A node stuck in 'Inactive' because its 'on_configure' callback returned FAILURE (e.g. couldn't open a sensor device) will never publish anything, and downstream nodes waiting for that data simply see no messages with no obvious top-level error -- the failure is buried in the lifecycle node's own logs/state, only visible via 'ros2 lifecycle get <node>'. Also, forgetting that LifecyclePublisher.publish() is a no-op while Inactive leads to 'my publish() call did nothing and didn't error' confusion.
8|⚪ T3 ROS2 Core|Development|Node lifecy.real_example: Nav2's lifecycle_manager reports the system is 'active', but the robot doesn't move when sent a goal -- 'ros2 lifecycle get /controller_server' reveals it's stuck in 'inactive' because its on_activate() failed silently due to a missing plugin parameter; the lifecycle_manager's bringup sequence didn't surface this as a hard failure, just left that one node un-activated.

8|⚪ T3 ROS2 Core|Development|Custom mess.what_it_is: Custom interface definitions -- '.msg' (topic message), '.srv' (service request/response), and '.action' (action goal/result/feedback) files -- let developers define their own strongly-typed data structures for ROS2 communication, beyond the standard interfaces provided by common_interfaces (std_msgs, geometry_msgs, sensor_msgs, etc.).
8|⚪ T3 ROS2 Core|Development|Custom mess.why_it_exists: Standard message types cover generic data (a Twist for velocity, a PoseStamped for a pose) but real applications need domain-specific structures -- e.g. a 'DetectedObject' message with a class label, confidence, and bounding box, or a custom 'Inspect' action for a robotic inspection task. Defining these as first-class typed interfaces (rather than ad-hoc JSON in a String message) gives type safety, code generation, and tooling support (ros2 interface show, IDE autocomplete) across languages.
8|⚪ T3 ROS2 Core|Development|Custom mess.how_it_works: A '.msg' file lists fields as 'type name' lines (e.g. 'float64 confidence', 'string label', with optional constants and arrays); '.srv' files have a request section, '---', then a response section; '.action' files have Goal, '---', Result, '---', Feedback sections. These live in a dedicated 'msg/', 'srv/', 'action/' directory of an 'interface package' (often a package with no code, just interface definitions, e.g. 'my_robot_interfaces'), declared in CMakeLists.txt via 'rosidl_generate_interfaces'. The build (rosidl) generates C++ structs and Python classes (plus serialization code) automatically.
8|⚪ T3 ROS2 Core|Development|Custom mess.use_when: Any domain-specific data structure exchanged repeatedly between nodes -- detection results, custom commands, robot-specific status/diagnostics, application-specific action goals (e.g. 'Dock', 'PickObject').
8|⚪ T3 ROS2 Core|Development|Custom mess.avoid_when: Don't define a custom message when a standard one (possibly with a 'Stamped' or array variant) already fits -- reusing common_interfaces maximizes compatibility with existing tools (RViz displays, rqt plugins, Nav2) that expect standard types. Also avoid putting a custom message and the nodes that use it in the same package if other packages need to depend on just the interface -- circular dependencies result; use a dedicated interface-only package.
8|⚪ T3 ROS2 Core|Development|Custom mess.what_goes_wrong: Changing a custom message's fields (renaming, reordering, changing types) is a breaking change for any other package built against the old definition -- if not all packages are rebuilt together, you get runtime type mismatches that 'ros2 topic info --verbose' may not even flag clearly (different versions can have the same type name but different hashes, causing DDS-level incompatibility). Also, putting message definitions in the same package as nodes that use them is a common beginner mistake that creates circular build dependencies once a second package wants to use the message.
8|⚪ T3 ROS2 Core|Development|Custom mess.real_example: A team adds a new required field to a custom 'DetectionArray.msg' and rebuilds the perception package, but a separate tracking package (built in a different workspace/container image) still has the old generated code -- the two processes' DDS type hashes for 'DetectionArray' no longer match, so the topic silently fails to connect, surfacing only as 'tracking node isn't receiving detections' with no type-mismatch error visible without comparing type hashes via 'ros2 interface show' in each environment.

8|⚪ T3 ROS2 Core|Development|ROS2 parame.what_it_is: YAML parameter files declare initial values for one or more nodes' parameters in a structured, version-controllable file, loaded at launch time via a launch file's 'parameters=[...]' argument on a Node action, as an alternative to hardcoding defaults or passing many '-p' CLI overrides.
8|⚪ T3 ROS2 Core|Development|ROS2 parame.why_it_exists: Real deployments need dozens to hundreds of tuned parameter values (controller gains, sensor calibration offsets, costmap settings) that differ per robot or environment. Keeping these in YAML files -- separate from code and from launch logic -- lets teams version, diff, and review tuning changes, and swap entire configuration sets (e.g. 'robot_a_params.yaml' vs 'robot_b_params.yaml') without touching launch files or code.
8|⚪ T3 ROS2 Core|Development|ROS2 parame.how_it_works: A YAML file's top-level keys are node names (or '/**' as a wildcard applying to all nodes), with a nested 'ros__parameters:' map of parameter name/value pairs, e.g. '/my_node:\n  ros__parameters:\n    kp: 1.5'. A launch file passes the file path in a Node action's 'parameters' list; at startup, the node's declared parameters are initialized from matching entries in the YAML (the node must still call 'declare_parameter' for each -- the YAML only supplies initial values, it doesn't implicitly declare them).
8|⚪ T3 ROS2 Core|Development|ROS2 parame.use_when: Any non-trivial set of tuned parameters for a node, especially when the same node is reused across robots/environments with different configs (load 'sim_params.yaml' vs 'real_robot_params.yaml'); storing calibration values, controller gains, and topic remapping-adjacent configuration alongside source code under version control.
8|⚪ T3 ROS2 Core|Development|ROS2 parame.avoid_when: Don't put parameters that need to vary at runtime (not just at launch) solely in YAML -- they're read at startup; runtime changes need 'ros2 param set' or a dynamic-reconfigure-style mechanism plus an on-set-parameters callback in the node. Also avoid one giant YAML file with every node's parameters for a huge system if it makes per-subsystem reuse and review harder -- splitting by subsystem with includes is often cleaner.
8|⚪ T3 ROS2 Core|Development|ROS2 parame.what_goes_wrong: The node name (and namespace) in the YAML's top-level key must exactly match the node's fully-qualified name at runtime, including any namespace applied by the launch file -- a mismatch means the parameters are silently not applied and the node falls back to its 'declare_parameter' defaults, with no warning that the YAML was effectively ignored. Also, a parameter present in YAML but never 'declared' in the node's code raises an error (or is ignored, depending on 'allow_undeclared_parameters') rather than being silently available.
8|⚪ T3 ROS2 Core|Development|ROS2 parame.real_example: A 'planner_params.yaml' has a top-level key '/planner_server:' but the node is actually launched with namespace '/robot1', making its fully-qualified name '/robot1/planner_server' -- the YAML's parameters don't match and are silently skipped; the planner runs entirely on its code-level defaults, and the carefully-tuned values in the YAML have zero effect, discovered only by 'ros2 param get /robot1/planner_server some_tuned_value' returning the default instead of the YAML value.

8|⚪ T3 ROS2 Core|Development|tf2 — trans.what_it_is: tf2 is ROS2's library for tracking the relative position and orientation (transforms) between any number of coordinate frames over time -- e.g. 'map', 'odom', 'base_link', 'camera_link', 'laser_frame' -- organized as a tree, with lookups available at arbitrary timestamps.
8|⚪ T3 ROS2 Core|Development|tf2 — trans.why_it_exists: A robot has many sensors and links, each with its own coordinate frame, and these relationships change over time (the robot moves, joints rotate, localization updates). Every perception, planning, and control component needs to ask 'where is point P, expressed in frame X, given as frame Y at time T' -- tf2 provides a single, consistent answer to that question system-wide instead of every node tracking transforms itself.
8|⚪ T3 ROS2 Core|Development|tf2 — trans.how_it_works: Nodes broadcast transforms by publishing 'geometry_msgs/TransformStamped' messages on '/tf' (dynamic, e.g. odom->base_link from odometry, or joint transforms from robot_state_publisher) or '/tf_static' (static, e.g. base_link->lidar_frame, published once with transient-local QoS). A 'tf2_ros::Buffer' + 'TransformListener' subscribes to both topics and maintains a time-indexed tree of all frames; any node can call 'lookupTransform(target_frame, source_frame, time)' to get the transform, with interpolation/extrapolation handling for slightly different timestamps.
8|⚪ T3 ROS2 Core|Development|tf2 — trans.use_when: Any time data needs to move between coordinate frames -- transforming a LiDAR point cloud (in 'laser_frame') into 'base_link' or 'map' for obstacle avoidance, computing where the robot is relative to a detected object, or rendering everything in RViz2 relative to a fixed frame.
8|⚪ T3 ROS2 Core|Development|tf2 — trans.avoid_when: Don't publish high-frequency dynamic transforms for things that are actually static (e.g. a fixed sensor mount) -- use '/tf_static' instead, both for correctness (late joiners get it) and to avoid flooding '/tf'. Also avoid creating tf trees with multiple parents for the same frame (not a tree anymore) -- tf2 assumes a strict tree and will throw errors or give undefined results with multiple parents.
8|⚪ T3 ROS2 Core|Development|tf2 — trans.what_goes_wrong: 'Lookup would require extrapolation into the future/past' errors are extremely common -- they happen when a node requests a transform at a timestamp tf2 doesn't have data for yet (clock sync issues, or asking for 'latest' transform with a stale stamped message). Another classic: a disconnected tf tree -- two separate trees (e.g. 'map'->'odom'->'base_link' from localization, and a separate 'base_link'->'camera' from robot_state_publisher that never got linked because robot_state_publisher wasn't started) -- causes 'frame X does not exist' errors for any cross-tree lookup.
8|⚪ T3 ROS2 Core|Development|tf2 — trans.real_example: A perception node trying to transform detections from 'camera_link' to 'map' intermittently throws 'Lookup would require extrapolation into the future' -- the camera node timestamps messages using the camera driver's hardware clock, which is slightly ahead of the system clock that the localization node uses for its 'map'->'odom' broadcasts, so tf2 occasionally doesn't yet have a 'map'->'odom' sample for the camera's (slightly future) timestamp; using 'waitForTransform' with a timeout, or syncing clocks via chrony/PTP, fixes it.

8|⚪ T3 ROS2 Core|Development|URDF/xacro.what_it_is: URDF (Unified Robot Description Format) is an XML format describing a robot's physical structure -- links (rigid bodies with visual/collision geometry and inertial properties) and joints (connections between links, with type, axis, limits) -- and xacro is a macro language layered on top of URDF to reduce repetition (variables, math expressions, reusable macros, conditionals).
8|⚪ T3 ROS2 Core|Development|URDF/xacro.why_it_exists: Nearly everything downstream -- TF tree structure, RViz visualization, collision checking for motion planning (MoveIt), physics simulation (Gazebo), and ros2_control's hardware abstraction -- needs a formal description of the robot's kinematic structure and geometry. URDF is that single source of truth; xacro exists because raw URDF for anything beyond a toy robot is extremely repetitive (e.g. 4 nearly-identical wheel joints, or a 7-DOF arm with similar link/joint patterns).
8|⚪ T3 ROS2 Core|Development|URDF/xacro.how_it_works: A URDF file defines '<link>' elements (each with optional '<visual>', '<collision>', '<inertial>' blocks) connected by '<joint>' elements specifying a type (revolute, prismatic, fixed, continuous, etc.), parent/child links, origin offset, and axis/limits. xacro files ('.urdf.xacro') use '<xacro:property>', '<xacro:macro>', and '${...}' expressions, and are processed ('xacro' command, or automatically by 'robot_state_publisher' via the 'robot_description' parameter) into plain URDF/XML before being consumed. 'robot_state_publisher' reads the URDF and publishes '/tf_static' transforms for all fixed joints and '/tf' for movable joints based on '/joint_states'.
8|⚪ T3 ROS2 Core|Development|URDF/xacro.use_when: Describing any physical robot for simulation, visualization, motion planning, or control -- essentially mandatory for using RViz2 robot models, MoveIt, Gazebo, or ros2_control. Use xacro (not raw URDF) for any robot with repeated structures (multiple wheels/legs/fingers, symmetric arms) or values that should be parameterized (link lengths, masses).
8|⚪ T3 ROS2 Core|Development|URDF/xacro.avoid_when: Don't hand-author raw, fully-expanded URDF for any non-trivial robot -- maintenance becomes a nightmare when a dimension changes and has to be updated in a dozen places; use xacro macros and properties from the start. Also, don't put simulation-only or control-only tags directly in the core URDF if multiple consumers (RViz, Gazebo, MoveIt) need different subsets -- use xacro conditionals or separate included files for plugin-specific blocks (e.g. Gazebo '<gazebo>' tags).
8|⚪ T3 ROS2 Core|Development|URDF/xacro.what_goes_wrong: Incorrect or missing '<inertial>' values (zero or wildly unrealistic mass/inertia) cause physics simulations in Gazebo to behave erratically -- the robot flies apart, jitters, or sinks through the floor, with no error message pointing at the URDF as the cause. Also, a joint's '<origin>' or '<axis>' sign error produces a TF tree that 'looks' connected but has links in the wrong place/orientation, which often isn't obvious until something downstream (a gripper, a sensor) is visibly misaligned in RViz.
8|⚪ T3 ROS2 Core|Development|URDF/xacro.real_example: A newly-added robotic arm link appears correctly in RViz when the robot is stationary, but during Gazebo simulation the arm violently oscillates and the whole robot model jitters across the floor -- the cause is a forgotten '<inertial>' block on that link, which Gazebo defaults to zero mass/inertia, creating a physically invalid rigid body that the physics engine can't stabilize.

8|⚪ T3 ROS2 Core|Development|Gazebo/Igni.what_it_is: Gazebo (now branded 'Gazebo' / formerly 'Ignition Gazebo' for the newer generation, distinct from 'Gazebo Classic') is a 3D physics-based robot simulator that loads a robot's URDF/SDF description and simulates sensors (cameras, LiDAR, IMU), physics (collisions, dynamics via ODE/Bullet/DART), and environments, integrated with ROS2 via the 'ros_gz' bridge packages.
8|⚪ T3 ROS2 Core|Development|Gazebo/Igni.why_it_exists: Testing robot software on real hardware is slow, expensive, and risky (a buggy nav stack can crash a real robot into a wall or a person). Simulation lets developers iterate on perception, planning, and control algorithms against realistic physics and sensor models, run automated regression tests, and generate synthetic sensor data, all without hardware -- and lets CI pipelines test full software stacks.
8|⚪ T3 ROS2 Core|Development|Gazebo/Igni.how_it_works: A simulated robot is described in SDF (Gazebo's native format, often generated from URDF/xacro via 'gz_ros2_control' or direct conversion) and spawned into a Gazebo world. Gazebo's physics engine steps the simulation, computing collisions and dynamics; sensor plugins generate simulated sensor_msgs data (camera images, LiDAR scans, IMU readings) and 'ros_gz_bridge' relays these (and command topics like '/cmd_vel') between Gazebo's internal transport and ROS2 topics, so ROS2 nodes interact with the simulation exactly as they would a real robot.
8|⚪ T3 ROS2 Core|Development|Gazebo/Igni.use_when: Developing and testing navigation, perception, and manipulation algorithms before deploying to hardware; running automated integration tests in CI without physical robots; generating synthetic labeled sensor data for training perception models; testing multi-robot scenarios that would be impractical to set up physically.
8|⚪ T3 ROS2 Core|Development|Gazebo/Igni.avoid_when: Don't treat simulation results as a guarantee of real-world performance -- the 'sim-to-real gap' (friction models, sensor noise characteristics, lighting, unmodeled dynamics) means algorithms tuned purely in sim can fail on hardware; always validate on real hardware before deployment. Also, full physics simulation with high-fidelity sensors (especially photorealistic rendering) is computationally heavy -- for pure logic/algorithm testing without physical realism, lighter-weight stubs or unit tests may be more appropriate.
8|⚪ T3 ROS2 Core|Development|Gazebo/Igni.what_goes_wrong: A common gotcha is forgetting that simulated time and wall-clock time diverge -- nodes must set 'use_sim_time:=true' to consume '/clock' from Gazebo, or TF lookups, message filters, and timeouts behave inconsistently (sim runs faster or slower than real time, especially under heavy load). Also, default friction/inertia values in URDF/SDF that weren't carefully tuned can make a robot in simulation behave nothing like the real one -- e.g. wheels that slip unrealistically, causing a nav stack tuned in sim to be miscalibrated on hardware.
8|⚪ T3 ROS2 Core|Development|Gazebo/Igni.real_example: A nav stack works perfectly in Gazebo but the robot's odometry is wildly inaccurate on real hardware -- the simulated diff-drive plugin used perfect, noise-free wheel odometry, while the real robot's wheel encoders have slip and quantization error; the nav stack's EKF was never tuned against realistic odometry noise because the simulation never exhibited it, so sensor fusion parameters tuned in sim don't generalize.

8|⚪ T3 ROS2 Core|Development|Isaac Sim —.what_it_is: NVIDIA Isaac Sim is a GPU-accelerated, photorealistic robotics simulator built on the Omniverse platform (using the USD -- Universal Scene Description -- format), providing high-fidelity rendering, PhysX-based physics, and synthetic data generation, with ROS2 bridges for integration.
8|⚪ T3 ROS2 Core|Development|Isaac Sim —.why_it_exists: Modern robot perception increasingly relies on learned (deep learning) models -- object detection, segmentation, depth estimation -- which need large amounts of labeled, photorealistic training data and benefit from domain randomization (varying lighting, textures, object placement) that's impractical to collect physically. Isaac Sim targets this gap: combining accurate physics (for manipulation/locomotion) with rendering quality high enough to train vision models that transfer to the real world (sim-to-real).
8|⚪ T3 ROS2 Core|Development|Isaac Sim —.how_it_works: Robots and environments are represented as USD scenes; Isaac Sim's PhysX engine simulates rigid/articulated body dynamics, while its RTX-based renderer produces photorealistic camera images, depth, segmentation masks, and other sensor outputs. The 'ROS2 bridge' extension publishes simulated sensor data and TF, and subscribes to control commands, similar in spirit to Gazebo's ros_gz_bridge but within the Omniverse ecosystem. Isaac Lab (built on Isaac Sim) adds RL training environments (parallel simulated environments on GPU for fast RL rollout collection).
8|⚪ T3 ROS2 Core|Development|Isaac Sim —.use_when: Training perception models that need photorealistic synthetic data with domain randomization; reinforcement learning for locomotion/manipulation policies (via Isaac Lab) where thousands of parallel simulated environments running on GPU dramatically speed up training; high-fidelity digital-twin work where rendering quality and physics accuracy both matter.
8|⚪ T3 ROS2 Core|Development|Isaac Sim —.avoid_when: Don't use Isaac Sim for simple 2D navigation testing or basic integration testing where Gazebo's lighter weight and simpler setup is more practical -- Isaac Sim has a much higher hardware bar (requires a capable NVIDIA GPU) and steeper learning curve (USD, Omniverse). Also avoid it if your team's workflow is deeply ROS-centric and you need the broadest compatibility with existing ROS2 simulation tooling/tutorials, where Gazebo remains the more standard choice.
8|⚪ T3 ROS2 Core|Development|Isaac Sim —.what_goes_wrong: Isaac Sim's resource requirements (a recent NVIDIA RTX GPU with substantial VRAM) are a common blocker -- teams without the right hardware can't run it at all, or run it so slowly that iteration is painful, leading to abandoned setups. Also, the USD-based asset pipeline and Omniverse-specific concepts (stages, prims, layers) have a learning curve distinct from URDF/SDF, and converting existing URDF robots into well-behaved USD assets (correct physics properties, joint drives) often requires non-trivial extra work.
8|⚪ T3 ROS2 Core|Development|Isaac Sim —.real_example: A research team adopts Isaac Sim to train an object-detection model with domain-randomized synthetic data, expecting a quick win -- but their existing URDF robot model, when imported, has joints with incorrect drive stiffness/damping defaults, causing the robot arm to oscillate uncontrollably in simulation; they spend a significant chunk of the project tuning USD physics properties that had sensible defaults in their previous Gazebo setup.

8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|SLAM & Loca.what_it_is: SLAM is the problem (and family of algorithms) of simultaneously building a map of an unknown environment and estimating the robot's own pose within that map, using only the robot's sensors (typically LiDAR, cameras, and odometry) -- a classic chicken-and-egg problem since accurate mapping needs known pose and accurate localisation needs a known map.
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|SLAM & Loca.why_it_exists: Robots operating in unknown or changing environments (warehouses before a map exists, exploration robots, new construction sites) can't rely on a pre-built map and external positioning (GPS is unavailable/unreliable indoors). SLAM lets a robot bootstrap its own spatial understanding from scratch, which is foundational for nearly all autonomous mobile robot navigation.
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|SLAM & Loca.how_it_works: Most SLAM systems combine: (1) front-end odometry/scan-matching that estimates incremental motion between consecutive sensor readings (e.g. matching successive LiDAR scans or visual features), (2) loop-closure detection that recognizes when the robot has returned to a previously-visited place, and (3) a back-end optimizer (pose graph optimization or a filter like an EKF/particle filter) that globally adjusts all past poses and the map to be consistent once loop closures are found, correcting accumulated drift.
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|SLAM & Loca.use_when: Building a map of a new environment (mapping mode) before deploying for autonomous navigation; environments where GPS is unavailable (indoors, underground, dense urban) and a pre-existing map doesn't exist or needs updating; robots that need to operate in environments that change over time.
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|SLAM & Loca.avoid_when: Don't run full SLAM continuously in a static, already-mapped environment where localisation against a fixed map (AMCL) is sufficient and computationally cheaper -- SLAM's ongoing map updates and loop-closure search cost CPU that pure localisation doesn't need. Also, in GPS-rich outdoor environments with good RTK GPS, GPS-based localisation may be simpler and more robust than visual/LiDAR SLAM alone.
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|SLAM & Loca.what_goes_wrong: Drift accumulates between loop closures -- in long corridors or featureless environments (e.g. a long straight hallway with identical-looking walls), scan-matching has little to constrain it, and the map can develop visible 'bends' or 'doubling' of corridors until a loop closure corrects it retroactively. 'Perceptual aliasing' -- two different places that look similar (e.g. identical warehouse aisles) -- can cause false loop closures, which can catastrophically warp the map when the back-end 'corrects' based on a wrong match.
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|SLAM & Loca.real_example: A warehouse robot building a map of a long aisle-based facility produces a map where two parallel aisles end up overlapping -- the LiDAR scans in each aisle look nearly identical (same shelving, same spacing), and the SLAM system's loop-closure detector matches the robot's position in aisle 5 to a previously-visited pose in aisle 3, snapping the pose graph into an incorrect configuration that takes a manual map edit (or disabling that loop closure) to fix.

8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|SLAM & Loca.what_it_is: slam_toolbox (by Steve Macenski) is the de facto standard 2D LiDAR SLAM package for ROS2, providing online (real-time) and offline (lifelong) mapping, map serialization/deserialization, and pose-graph-based loop closure, replacing ROS1's gmapping/karto-based approaches.
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|SLAM & Loca.why_it_exists: ROS1's SLAM options (gmapping, hector_slam, karto) were either not ported well to ROS2, lacked modern pose-graph optimization, or didn't support saving/loading/continuing a map session. slam_toolbox was purpose-built for ROS2 to provide a maintained, feature-complete 2D SLAM solution that integrates cleanly with Nav2.
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|SLAM & Loca.how_it_works: slam_toolbox subscribes to '/scan' (LaserScan) and odometry/TF, performs scan matching (using Ceres-based optimization) to estimate the robot's incremental motion, builds an occupancy grid map, and runs pose-graph SLAM with loop closure in the background. It supports multiple modes: 'mapping' (build a new map from scratch), 'localization' (localize within a previously-saved map, similar to AMCL but using the same scan-matching backend), and 'lifelong' (continuously update/extend an existing map as the robot operates over time). Maps can be serialized ('.posegraph' + '.data') for later continuation, distinct from the simple image-based '.pgm'/'.yaml' map format.
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|SLAM & Loca.use_when: Building 2D occupancy grid maps with a LiDAR-equipped ground robot in ROS2 -- the default choice for most 2D indoor/warehouse mapping; needing to pause and resume mapping sessions, merge maps, or continuously update a map over the robot's lifetime (lifelong mapping mode).
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|SLAM & Loca.avoid_when: Don't use slam_toolbox for 3D mapping or visual SLAM -- it's fundamentally a 2D LiDAR-based system; for 3D environments (multi-level, complex terrain) or camera-based SLAM, look at RTAB-Map, Cartographer (3D mode), or visual-inertial SLAM. Also, for pure localisation against an already-good static map with no need for ongoing map updates, AMCL is lighter-weight.
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|SLAM & Loca.what_goes_wrong: Running slam_toolbox in 'mapping' mode with poor-quality odometry (e.g. a skid-steer robot with significant wheel slip) can produce maps with visible distortion that loop closures only partially fix -- the scan matcher fights bad odometry priors. Also, switching from 'mapping' to 'localization' mode requires loading the serialized pose graph (not just the image map) to retain the full SLAM state -- loading only the '.yaml'/'.pgm' map and expecting slam_toolbox's localization mode to behave identically to AMCL is a common point of confusion.
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|SLAM & Loca.real_example: A team maps a warehouse with slam_toolbox, saves the map, and switches to 'localization' mode for daily operation -- but they only saved the image-based map ('.pgm'/'.yaml'), not the serialized pose graph ('.posegraph'/'.data'). slam_toolbox's localization mode starts with an empty pose graph and behaves erratically until they realize they need 'ros2 run slam_toolbox deserialize_map' with the full serialized session, not just the occupancy grid image.
