8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|SLAM & Loca.what_it_is: Cartographer is Google's open-source SLAM library supporting both 2D and 3D LiDAR (and multi-sensor) mapping, using submap-based local SLAM combined with global pose-graph optimization and branch-and-bound loop closure search.
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|SLAM & Loca.why_it_exists: Before slam_toolbox matured, Cartographer was one of the few production-grade, actively-maintained SLAM systems with strong 3D support and a track record from Google's own robotics/mapping use cases (it was originally developed for backpack-mounted mapping systems). It remains relevant for 3D LiDAR SLAM and multi-sensor fusion scenarios.
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|SLAM & Loca.how_it_works: Cartographer builds local 'submaps' by accumulating consecutive scans into small, locally-consistent grids using scan-to-submap matching (with a correlative scan matcher and Ceres-based optimization). Periodically, it runs global SLAM: a pose graph connects submaps, and a branch-and-bound search efficiently finds loop-closure constraints between submaps, after which Ceres optimizes the entire pose graph to minimize global error. It supports 2D (LaserScan-based) and 3D (multiple LiDARs/point clouds + IMU) configurations via YAML 'Lua' configuration files.
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|SLAM & Loca.use_when: 3D LiDAR SLAM (multi-layer or full 3D point clouds, e.g. with a 3D spinning LiDAR or multiple 2D LiDARs at different heights); scenarios needing tight IMU integration for local SLAM accuracy; multi-sensor configurations where Cartographer's flexible Lua-based sensor configuration fits better than slam_toolbox's more 2D-focused design.
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|SLAM & Loca.avoid_when: For straightforward 2D single-LiDAR ground-robot mapping in ROS2, slam_toolbox is generally simpler to configure and better integrated with Nav2's ecosystem -- don't reach for Cartographer's more complex Lua configuration unless you need its 3D/multi-sensor capabilities. Also, Cartographer's ROS2 support and community activity has historically lagged slam_toolbox's, so check current maintenance status before committing.
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|SLAM & Loca.what_goes_wrong: Cartographer's many tunable parameters (submap size, scan matcher search windows, optimization thresholds) in its Lua configuration files have a steep learning curve -- default configurations tuned for one robot/sensor setup (e.g. Google's original backpack mapper) often perform poorly out-of-the-box on a different robot, and tuning requires understanding the underlying submap/pose-graph architecture, not just trial-and-error parameter sweeps.
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|SLAM & Loca.real_example: A team adapts a Cartographer 3D configuration originally tuned for a spinning 3D LiDAR to their robot's setup of three stacked 2D LiDARs -- the default 'num_range_data' (scans per submap) and voxel filter settings produce extremely sparse submaps because the per-scan point density is much lower than the original 3D LiDAR, leading to poor scan matching; they have to substantially re-tune the Lua config's point cloud accumulation parameters for their sensor density.

8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|SLAM & Loca.what_it_is: ORB-SLAM3 is a feature-based visual (and visual-inertial) SLAM system that works with monocular, stereo, or RGB-D cameras, tracking ORB (Oriented FAST and Rotated BRIEF) feature points across frames to estimate camera pose and build a sparse 3D map, with multi-map support for relocalization across sessions.
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|SLAM & Loca.why_it_exists: LiDAR is expensive, power-hungry, and sometimes impractical (small drones, AR/VR devices, low-cost robots), while cameras are cheap, lightweight, and ubiquitous. Visual SLAM extracts 3D structure and motion from camera images alone (or with IMU for visual-inertial SLAM), enabling SLAM on platforms where LiDAR isn't viable.
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|SLAM & Loca.how_it_works: ORB-SLAM3 detects ORB features in each frame, matches them against the local map and across frames to estimate camera motion (tracking thread), maintains a sparse map of 3D landmarks with periodic local bundle adjustment (mapping thread), and runs place recognition (DBoW2 bag-of-words) for loop closure and relocalization (a separate thread). Its multi-map system can maintain disconnected map segments (e.g. after tracking loss) and merge them when overlap is recognized, and it supports tightly-coupled visual-inertial fusion when an IMU is available.
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|SLAM & Loca.use_when: Camera-only or camera+IMU platforms needing 6-DOF pose estimation and sparse mapping -- drones, AR/VR headsets, mobile robots without LiDAR, or as a complementary localisation source alongside LiDAR SLAM. Monocular setups in particular benefit from ORB-SLAM3's robustness to tracking loss via its multi-map/relocalization design.
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|SLAM & Loca.avoid_when: Don't expect monocular visual SLAM to produce metrically-accurate maps without scale information (an IMU, stereo baseline, or known object size) -- monocular SLAM is scale-ambiguous by nature. Also avoid pure visual SLAM in low-texture (blank walls), repetitive-texture, or poorly-lit environments where feature tracking fails -- LiDAR or depth-camera-based SLAM is more robust there.
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|SLAM & Loca.what_goes_wrong: Monocular ORB-SLAM3 can lose tracking entirely during fast rotation or motion blur (too few/poor feature matches between consecutive frames), causing it to start a new disconnected map segment -- if it never re-recognizes the earlier map, the trajectory has an unrecoverable discontinuity. Also, scale drift in monocular mode (without IMU) means distances slowly become inaccurate over long trajectories, since there's no absolute scale reference being continuously reinforced.
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|SLAM & Loca.real_example: A drone running monocular ORB-SLAM3 performs a rapid yaw maneuver during a turn, causing severe motion blur; tracking is lost for about a second, and ORB-SLAM3 starts a new map. When the drone later revisits the starting area, place recognition successfully merges the two maps -- but the trajectory segment during the lost-tracking period has no pose estimate at all, leaving a gap that downstream consumers (e.g. a logger expecting continuous pose) must handle.

8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|SLAM & Loca.what_it_is: RTAB-Map (Real-Time Appearance-Based Mapping) is a graph-based SLAM library designed around RGB-D (and stereo/LiDAR) sensors, producing both 2D occupancy grids and dense 3D point cloud / mesh maps, with a strong focus on large-scale, real-time loop closure via an incremental appearance-based memory management scheme.
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|SLAM & Loca.why_it_exists: Cheap RGB-D cameras (Intel RealSense, ZED, Kinect-style sensors) provide dense depth alongside color, enabling dense 3D mapping that pure 2D LiDAR SLAM can't produce -- useful for robots needing 3D obstacle awareness (e.g. detecting overhangs, stairs) and for applications wanting a visually rich 3D map, not just a 2D occupancy grid. RTAB-Map's memory-management approach also targets large-scale, long-duration mapping where naive loop-closure search would become too slow.
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|SLAM & Loca.how_it_works: RTAB-Map performs visual odometry (or accepts external odometry) and builds a graph of poses linked by RGB-D 'signatures'. Loop closure uses a bag-of-words appearance model to efficiently retrieve similar past locations, with a 'working memory / long-term memory' scheme that keeps only recently/frequently-relevant locations in active memory for real-time performance, transferring older ones to long-term memory and retrieving them only when revisited. It outputs both a 2D occupancy grid (projected from 3D data, usable directly by Nav2) and optionally a dense 3D point cloud or mesh.
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|SLAM & Loca.use_when: Robots with RGB-D or stereo cameras (with or without LiDAR) needing both 2D navigation maps and 3D scene understanding (for obstacle detection beyond a single LiDAR plane, or for visualization/inspection); long-duration mapping sessions where memory management for loop closure scalability matters.
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|SLAM & Loca.avoid_when: Don't use RTAB-Map's full dense 3D mapping if you only need 2D LiDAR-based occupancy grids for navigation -- slam_toolbox is lighter-weight and purpose-built for that. RGB-D sensors also have limited range and field of view compared to LiDAR and struggle outdoors in bright sunlight, so for large outdoor environments LiDAR-based SLAM is generally more robust.
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|SLAM & Loca.what_goes_wrong: RGB-D depth sensors have limited effective range (often a few meters) and degrade in direct sunlight (structured-light/ToF interference) -- RTAB-Map's map quality drops sharply outdoors or in large open spaces where the depth camera simply can't see far enough to constrain the map, producing sparse or noisy regions. Also, RTAB-Map's memory-management thresholds, if too aggressive, can move locations to long-term memory before a loop closure is found, causing missed loop closures that a more naive (but slower) full-search approach would have caught.
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|SLAM & Loca.real_example: A robot mapping a large open warehouse with an RGB-D camera produces a 2D occupancy grid with large 'unknown' gaps down the center of wide aisles -- the depth camera's effective range (around 4-5m) can't reach the far walls/shelves across the aisle width, so RTAB-Map has no depth data to populate those cells, even though the area is clearly visible and well-lit in the RGB image; adding a 2D LiDAR alongside the RGB-D camera for the occupancy grid (using RTAB-Map's LiDAR+RGB-D fusion mode) fills the gaps.

8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|SLAM & Loca.what_it_is: An occupancy grid map represents an environment as a regular grid of cells, each holding a probability (or log-odds value) that the cell is occupied by an obstacle, free space, or unknown -- the standard map representation produced by 2D SLAM and consumed by Nav2's costmaps.
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|SLAM & Loca.why_it_exists: Robots need a representation of 'where can I drive' that's simple to update incrementally from noisy sensor data, simple to reason about for path planning (grid-based search algorithms operate directly on it), and simple to visualize and save/load. A probabilistic grid handles sensor noise gracefully -- repeated observations reinforce or weaken a cell's occupancy estimate rather than a single noisy reading causing a hard binary flip.
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|SLAM & Loca.how_it_works: Each cell's occupancy is updated using a sensor model and Bayes' rule (often implemented as log-odds updates for numerical stability and efficiency): a LiDAR beam that passes through a cell without hitting anything decreases that cell's occupancy probability (it's likely free), while a beam that terminates in a cell increases it (likely occupied). Cells never observed remain at a 'unknown' prior (typically 0.5 probability, often visualized as gray). The standard ROS2 serialization is a '.pgm' grayscale image (pixel intensity encodes occupancy) plus a '.yaml' file with resolution, origin, and thresholds.
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|SLAM & Loca.use_when: 2D ground robot navigation -- as the static map layer for Nav2 costmaps, as the output format for slam_toolback/gmapping-style 2D SLAM, and as a simple, universally-supported map format for visualization and path planning.
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|SLAM & Loca.avoid_when: Don't use occupancy grids for representing 3D structure (overhangs, multi-level environments, drones) -- a 2D grid can't represent 'free below, occupied above' at the same (x,y); use 3D representations (octomaps, voxel grids, or RTAB-Map's 3D output) for those cases. Also, for very large environments, a single fine-resolution grid can become memory-prohibitive -- consider hierarchical or rolling-window (local costmap) representations.
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|SLAM & Loca.what_goes_wrong: Resolution choice is a recurring tradeoff bug: too coarse (e.g. 10cm cells) and narrow doorways/corridors can appear blocked (a cell is marked occupied if any part of it has an obstacle, so thin obstacles get 'fattened'); too fine (e.g. 1cm) and memory/CPU for costmap inflation and planning blow up. Also, '.pgm'/'.yaml' map files have an 'origin' and 'resolution' that must match what the localisation/planning stack expects -- a map saved with one resolution but loaded with mismatched costmap inflation parameters can make a perfectly navigable corridor appear impassable.
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|SLAM & Loca.real_example: A robot's Nav2 stack reports 'no valid path found' for a goal down a corridor that's clearly open in RViz -- the map was saved at 5cm resolution, but the global costmap's 'inflation_radius' was tuned assuming a 10cm-resolution map (copied from a different robot's config), so the inflation layer expands obstacles roughly twice as far as intended in metric terms, narrowing the corridor below the robot's footprint in the costmap even though the raw occupancy grid shows it as passable.

8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|SLAM & Loca.what_it_is: AMCL (Adaptive Monte Carlo Localization) is a particle-filter-based localisation algorithm that estimates a robot's pose within a known, pre-built occupancy grid map by maintaining a population of weighted pose hypotheses ('particles') that converge toward the true pose as sensor data arrives.
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|SLAM & Loca.why_it_exists: Once a map exists (from SLAM), running full SLAM continuously is unnecessary and wasteful -- the robot just needs to know 'where am I on this known map'. Particle filters handle the non-Gaussian, multi-modal uncertainty common at startup (the robot could be anywhere -- 'global localization') better than a single-hypothesis filter like a Kalman filter, and AMCL's 'adaptive' part dynamically adjusts the number of particles based on localisation confidence for efficiency.
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|SLAM & Loca.how_it_works: Each particle represents a hypothesized (x, y, theta) pose. On each odometry update, particles are moved according to a motion model with noise; on each LiDAR scan, each particle's weight is updated based on how well the scan matches the map from that particle's hypothesized pose (the sensor model, e.g. likelihood field model). Particles are then resampled proportional to their weights (low-weight hypotheses die out, high-weight ones multiply), and KLD-sampling adaptively varies particle count -- many particles when uncertain (e.g. at startup, 'global localization'), few once converged for efficiency.
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|SLAM & Loca.use_when: Localising a robot within a pre-existing, static (or mostly static) occupancy grid map -- the standard Nav2 localisation approach for most indoor wheeled robots once a map has been built and saved.
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|SLAM & Loca.avoid_when: Don't use AMCL in environments that change significantly from the saved map (major rearrangements, new walls) -- it will struggle to localise against a stale map; re-map or use a SLAM system with map-update capability (slam_toolbox lifelong mode). Also, AMCL assumes a 2D world with a roughly planar robot -- it's not appropriate for 3D localisation (drones, uneven terrain robots needing 6-DOF pose).
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|SLAM & Loca.what_goes_wrong: 'Particle deprivation' / kidnapped robot problem -- if the robot is moved without odometry registering it (picked up and placed elsewhere, or severe wheel slip), all particles converge around the old (now wrong) pose and AMCL can't recover without manual re-initialization or a large 'global localization' particle spread. Also, AMCL's performance is very sensitive to its motion model noise parameters ('alpha1'-'alpha4') -- if set too low relative to the robot's actual odometry noise, particles converge prematurely to a wrong pose; too high, and localisation never tightens up, causing jittery TF.
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|SLAM & Loca.real_example: After an operator manually pushes a robot out of the way (e.g. to let a forklift pass) without disabling localisation, AMCL's particle cloud stays clustered around the robot's pre-push position -- the robot's 'localized' pose in RViz doesn't match its actual position, and Nav2 then plans a path based on the wrong pose, driving the robot in the wrong direction until someone notices and triggers a 'global localization' or manual pose reset via the '2D Pose Estimate' tool.

8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|SLAM & Loca.what_it_is: The Extended Kalman Filter is a recursive Bayesian state estimator that fuses multiple noisy sensor sources (wheel odometry, IMU, GPS) into a single best-estimate of the robot's pose and velocity, handling the non-linear motion/observation models common in robotics by linearizing them around the current estimate (via Jacobians).
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|SLAM & Loca.why_it_exists: No single sensor gives a complete, accurate picture of robot state -- wheel odometry drifts over time, IMUs drift in orientation/bias, GPS is noisy and unavailable indoors. An EKF combines these complementary sources, weighting each by its uncertainty, to produce a smoother, more accurate, continuously-updated state estimate than any single sensor alone -- this is the role of 'robot_localization' (ekf_node) in the ROS2 navigation stack, typically producing the 'odom' -> 'base_link' transform.
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|SLAM & Loca.how_it_works: The EKF maintains a state vector (e.g. x, y, theta, and their velocities) and a covariance matrix representing uncertainty. On each timestep, a 'predict' step propagates the state forward using a motion model (and grows uncertainty); on each sensor measurement, an 'update' step computes the difference between predicted and observed measurement (the 'innovation'), and adjusts the state estimate toward the measurement weighted by the Kalman gain (which depends on relative uncertainties). Because motion and observation models in robotics are non-linear (e.g. theta wraps around, rotations are non-linear), the EKF linearizes them locally using Jacobian matrices at each step.
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|SLAM & Loca.use_when: Fusing wheel odometry + IMU (and optionally GPS) into a single continuous local pose estimate -- the standard 'robot_localization' setup providing 'odom' frame in the TF tree, which downstream consumers (Nav2, controllers) rely on for smooth, continuous (if drifting) pose estimates between discrete AMCL/SLAM corrections.
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|SLAM & Loca.avoid_when: Don't rely on EKF alone for global localisation (correcting drift against a map) -- it has no concept of a map and will happily integrate drifting sensors forever, accumulating error; pair it with AMCL or SLAM for the 'map' -> 'odom' correction. Also, for highly non-linear systems or significantly non-Gaussian noise/multi-modal uncertainty (e.g. global localisation from scratch), a particle filter (AMCL) or Unscented Kalman Filter is more appropriate than a linearized EKF.
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|SLAM & Loca.what_goes_wrong: Incorrectly configured sensor covariances (telling the EKF a noisy sensor is very accurate, or vice versa) cause the filter to either ignore good data or over-trust bad data -- e.g. trusting GPS too much in an EKF feeding the 'odom' frame causes visible 'jumps' in robot pose whenever GPS has a noisy fix, since GPS belongs in the 'map'-level fusion, not 'odom'. Also, EKF linearization errors can cause the filter to diverge (covariance shrinks to overconfidence while the estimate is actually wrong) if the motion model is very non-linear relative to the timestep (e.g. fast rotation with a large dt).
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|SLAM & Loca.real_example: A robot's 'odom' frame, fused from wheel odometry and IMU via an EKF (robot_localization), exhibits sudden jumps whenever the robot drives near a metal shelf -- the IMU's magnetometer-based yaw (if included) is affected by magnetic interference from the shelving, and because the EKF's IMU orientation covariance was configured as very low (high trust), each magnetic disturbance causes a sharp, physically-impossible jump in the fused yaw estimate; excluding the magnetometer-derived yaw from the EKF input fixes it.

8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|SLAM & Loca.what_it_is: The Unscented Kalman Filter is an alternative to the EKF for non-linear state estimation that avoids explicit linearization (Jacobians) by propagating a small, deterministic set of sample points ('sigma points') through the true non-linear functions and reconstructing the mean/covariance from the transformed points -- generally more accurate for strongly non-linear systems at moderate extra computational cost.
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|SLAM & Loca.why_it_exists: The EKF's first-order linearization (Jacobians) can introduce significant error when motion or observation models are highly non-linear (e.g. large rotations per timestep, or sensor models with strong non-linearities) -- errors that compound over time. The UKF's 'unscented transform' captures the non-linear mapping's effect on the distribution's mean and covariance more accurately without requiring derivatives, at the cost of more function evaluations per step (typically 2n+1 sigma points for an n-dimensional state).
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|SLAM & Loca.how_it_works: At each step, the UKF deterministically generates a set of 'sigma points' around the current state estimate (chosen based on the current covariance, via a scaled unscented transform), passes each sigma point through the actual non-linear motion/observation function (no linearization needed), and recombines the transformed points (weighted mean and covariance) to get the predicted state and covariance. The rest of the filter (Kalman gain, update step) proceeds analogously to a standard Kalman filter but using these recomputed statistics.
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|SLAM & Loca.use_when: Robot localisation/odometry fusion where motion is highly non-linear relative to the update rate -- e.g. fast-rotating platforms, or systems where EKF performance has been observed to degrade (divergence, inconsistent covariance). 'robot_localization' in ROS2 offers both 'ekf_node' and 'ukf_node' with the same interface, so switching is often a drop-in configuration change to compare.
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|SLAM & Loca.avoid_when: For most wheeled ground robots with modest accelerations and update rates around 30-50Hz, the EKF's linearization error is small enough that the UKF's extra computation isn't worth it -- default to EKF unless you've observed specific non-linearity-related issues. Also, the UKF doesn't help with non-Gaussian or multi-modal uncertainty (global localisation 'kidnapped robot' scenarios) -- that still needs a particle filter.
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|SLAM & Loca.what_goes_wrong: Because the UKF and EKF share the same 'robot_localization' configuration interface (sensor covariances, process noise), teams sometimes swap one for the other expecting a free accuracy improvement without re-tuning -- but the UKF's sigma-point spread is sensitive to the same covariance parameters, and a configuration poorly tuned for the EKF may not automatically perform better with the UKF; the gains are most visible specifically when EKF linearization error was the actual problem, not a general 'better filter' button.
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|SLAM & Loca.real_example: A fast-spinning robot platform (e.g. a turret-mounted sensor rotating independently of the base) shows EKF-based orientation estimates that drift noticeably during rapid spins -- switching 'robot_localization' from 'ekf_node' to 'ukf_node' with the same sensor configuration measurably reduces orientation error during spins, because the UKF's sigma-point propagation through the rotation's true non-linear dynamics avoids the EKF's linearization error that compounds at high angular velocity.

8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|SLAM & Loca.what_it_is: Multi-sensor fusion combines complementary localisation sources -- wheel/visual odometry (relative motion), IMU (orientation, acceleration), LiDAR-based scan matching or SLAM (absolute position relative to a map), and GPS (absolute global position, outdoors) -- typically in a layered architecture: a fast local fuser (EKF/UKF combining odometry+IMU) feeding 'odom', corrected periodically by a global localiser (AMCL/SLAM, and/or GPS) providing 'map' -> 'odom'.
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|SLAM & Loca.why_it_exists: Each sensor has complementary strengths and weaknesses: wheel odometry is smooth and high-rate but drifts (especially with slip); IMU gives accurate short-term orientation/acceleration but drifts in position when double-integrated and has bias; LiDAR/SLAM gives drift-free absolute position relative to a map but at lower rate and can fail in feature-poor areas; GPS gives global absolute position but is noisy, low-rate, and unavailable indoors. No single source is sufficient for robust, continuous, accurate localisation across all conditions.
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|SLAM & Loca.how_it_works: A common ROS2 pattern: an EKF/UKF ('ekf_filter_node_odom') fuses wheel odometry + IMU at high rate to produce a smooth 'odom' -> 'base_link' transform (locally accurate, but drifts globally). A second EKF/UKF ('ekf_filter_node_map') additionally fuses GPS (converted to a local Cartesian frame via 'navsat_transform_node') and/or pose corrections from AMCL/SLAM to produce 'map' -> 'odom', correcting the drift of the first layer periodically/discretely. This two-layer (continuous local + discontinuous global correction) architecture avoids feeding low-rate, occasionally-jumpy absolute sources directly into the smooth local estimate.
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|SLAM & Loca.use_when: Any outdoor mobile robot needing both smooth local control (requires continuous, low-latency 'odom') and globally-accurate, drift-free position (requires GPS/SLAM corrections) -- the standard architecture for outdoor AMRs, agricultural robots, and delivery robots using 'robot_localization' with this dual-EKF setup.
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|SLAM & Loca.avoid_when: Don't fuse GPS directly into the same EKF that produces 'odom' if smooth local motion matters -- GPS jumps (multipath, satellite dropout) will inject discontinuities into 'odom', which controllers and local planners assume is smooth and continuous; keep GPS fusion in the separate 'map'-level EKF. Also, indoors (no GPS), this architecture simplifies to odometry+IMU for 'odom' and AMCL/SLAM for 'map' corrections -- don't configure a 'navsat_transform_node' pipeline for purely indoor robots.
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|SLAM & Loca.what_goes_wrong: GPS dropout/reacquisition near buildings or under tree cover causes sudden large position 'jumps' when GPS comes back after being lost -- if this is fed into the same filter as 'odom', the robot's local frame jumps discontinuously, which can cause a local planner to suddenly think it's inside an obstacle or far from its planned path. Also, IMU yaw drift (especially with cheap MEMS IMUs lacking a magnetometer, or with magnetometers disturbed by motors/metal) accumulates over time in the 'odom' frame, becoming the dominant error source corrected only by the lower-rate global layer (GPS heading or SLAM/AMCL).
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|SLAM & Loca.real_example: An outdoor delivery robot's local costmap occasionally shows the robot 'jumping' several meters and briefly reports false obstacles all around it after passing under a tree canopy -- GPS was fused directly into the same EKF producing 'odom', and the multi-second GPS dropout under the canopy caused the filter's position estimate to drift (odometry-only), then snap back sharply when GPS reacquired with a different (corrected) fix; restructuring to a two-layer EKF (GPS only in the 'map'-level filter) keeps 'odom' smooth through the dropout while still correcting global position less abruptly.

8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Nav2 Naviga.what_it_is: Nav2 is ROS2's modular autonomous navigation framework -- the successor to ROS1's move_base -- structured as a set of independent lifecycle-managed servers (planner, controller, behavior, smoother, costmaps, BT navigator) coordinated by a Behavior Tree that decides which servers to call, in what order, and how to react to failures.
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Nav2 Naviga.why_it_exists: ROS1's move_base used a rigid state machine (plan -> execute -> recover-on-failure -> retry) that was hard to customize -- adding a new recovery strategy or changing the failure-handling logic meant patching move_base's C++ internals. Nav2's BT-based architecture makes the high-level navigation logic itself data (an XML behavior tree), so operators can add custom recoveries, change retry logic, or insert new behaviors (e.g. 'wait for a door to open') without touching the core servers' code.
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Nav2 Naviga.how_it_works: The BT Navigator loads an XML behavior tree (e.g. 'navigate_to_pose_w_replanning_and_recovery.xml') containing nodes that call into action servers: 'ComputePathToPose' (planner server), 'FollowPath' (controller server), and recovery actions ('Spin', 'BackUp', 'Wait', 'ClearCostmap'). The BT ticks repeatedly, and standard BT control-flow nodes (Sequence, Fallback/ReactiveFallback, Recovery) determine what happens on success or failure of each action -- e.g. 'if FollowPath fails, try ClearCostmap then retry; if that also fails, fall back to a different recovery'. Each server (planner, controller, etc.) is itself a lifecycle node, managed by the 'lifecycle_manager' for coordinated startup.
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Nav2 Naviga.use_when: Any ROS2 autonomous navigation task -- it's the standard, actively-maintained navigation stack for ROS2 ground robots. Use the BT architecture's customizability when you need non-default recovery sequences, custom behaviors (e.g. 'request elevator', 'honk before backing up'), or different navigation modes (e.g. a 'docking' BT vs a 'normal navigation' BT) selectable per goal.
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Nav2 Naviga.avoid_when: For very simple, fixed-sequence navigation needs, the default BT XML is usually sufficient -- don't over-engineer custom BTs when the standard 'navigate_to_pose' behavior already does what you need. Also, BTs are for orchestration of existing servers, not a place to implement new core algorithms (planning math belongs in a planner plugin, not a BT custom node).
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Nav2 Naviga.what_goes_wrong: Editing the BT XML incorrectly (wrong port names, mismatched node names between XML and registered plugins) fails silently or with cryptic BT-library errors at runtime, often only discovered when a specific recovery path is exercised for the first time in production. Also, because each server is a lifecycle node managed by lifecycle_manager, if one server fails to activate (e.g. a misconfigured planner plugin), the whole system can appear 'up' in 'ros2 lifecycle list' summary while one critical server is silently inactive, and navigation goals simply never complete.
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Nav2 Naviga.real_example: A team adds a custom 'wait for door' behavior to their navigation BT XML, referencing a BT node class name that doesn't match what they registered in their BT navigator's plugin list (a typo: 'WaitForDoor' vs 'WaitForDoorOpen') -- the BT navigator fails to construct the tree at startup with an error buried in the logs, and 'ros2 launch' appears to succeed, but 'navigate_to_pose' goals are rejected immediately with 'failed to load behavior tree', which the team initially mistook for a costmap configuration issue.

8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Nav2 Naviga.what_it_is: Nav2 costmaps are layered 2D grids (a 'global' costmap covering the whole map, and a smaller 'local' costmap in a rolling window around the robot) where each cell holds a cost value representing how undesirable/dangerous it is to drive there, built by combining multiple independently-configurable 'layers' -- most commonly static, obstacle (voxel/obstacle layer from live sensors), and inflation.
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Nav2 Naviga.why_it_exists: Path and trajectory planning need more than a binary 'free/occupied' map -- they need a notion of 'how close is too close to an obstacle' (so robots don't hug walls), and they need to combine a known static map with live sensor data (dynamic obstacles like people, moved furniture) without re-running SLAM. The layered architecture lets each concern (static map, live obstacles, safety margins, custom zones) be handled by an independent, swappable plugin that's combined into one final costmap.
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Nav2 Naviga.how_it_works: The 'static layer' loads the pre-built occupancy grid map (from SLAM) as a baseline. The 'obstacle layer' (or 'voxel layer' for 3D) marks cells as occupied based on live sensor data (LiDAR scans, point clouds) via raytracing -- marking hit cells occupied and clearing cells the sensor saw through as free, with the local costmap continuously updating as the robot moves. The 'inflation layer' takes all 'lethal' obstacle cells and spreads a cost gradient outward (decaying with distance, up to 'inflation_radius'), so cells near (but not touching) obstacles get progressively higher cost -- this is what makes planners prefer the center of corridors over hugging walls. Layers are combined (typically by taking the max cost per cell across layers).
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Nav2 Naviga.use_when: Configuring Nav2 for any robot -- nearly every deployment uses at least static + obstacle + inflation layers; tune 'inflation_radius' and 'cost_scaling_factor' based on robot footprint and desired clearance from obstacles.
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Nav2 Naviga.avoid_when: Don't set 'inflation_radius' larger than necessary for the environment -- in narrow environments (warehouse aisles), an inflation radius tuned for a wide-open lobby can inflate obstacle costs across the entire width of a corridor, making the planner think it's impassable even though the robot would physically fit. Also, don't rely solely on the obstacle layer for safety-critical stopping -- it's a planning input, not a substitute for a dedicated safety/collision-monitor system with independent sensors.
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Nav2 Naviga.what_goes_wrong: Sensor mounting height/angle issues cause the obstacle layer to mark the floor itself as an obstacle (if a LiDAR or depth camera's beams clip the ground at certain ranges), filling the costmap with phantom obstacles that block all paths -- this manifests as 'robot won't move, costmap looks solid red in RViz' with no software bug at all, just a sensor calibration/mounting issue. Inflation layer cost-scaling-factor too aggressive can also make the entire map 'expensive' near any obstacle, causing the planner to take bizarre detours to avoid minor cost gradients.
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Nav2 Naviga.real_example: A robot's local costmap shows the entire area in front of it as 'lethal obstacle' (max cost) even in open space -- the 2D LiDAR is mounted slightly tilted downward, so at certain ranges its beams hit the floor instead of passing over it; the obstacle layer correctly marks every floor-hit as an obstacle per its configuration, filling the costmap with a false 'wall' a few meters ahead. The fix is mechanical (re-level the LiDAR mount) plus adjusting the obstacle layer's minimum/maximum height filtering to ignore returns near floor height.

8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Nav2 Naviga.what_it_is: The global planner computes a path from the robot's current pose to a goal pose across the entire (static) global costmap, ignoring fine-grained dynamics -- Nav2 ships multiple interchangeable planner plugins, most commonly 'NavFn' (a Dijkstra/A*-based grid planner, the long-standing default) and the 'Smac Planner' family (including Smac Hybrid-A* for car-like/non-holonomic robots).
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Nav2 Naviga.why_it_exists: Different robots and environments need different planning algorithms: a simple differential-drive robot in an indoor environment is well-served by a fast grid search (NavFn) that ignores kinematics, but a car-like robot (with a minimum turning radius) needs a planner that respects its kinematic constraints (Hybrid-A*) to produce drivable paths, not just geometrically-shortest ones. Nav2's plugin architecture lets the same BT-based navigation stack use whichever planner fits the robot.
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Nav2 Naviga.how_it_works: NavFn computes a potential field over the costmap (similar to Dijkstra's algorithm / wavefront propagation from the goal) and extracts a path by gradient descent from the start, producing a path that minimizes cost but treats the robot as a point that can rotate freely in place. Smac Planner's Hybrid-A* variant searches in (x, y, theta) space using motion primitives that respect the robot's minimum turning radius (and optionally reverse motion), producing paths that a car-like or large differential-drive robot can actually follow without needing to pivot in place. Both expose the 'ComputePathToPose' action interface used by the BT.
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Nav2 Naviga.use_when: NavFn (or its modern equivalent, Smac 2D) for differential-drive or omnidirectional robots that can rotate freely -- the common default for indoor AMRs. Smac Hybrid-A* for car-like (Ackermann-steered) robots, large robots with significant turning radius constraints, or any robot where in-place rotation isn't possible/desirable.
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Nav2 Naviga.avoid_when: Don't use a kinematically-unconstrained planner (NavFn) for a robot that physically cannot follow the resulting paths (e.g. a car that can't pivot in place) -- the local controller will struggle or fail to track geometrically-valid-but-kinematically-infeasible paths. Conversely, don't use the heavier Hybrid-A* search for a simple differential-drive robot in an open environment where it adds planning latency with no benefit over NavFn.
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Nav2 Naviga.what_goes_wrong: Choosing NavFn for a non-holonomic robot produces globally-optimal-looking paths that include sharp turns or paths that double back -- the local controller (e.g. a DWB tuned for differential drive assumptions on a car-like robot) then either fails to follow them or produces jerky, unsafe motion trying to approximate impossible maneuvers. Also, Smac planners' motion-primitive lookup tables must be generated/configured for the robot's actual minimum turning radius -- using default parameters tuned for a different robot's turning radius produces paths that are either overly conservative (wide unnecessary loops) or still kinematically infeasible.
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Nav2 Naviga.real_example: A car-like delivery robot using the default NavFn planner repeatedly gets stuck trying to execute a planned path that requires a 3-point turn in a narrow aisle -- the global plan is geometrically valid (shortest path through the costmap) but assumes the robot can rotate in place, which it can't. Switching the global planner to Smac Hybrid-A* with the robot's actual minimum turning radius configured produces paths with wider, drivable curves instead of in-place pivots, and the robot completes the same routes without getting stuck.

8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Nav2 Naviga.what_it_is: The local planner (controller server in Nav2 terminology) takes the global path and the robot's immediate surroundings (local costmap) and computes real-time velocity commands ('/cmd_vel') to follow the path while avoiding dynamic obstacles -- Nav2's main controller plugins are 'DWB' (Dynamic Window approach-based) and the newer 'MPPI' (Model Predictive Path Integral) controller.
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Nav2 Naviga.why_it_exists: The global plan is computed against a static snapshot of the map and doesn't account for moving obstacles (people, other robots) or the robot's exact dynamic constraints (acceleration limits, current velocity) at every instant. The local planner runs at high frequency (10-20Hz+), continuously re-evaluating the immediate situation and producing velocity commands that balance 'follow the global path' against 'avoid what I can currently see', reacting to changes the global planner never knew about.
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Nav2 Naviga.how_it_works: DWB samples a set of candidate velocity commands (within the robot's dynamic feasibility window -- reachable velocities given current velocity and acceleration limits), simulates each candidate's short-term trajectory, scores them against multiple configurable 'critics' (path alignment, goal alignment, obstacle proximity, etc.), and picks the best-scoring command -- a discretized sample-and-score approach. MPPI instead uses a sampling-based model-predictive control approach: it samples many random perturbations of a control sequence, simulates each (via a robot motion model) over a longer horizon, weights them by a cost function (path following, obstacle cost, etc.), and computes a weighted-average 'optimal' control -- repeated every control cycle (receding horizon), generally producing smoother, more dynamically-aware behavior than DWB's discrete sampling.
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Nav2 Naviga.use_when: DWB for robots and use-cases where its long track record, simpler tuning model (per-critic weights), and lower computational cost are preferred -- many production indoor AMRs. MPPI for robots needing smoother trajectories, better handling of dynamic obstacles, or where DWB's discretized velocity sampling produces visibly jerky motion -- MPPI has become the recommended default for new Nav2 deployments due to generally better obstacle avoidance and smoother paths.
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Nav2 Naviga.avoid_when: Don't use MPPI on severely compute-constrained platforms without verifying it meets the required control-loop rate -- its sampling-based optimization (many simulated rollouts per cycle) is more CPU-intensive than DWB's critic evaluation, though tunable via sample count/horizon. Don't expect either local planner to fix a fundamentally bad global plan -- if the global path routes through an area the robot truly can't traverse, local planning will just get stuck or trigger recoveries repeatedly.
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Nav2 Naviga.what_goes_wrong: DWB's per-critic weight tuning is famously fiddly -- increasing 'obstacle' critic weight to make the robot more cautious can inadvertently make it ignore the path-following critics near obstacles, causing the robot to stop or oscillate rather than carefully proceed. MPPI's behavior is sensitive to its cost function weights and the accuracy of its motion model -- an inaccurate model (e.g. wrong max acceleration) can cause MPPI to compute velocity commands the robot's low-level controller then can't actually achieve, leading to path-tracking error that MPPI keeps 'correcting' for, producing oscillation.
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Nav2 Naviga.real_example: A robot using DWB oscillates left-right while passing through a doorway -- the 'path_align' and 'obstacle' critics are both weighted highly, and as the robot approaches the doorway, the obstacle critic (seeing the door frame on both sides) and the path-align critic disagree on the best heading from one control cycle to the next, causing the selected velocity command to flip-flop between favoring each critic. Reducing the obstacle critic's weight slightly, or switching to MPPI (whose trajectory-level cost evaluation handles this geometry more smoothly), resolves the oscillation.

8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Nav2 Naviga.what_it_is: Within Nav2 specifically, the BT Navigator loads an XML tree built from BehaviorTree.CPP (BT.CPP) primitives -- Nav2-specific 'leaf' nodes like 'ComputePathToPose', 'FollowPath', 'Spin', 'Wait', 'BackUp', 'ClearEntireCostmap', combined with BT.CPP's generic control nodes (Sequence, Fallback/ReactiveFallback, RecoveryNode, PipelineSequence) to define exactly how a navigation request is executed and recovered from.
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Nav2 Naviga.why_it_exists: This is a second occurrence -- the earlier 'Nav2 architecture' note covered why Nav2 uses a behavior tree at all (data-driven, customizable navigation logic vs. move_base's hardcoded state machine). This note covers the practical mechanics of working with Nav2's specific BT.CPP trees: what nodes exist, how the default trees ('navigate_to_pose_w_replanning_and_recovery.xml', etc.) are structured, and how to read/modify them.
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Nav2 Naviga.how_it_works: Nav2's default 'navigate_to_pose' tree is roughly: a 'RecoveryNode' wraps a 'PipelineSequence' of [ComputePathToPose -> FollowPath]; if either fails, the RecoveryNode's second child (a recovery Fallback of ClearCostmap/Spin/Wait/BackUp) runs before retrying, up to a configured number of times. A 'RateController' decorator wraps the planner call so replanning happens periodically (e.g. every 1 second) rather than only on failure, giving 'replanning' behavior. Data flows between BT nodes via a shared 'blackboard' (e.g. the computed path is written to a blackboard key by ComputePathToPose and read by FollowPath). Each leaf node corresponds to a registered C++ plugin class loaded by the BT navigator.
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Nav2 Naviga.use_when: Customizing Nav2's navigation logic -- adding a new recovery step, changing replanning frequency (RateController period), creating alternate trees for different scenarios (e.g. a 'docking' tree vs a 'normal navigation' tree, selectable via the action request's 'behavior_tree' field), or debugging why a particular failure/recovery sequence did or didn't trigger.
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Nav2 Naviga.avoid_when: Don't write custom BT XML changes without testing them in simulation first -- a malformed tree (mismatched port names, wrong node class names) fails at BT construction time, often with non-obvious error messages, and a logically-wrong tree (e.g. an infinite retry loop with no escalation) can leave a robot endlessly attempting and failing a recovery in production.
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Nav2 Naviga.what_goes_wrong: A common mistake is editing the 'navigate_to_pose' XML's RecoveryNode retry count to a high number 'to make navigation more robust', which instead means the robot spends minutes cycling through Spin/Wait/ClearCostmap/retry before finally reporting failure -- from an operator's perspective the robot just looks 'stuck' for a long time with no clear error. Another: blackboard key name mismatches between a custom BT node's output port and what a downstream node expects to read silently results in that downstream node operating on stale or default data.
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Nav2 Naviga.real_example: A team adds a custom 'NotifyOperator' BT node inside the recovery Fallback, intending it to fire after all standard recoveries (Spin, Wait, ClearCostmap) fail -- but they place it as the FIRST child of the Fallback instead of the last, so BT.CPP's Fallback semantics mean 'NotifyOperator' runs (and 'succeeds' immediately, since notification always 'succeeds') before Spin/Wait/ClearCostmap ever get a chance, short-circuiting all the real recovery behaviors -- the robot notifies the operator on every single planning hiccup instead of only as a last resort.

8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Nav2 Naviga.what_it_is: Recovery behaviours are short, self-contained actions Nav2 invokes when normal navigation (planning or path-following) fails, intended to clear the cause of the failure and allow a retry -- the most common built-in recoveries are 'ClearEntireCostmap'/'ClearCostmapAroundRobot' (clear stale obstacle data), 'Spin' (rotate in place, often to clear costmap via fresh sensor sweeps or unstick a localisation issue), 'BackUp' (reverse a short distance), and 'Wait' (pause, e.g. for a dynamic obstacle to move).
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Nav2 Naviga.why_it_exists: Many navigation failures are transient and self-resolving with the right nudge: a costmap can have stale 'phantom' obstacles from a sensor glitch or a person who has since moved away (cleared by ClearCostmap or by Spin refreshing the sensor view); a robot can be 'too close' to an obstacle for the local planner to find any valid trajectory (resolved by backing up to create space); a temporarily-blocking obstacle (person standing in a doorway) may simply move if the robot waits briefly. Recoveries handle these common cases automatically rather than immediately failing the whole navigation task.
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Nav2 Naviga.how_it_works: Each recovery is implemented as its own Nav2 action server/plugin (e.g. the 'behavior_server' hosts Spin, BackUp, Wait, DriveOnHeading as 'nav2_behaviors' plugins; costmap clearing is a service call to the costmap nodes). In the default BT, a 'RecoveryNode' control node wraps the main navigation pipeline: on failure, its recovery child (often a Fallback sequence trying ClearCostmap, then Spin, then Wait, then BackUp, in some configured order) executes before the main pipeline is retried, up to a configured retry count.
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Nav2 Naviga.use_when: Any production Nav2 deployment -- recoveries are essential for robustness against transient costmap noise, momentarily-blocked paths, and minor localisation hiccups; tune the recovery sequence and retry counts to match the environment (e.g. more aggressive Wait-based recoveries in human-populated spaces where obstacles are often transient people).
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Nav2 Naviga.avoid_when: Don't rely on 'Spin' as a recovery in very tight spaces -- a robot that can't find a valid path partly because it's wedged close to obstacles may not have room to spin safely, and the spin itself could cause a collision. Also, don't configure unlimited or very high retry counts for recoveries that won't resolve a persistent (non-transient) failure -- e.g. repeatedly backing up and retrying toward a goal that's genuinely unreachable just wastes time before eventually failing anyway.
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Nav2 Naviga.what_goes_wrong: 'BackUp' recoveries in environments with obstacles behind the robot (common in narrow aisles) can cause the robot to back into something it didn't sense was there (e.g. a rear blind spot with no rear-facing sensor) -- a recovery meant to create space instead causes a collision. Also, 'ClearEntireCostmap' as a first-resort recovery can be too aggressive: it clears genuinely-present obstacles from the costmap too, so the robot may briefly 'forget' about a real obstacle and plan a path through it until the next sensor update repopulates the costmap.
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Nav2 Naviga.real_example: A robot operating in a busy aisle repeatedly fails to find a local plan because a person is standing in its path, triggers ClearEntireCostmap as its first recovery (clearing the person from the costmap), immediately replans a path 'through' where the person is standing (now invisible to the costmap), and only re-detects the obstacle on the very next sensor scan -- producing a visible 'lurch toward the person, then stop again' pattern. Reordering recoveries to try 'Wait' before 'ClearEntireCostmap' lets transient obstacles resolve themselves first without this lurching.

8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Nav2 Naviga.what_it_is: Waypoint navigation (Nav2's 'FollowWaypoints' action) drives the robot through an ordered sequence of poses, executing the 'navigate_to_pose' behavior for each waypoint in turn, optionally running a 'waypoint task executor' plugin (e.g. pause for a photo, wait for a docking action) at each stop.
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Nav2 Naviga.why_it_exists: Many real tasks aren't 'go to one place' but 'visit these N locations in order' -- a security patrol robot, an inspection robot checking multiple stations, or a delivery robot dropping off at several rooms. Rather than every application re-implementing 'loop over goals, call navigate_to_pose, handle failures', Nav2 provides this as a single action with configurable failure-handling policy (stop on first failure, or skip failed waypoints and continue).
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Nav2 Naviga.how_it_works: A client sends a 'FollowWaypoints' goal containing a list of PoseStamped goals. The waypoint follower iterates through them, internally invoking 'navigate_to_pose' for each (the same BT-based navigation described elsewhere). Between (or at) each waypoint, an optional 'waypoint_task_executor' plugin runs (e.g. 'WaitAtWaypoint' pauses for a configured duration, or a custom plugin could trigger a camera capture or a docking sequence). The action reports which waypoints succeeded/failed via feedback, and an 'on failure' policy determines whether to abort the whole sequence or continue to the next waypoint.
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Nav2 Naviga.use_when: Multi-stop missions -- patrol routes, multi-room delivery, inspection rounds with stop-and-perform-task semantics at each waypoint.
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Nav2 Naviga.avoid_when: Don't use FollowWaypoints for tasks needing complex inter-waypoint logic (e.g. 'go to waypoint 3 only if waypoint 2's inspection found an anomaly') -- that conditional logic belongs in a higher-level task/mission layer (or a custom BT) that calls individual navigation actions, not in the linear FollowWaypoints sequence. Also avoid extremely long waypoint lists where a single early failure (with 'stop on failure' policy) wastes the entire remaining mission -- consider a 'skip failed waypoints' policy for long patrol routes.
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Nav2 Naviga.what_goes_wrong: With the default 'stop on failure' policy, a single unreachable waypoint (e.g. a temporarily-blocked doorway) aborts the entire remaining route, even if waypoints 4-10 are all perfectly reachable -- for patrol-style missions this is often the wrong default and needs explicit configuration to 'skip and continue'. Also, waypoint task executors that block for a long time (e.g. waiting for a slow docking sequence) block the entire FollowWaypoints action with no separate timeout, so a stuck task executor stalls the whole mission with feedback that just stops updating.
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Nav2 Naviga.real_example: A security patrol robot's nightly route aborts at waypoint 3 of 12 because a cleaning cart was temporarily blocking that location -- with the default failure policy, the robot simply stops and reports 'mission failed', skipping waypoints 4-12 entirely (including areas that were perfectly accessible), and the gap isn't noticed until the morning review of patrol logs shows 9 unvisited locations.

8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Nav2 Naviga.what_it_is: 'navigate_to_pose' is Nav2's core action interface -- a client sends a single target Pose (in the 'map' frame), and the BT Navigator executes the full plan-and-follow-with-recovery behavior tree to drive the robot there, reporting periodic feedback (distance remaining, estimated time, number of recoveries attempted) and a final result (succeeded, canceled, or failed with a specific error code).
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Nav2 Naviga.why_it_exists: This is the single, stable, high-level entry point that essentially every navigation interaction in Nav2 ultimately goes through -- whether a user clicks a goal in RViz2 ('2D Goal Pose' tool publishes to this action), a waypoint follower invokes it per-waypoint, or an autonomy stack requests it programmatically (e.g. via the Simple Commander API). Having one well-defined action with feedback and cancellation, rather than many bespoke interfaces, is what makes Nav2 composable.
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Nav2 Naviga.how_it_works: A client (RViz2, a Python script, another BT) sends a 'nav2_msgs/action/NavigateToPose' goal with a target PoseStamped. The BT Navigator's executor begins ticking the loaded behavior tree (described in the BT notes), which internally calls 'ComputePathToPose' (planner server) and 'FollowPath' (controller server), with recoveries as needed. Feedback messages are published periodically (current pose, distance/time remaining, number of recoveries). On completion, a result code and message indicate success or the specific failure mode (e.g. 'NO_VALID_CONTROL', 'PATIENCE_EXCEEDED', 'FAILED_TO_FIND_VALID_PATH').
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Nav2 Naviga.use_when: Any single-goal navigation request -- the foundation that RViz2's goal tool, FollowWaypoints, and most custom mission code build on. Use the action's feedback to monitor progress (e.g. for a UI progress bar) and its cancellation to implement 'abort current goal' functionality.
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Nav2 Naviga.avoid_when: Don't poll the robot's position separately to determine 'are we there yet' when the action's feedback already provides distance/time remaining -- duplicating this logic is wasteful and can drift out of sync with the actual navigation state. Also don't send a new 'navigate_to_pose' goal without canceling/waiting for completion of a previous one if your client logic assumes only one goal is active -- Nav2 will preempt the previous goal, which may be surprising if the client didn't intend that.
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Nav2 Naviga.what_goes_wrong: Result error codes are often under-examined -- code that only checks 'did the action succeed (bool)' loses the specific failure reason (e.g. 'NO_VALID_CONTROL' vs 'FAILED_TO_FIND_VALID_PATH' vs 'PATIENCE_EXCEEDED' from taking too long), which matters enormously for automated retry/fallback logic (a 'no path found' failure might warrant trying a different goal, while a 'patience exceeded' failure on an otherwise-valid path might warrant a recovery and simple retry). Also, sending goals in a frame other than 'map' (or a frame without a valid TF chain to 'map') causes the action to fail immediately with a TF-related error that's easy to misattribute to planning logic.
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Nav2 Naviga.real_example: An application retries any failed 'navigate_to_pose' goal up to 3 times with the same target pose -- this works fine for transient 'PATIENCE_EXCEEDED' failures (a person briefly blocking the path), but for a goal pose that's actually inside a wall (a bad goal from an upstream mapping error), every retry fails identically with 'FAILED_TO_FIND_VALID_PATH', burning through all 3 retries (and the associated time) before the application gives up -- distinguishing the error codes would let it fail fast on the unreachable-goal case instead of wasting retries.

8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Nav2 Naviga.what_it_is: 'navigate_through_poses' is a Nav2 action that, given an ordered list of poses, computes and follows a single continuous path passing through all of them in sequence -- unlike FollowWaypoints, the robot does not stop, reorient, or run task executors at each intermediate pose; the poses act as path 'via points' for one continuous motion.
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Nav2 Naviga.why_it_exists: Sometimes the goal isn't 'visit these N places and do something at each' (FollowWaypoints) but 'drive smoothly along a route defined by these via-points without stopping' -- e.g. following a designated corridor route through a building rather than the shortest direct path, or producing smoother motion than repeatedly stopping at each waypoint and replanning from a standstill.
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Nav2 Naviga.how_it_works: The action passes the full list of poses to the planner ('ComputePathThroughPoses'), which produces a single path that passes through (or near) each intermediate pose en route to the final goal, then the controller follows this single path continuously -- the BT structure is analogous to 'navigate_to_pose' but with a multi-pose-aware planning call, so there's no stop/replan cycle between via-points the way there would be between consecutive FollowWaypoints goals.
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Nav2 Naviga.use_when: Defining a preferred route through intermediate points without stopping -- e.g. forcing a robot down a specific corridor (via-point in the corridor) rather than letting the planner find a shorter but undesirable route; producing smoother multi-segment motion than sequential navigate_to_pose calls, which each involve a full stop and replan.
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Nav2 Naviga.avoid_when: Don't use this when you actually need the robot to perform an action AT each intermediate point (use FollowWaypoints with task executors instead) -- navigate_through_poses has no concept of 'arriving' at intermediate poses, only passing through them en route. Also, if intermediate poses are far apart with very different headings, forcing a single continuous path through all of them may produce less direct or less natural motion than separate navigate_to_pose calls would.
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Nav2 Naviga.what_goes_wrong: Because intermediate poses are 'via points' for planning, not strict waypoints the robot must precisely reach, the actual path may pass somewhat near (not exactly through) each pose depending on the planner and costmap -- applications expecting precise via-point tracking (e.g. 'must pass within 10cm of this exact point for a sensor calibration check') may be surprised by the deviation. Also, a single very long multi-pose path means a single planning failure anywhere along the route fails the entire action, rather than getting partial progress as FollowWaypoints would report per-waypoint.
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Nav2 Naviga.real_example: A facility wants robots to always travel between two rooms via a specific main corridor (for predictability around people) rather than a shorter route through a back area -- adding a via-point pose in the main corridor to a 'navigate_through_poses' call reliably routes the robot that way; however, when the main corridor is temporarily fully blocked, the entire action fails (no path exists through all via-points), whereas a sequence of navigate_to_pose calls might have at least gotten partway via the back route before the final leg failed.

8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Nav2 Naviga.what_it_is: nav2_simple_commander is a Python library that wraps Nav2's action interfaces (navigate_to_pose, navigate_through_poses, follow_waypoints, spin, backup, etc.) and lifecycle management into simple, synchronous-feeling Python method calls (goToPose, followWaypoints, followPath, getResult, isTaskComplete), so mission scripts don't need to hand-write ROS2 action client boilerplate.
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Nav2 Naviga.why_it_exists: Writing a raw ROS2 action client (create client, send goal, handle goal-response future, handle feedback callback, handle result future) for every navigation call is verbose boilerplate that obscures the actual mission logic. For scripting autonomy demos, test missions, or simple task-execution layers, most developers want to write 'robot.goToPose(pose); while not robot.isTaskComplete(): print(robot.getFeedback())' -- Simple Commander provides exactly that ergonomic layer over the same underlying actions.
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Nav2 Naviga.how_it_works: A 'BasicNavigator' (or 'TaskResult'-returning equivalents) instance wraps an rclpy node; its methods (e.g. 'goToPose(pose)') create the appropriate action client, send the goal, and return immediately, with 'isTaskComplete()' polling the result future and 'getFeedback()'/'getResult()' exposing the action's feedback/result. It also wraps lifecycle bring-up/teardown ('lifecycleStartup', 'lifecycleShutdown') and costmap-clearing convenience methods, so a full mission script can manage the navigation stack's lifecycle and execute a sequence of goals in straightforward, readable Python.
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Nav2 Naviga.use_when: Writing mission/test scripts, demos, or simple autonomy layers in Python that need to sequence navigation goals, react to feedback/results, and manage the nav stack's lifecycle -- the recommended starting point for 'drive the robot through this sequence of behaviors' scripting rather than hand-rolled action clients.
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Nav2 Naviga.avoid_when: Don't build a production-grade, complex mission executor entirely on Simple Commander's polling-based 'isTaskComplete()' loops if you need sophisticated concurrent task management, multiple simultaneous action goals, or tight integration with a larger state machine/BT framework -- at that point, working with the action clients directly (or building a custom BT) gives more control. Simple Commander is an ergonomic convenience layer, not a full mission-planning framework.
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Nav2 Naviga.what_goes_wrong: The polling pattern ('while not isTaskComplete(): sleep/do other work') can mask the fact that 'rclpy.spin_once' or equivalent needs to be called for callbacks (feedback, result) to actually be processed -- a script that polls without spinning the node can get stuck waiting on a result that's actually already arrived but never processed. Also, scripts often forget to call 'lifecycleStartup()' and wait for it to complete before sending the first navigation goal, sending goals to a nav stack whose servers haven't finished activating yet, causing the first goal to fail or hang.
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Nav2 Naviga.real_example: A demo script using BasicNavigator sends a 'goToPose' goal immediately after constructing the navigator object, without calling 'lifecycleStartup()' (or without waiting for it to report active) -- the first goal silently fails because the planner/controller servers are still in the 'unconfigured' lifecycle state. The fix is calling 'navigator.lifecycleStartup()' and confirming active state (or waiting for 'navigator.waitUntilNav2Active()') before sending any goals.

8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Nav2 Naviga.what_it_is: Beyond the core static/obstacle/inflation layers, Nav2's costmap plugin architecture supports additional layers for application-specific behavior -- notably the 'Keepout Filter' (mask-based no-go/no-drive zones from a separate filter mask image) and 'Speed Filter' (zone-based speed limits), plus community/custom 'social' layers that add cost around detected humans for more cautious, proxemics-aware navigation.
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Nav2 Naviga.why_it_exists: Real deployments have requirements beyond 'avoid physical obstacles' -- a warehouse may have zones robots must never enter regardless of whether they're physically clear (a loading dock, a restricted area near machinery), certain zones may require reduced speed (near pedestrian crossings), and human-aware robots may need to maintain larger personal-space buffers around people than around inanimate obstacles. The costmap plugin architecture lets these policies be expressed as additional cost layers without modifying core planner/controller code.
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Nav2 Naviga.how_it_works: The 'Keepout Filter' uses a separate grayscale 'filter mask' image (same format as an occupancy grid map, but encoding 'keepout' regions instead of obstacles) aligned to the main map; cells marked in the mask are treated as lethal (or high-cost) regardless of sensor data, so planners route around them as if they were walls. The 'Speed Filter' similarly uses a mask image, but instead of adding cost, it publishes a speed-limit signal that the controller respects when the robot is within a masked zone. Social/human-aware layers (often custom or from community packages) subscribe to a people-detection topic and add a cost gradient (often Gaussian, proxemics-inspired) around each detected person's position, layered on top of the standard obstacle/inflation costs.
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Nav2 Naviga.use_when: Defining permanent no-go areas (docking station back-areas, restricted zones, areas under construction) via Keepout Filter; defining speed-restricted zones (near doors, blind corners, pedestrian areas) via Speed Filter; deploying robots in spaces with regular human traffic where extra clearance around people (beyond static-obstacle inflation) improves perceived safety and comfort.
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Nav2 Naviga.avoid_when: Don't use Keepout zones as the only mechanism for safety-critical exclusion (e.g. a genuinely hazardous machine area) -- costmap-based exclusion is a planning-level soft constraint, not a certified safety system; pair with hardware safety measures (e-stops, light curtains, physical barriers) for true hazards. Also, overly large social-layer cost gradients in densely populated environments can make the costmap appear 'full' of high cost everywhere, causing the planner to struggle to find any low-cost path through a crowd.
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Nav2 Naviga.what_goes_wrong: Keepout/speed filter masks must be precisely aligned (same resolution, origin, and dimensions) with the main map -- even small misalignments mean the 'no-go zone' ends up a meter or two off from where it's supposed to be, which may not be obvious until a robot enters an area it shouldn't (or refuses to enter an area it should). Also, social layers that update cost based on tracked people positions at the rate of a (possibly noisy/jittery) perception pipeline can cause the costmap -- and thus the local plan -- to fluctuate rapidly as detections jitter frame to frame, producing visibly nervous/twitchy robot motion near people.
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Nav2 Naviga.real_example: A warehouse deploys a Keepout Filter mask to block off a loading dock area, generated from a slightly different map version than the one currently loaded for navigation (created weeks apart, with the map having been re-saved with a different origin in the meantime) -- the keepout zone in the costmap ends up offset by about 1.5 meters from the actual loading dock boundary, so the robot is blocked from an area of open floor it should be able to use, while the actual loading dock remains accessible; regenerating the mask aligned to the current map fixes it.

8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Path Planni.what_it_is: Dijkstra's algorithm is a graph-search algorithm that finds the shortest (lowest-cost) path from a single source node to all other nodes in a weighted graph with non-negative edge weights, running in O((V+E) log V) time with a priority queue -- the foundation that NavFn-style robot path planners build on, treating the costmap grid as a graph where cells are nodes and edges connect neighboring cells weighted by traversal cost.
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Path Planni.why_it_exists: Robot path planning on a grid is fundamentally a shortest-path graph problem: find the lowest-cost route from the robot's current cell to the goal cell through a grid where each cell has a traversal cost (free space cheap, near obstacles expensive). Dijkstra's algorithm guarantees the globally optimal answer for this problem (given non-negative costs), which is why it (or its informed variant, A*) underlies most grid-based global planners.
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Path Planni.how_it_works: Maintain a priority queue of nodes ordered by tentative distance-from-source, initialized with the source at distance 0 and all others at infinity. Repeatedly pop the lowest-distance unvisited node, mark it visited, and 'relax' each of its neighbors (if reaching the neighbor through this node is cheaper than its current known distance, update it and re-add to the queue). When the queue is empty (or the goal is popped), every visited node has its guaranteed-shortest distance from the source. Because it explores in increasing order of distance from the source with no notion of 'direction toward goal', it explores roughly equally in all directions (a 'wavefront' expanding from the source).
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Path Planni.use_when: Computing shortest paths when you need guaranteed-optimal results and have no useful heuristic, or when you need distances/paths to MANY targets from one source simultaneously (Dijkstra naturally computes this; A* to a single goal does not directly generalize as efficiently). NavFn's potential-field approach is essentially Dijkstra/wavefront propagation from the goal outward.
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Path Planni.avoid_when: Don't use plain Dijkstra when you have a good heuristic and only care about a single source-goal pair -- A* with an admissible heuristic finds the same optimal path while exploring far fewer nodes, especially in open areas where Dijkstra wastes time exploring uniformly in all directions including away from the goal.
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Path Planni.what_goes_wrong: On large grid maps, Dijkstra's lack of goal-direction means it can explore huge swaths of the map before reaching the goal, especially in open spaces -- this manifests as noticeably higher planning latency and CPU usage compared to A* for the same map/goal, particularly disproportionate when the goal happens to be far from the start in an open area with few obstacles to 'guide' the wavefront.
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Path Planni.real_example: A robot's global planner (configured to use a pure Dijkstra-like NavFn variant) takes visibly longer to compute paths in a large open warehouse than in a cluttered area of similar size -- profiling shows the planner's wavefront expands almost uniformly across the entire open region before reaching the goal, whereas switching to an A*-based variant with a Euclidean heuristic biases the search toward the goal direction from the start, cutting planning time substantially in the open-area case.

8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Path Planni.what_it_is: A* is Dijkstra's algorithm augmented with a heuristic function h(n) estimating the remaining cost from node n to the goal -- it explores nodes in order of f(n) = g(n) + h(n) (cost-so-far plus estimated-cost-to-go), focusing the search toward the goal and finding the same optimal path as Dijkstra (if h is 'admissible', never overestimating) while typically expanding far fewer nodes.
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Path Planni.why_it_exists: Dijkstra wastes effort exploring in all directions with no notion of where the goal is. If you have any reasonable estimate of 'how far is this node from the goal' (which, for a robot on a grid, you almost always do -- straight-line distance), incorporating that estimate into the search order dramatically reduces the number of nodes explored, which matters for real-time replanning on large maps.
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Path Planni.how_it_works: Identical to Dijkstra's priority-queue structure, but the priority is f(n) = g(n) + h(n) instead of just g(n). If h(n) is admissible (never overestimates the true remaining cost) and consistent (satisfies a triangle-inequality-like property), A* is guaranteed to find the optimal path while exploring nodes roughly 'between' the start and goal rather than uniformly in all directions. Choice of h(n) (Manhattan, Euclidean, diagonal/octile distance) depends on the grid's allowed movement directions.
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Path Planni.use_when: The default choice for grid-based global path planning with a known goal location -- virtually all practical robot path planners use A* or a close variant (including weighted/anytime variants for real-time replanning under time pressure).
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Path Planni.avoid_when: Don't use A* if you need shortest paths to many different goals from one source (Dijkstra is more natural there) or if no reasonable heuristic exists for your cost structure (in which case A* degenerates to Dijkstra anyway, with extra heuristic-computation overhead). Also, a poorly-chosen (non-admissible) heuristic can make A* return suboptimal paths -- if optimality is required, verify the heuristic never overestimates true cost.
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Path Planni.what_goes_wrong: Using an inadmissible heuristic (e.g. a Euclidean-distance heuristic on a grid that only allows 4-directional movement, where Euclidean distance can underestimate the true grid distance... actually the more common bug is the reverse: using a heuristic that OVERESTIMATES, like diagonal/octile distance on a 4-connected grid) breaks the optimality guarantee silently -- A* still returns A path, just not necessarily the shortest one, and this can go unnoticed for a long time since the paths often 'look fine'. Tie-breaking in the priority queue when multiple nodes have equal f(n) can also produce visually unnatural 'zigzag' paths if not handled (a common practical fix is adding a small tie-breaking term favoring nodes closer to a straight line between start and goal).
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Path Planni.real_example: A grid planner configured for 8-directional movement (allows diagonal steps) uses a Manhattan-distance heuristic (which assumes only 4-directional movement and so OVERESTIMATES true cost when diagonal moves are cheaper) -- this inadmissible heuristic causes A* to occasionally return paths that are a few percent longer than optimal, a discrepancy that went unnoticed until someone compared planner output against a brute-force optimal solver on a small test map and found consistent small suboptimality; switching to octile distance (admissible for 8-connected grids) fixed it.

8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Path Planni.what_it_is: Heuristic functions h(n) used in A* estimate the remaining cost from a node to the goal -- Manhattan distance (|dx| + |dy|, for 4-connected grids), Euclidean distance (straight-line sqrt(dx^2+dy^2), for any-angle movement), and diagonal/octile distance (accounts for cheaper diagonal moves on 8-connected grids) are the standard choices, each matched to the grid's allowed movement model.
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Path Planni.why_it_exists: A* is only as good as its heuristic: too weak (e.g. always returning 0, which degenerates to Dijkstra) wastes the benefit of A*, while too strong (overestimating true cost) breaks the optimality guarantee. Matching the heuristic to the actual movement model -- how many directions the robot/grid allows, and at what relative cost -- is what keeps the heuristic both admissible (never overestimates) and as 'tight' (close to true cost) as possible for efficient search.
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Path Planni.how_it_works: Manhattan distance is exact for a 4-connected grid (only N/S/E/W moves, each cost 1) and admissible there, but overestimates if diagonal moves are allowed (since a diagonal move covers more Euclidean distance for the same '1 step' cost it would take 2 Manhattan steps to cover). Euclidean distance is admissible for any movement model (it's the true geometric lower bound, since no path can be shorter than a straight line) but is 'loose' (underestimates more) for grid movement restricted to 8 directions. Diagonal/octile distance (= max(|dx|,|dy|) + (sqrt(2)-1)*min(|dx|,|dy|) for unit diagonal cost sqrt(2)) is exact and admissible for 8-connected grids with that diagonal cost.
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Path Planni.use_when: Manhattan for 4-connected grids (no diagonal movement allowed); octile/diagonal distance for 8-connected grids (diagonal movement allowed at cost sqrt(2)); Euclidean distance for any-angle planners (Theta*, RRT-based methods) where movement isn't constrained to grid directions at all.
