8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Path Planni.avoid_when: Don't use Manhattan distance on an 8-connected grid (it overestimates, breaking admissibility) and don't use a heuristic of 0 'just to be safe' (correct but degenerates to Dijkstra, losing all of A*'s efficiency benefit). Also avoid heuristics that don't account for varying terrain cost (e.g. a costmap where some cells cost much more than others) -- a pure-distance heuristic that ignores cost weighting can be badly miscalibrated relative to g(n), which is in cost units, not distance units.
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Path Planni.what_goes_wrong: Mismatched units between h(n) and g(n) is a subtle but common bug -- if g(n) accumulates 'cost' (which includes inflation-layer penalties near obstacles, not just distance) but h(n) is pure geometric distance, the heuristic systematically underestimates near obstacles (where true cost-to-go is higher than distance suggests), which is technically still admissible (underestimating is safe) but makes the heuristic much less 'informative' near obstacles, causing A* to explore extra nodes specifically in cluttered regions.
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Path Planni.real_example: A planner using Euclidean-distance heuristic performs well in open areas but becomes noticeably slower specifically when paths must wind through cluttered regions with high inflation costs -- because the heuristic (pure distance) doesn't account for the inflation cost gradient that g(n) accumulates, the heuristic 'underestimates more' in cluttered areas, weakening A*'s pruning exactly where the search space is largest; some planners address this with a cost-aware heuristic that incorporates a rough estimate of inflation cost along the straight-line path.

8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Path Planni.what_it_is: Theta* is a variant of A* that produces 'any-angle' paths -- instead of restricting paths to grid-aligned edges (4 or 8 directions), it allows a node's parent to be ANY node with line-of-sight to it, producing paths with arbitrary angles that more closely resemble what a human would draw as the 'natural' shortest path, without the post-processing smoothing that grid-restricted A* paths typically need.
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Path Planni.why_it_exists: A*/Dijkstra on a grid produces paths constrained to the grid's discrete directions (e.g. only 0/45/90 degree turns on an 8-connected grid), which are provably longer than the true geometric shortest path and look 'jagged' or 'staircase-like' even when the environment has no obstacles forcing those turns. Theta* removes this artificial constraint while keeping A*'s efficient grid-based search structure, producing paths much closer to true shortest paths directly, without needing a separate path-smoothing post-process.
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Path Planni.how_it_works: Theta* runs essentially the same as A*, but when considering whether to update a neighbor's parent, it checks not just the current node but also the current node's PARENT -- if there's a clear line-of-sight from the neighbor to the current node's parent (checked via a line-of-sight/raycast test on the grid), the neighbor's parent is set directly to that grandparent (skipping the intermediate node), allowing the path to 'cut corners' at arbitrary angles rather than only at grid-cell boundaries.
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Path Planni.use_when: Generating global paths that will be directly followed (or lightly smoothed) by a controller, where grid-aligned zigzag paths would otherwise need significant smoothing; environments where natural-looking, geometrically-direct paths matter (e.g. paths shown to users, or paths for robots without strict grid-direction constraints).
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Path Planni.avoid_when: Don't use Theta* if your robot's motion is itself constrained to grid-like movements (rare in practice) -- the any-angle benefit is wasted. Also, the line-of-sight checks add per-node computational cost compared to plain A* -- for very large grids or very tight real-time replanning budgets, this overhead may matter, though it's usually modest.
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Path Planni.what_goes_wrong: Line-of-sight checks on a discretized grid are themselves an approximation (typically Bresenham-line-based) -- a line-of-sight check can pass even when the true continuous-space line would graze the corner of an obstacle cell, producing a path that's technically 'collision-free' according to the grid check but uncomfortably close to an obstacle corner in reality; this is usually mitigated by combining Theta* with inflation-layer costs (so 'close to obstacle' is expensive even if not literally colliding).
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Path Planni.real_example: A robot's global plan through an open room shows a sharp zigzag (a sequence of small 45-degree-alternating steps) using standard 8-connected A*, even though a single diagonal line would be shorter and obstacle-free -- switching the global planner to Theta* produces a single straight diagonal segment across the room instead, eliminating both the zigzag and the need for a path-smoother to clean it up before handing the path to the controller.

8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Path Planni.what_it_is: RRT (Rapidly-exploring Random Tree) is a sampling-based path planning algorithm that incrementally builds a tree of valid configurations by repeatedly sampling random points in the configuration space and extending the tree toward them, well-suited to high-dimensional spaces (robot arms with many joints) and continuous, non-grid state spaces where grid search (A*) becomes computationally infeasible.
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Path Planni.why_it_exists: Grid-based search (A*, Dijkstra) scales poorly with dimensionality -- a 6-DOF robot arm's configuration space, even coarsely discretized, has astronomically many grid cells. RRT avoids discretizing the space at all: by randomly sampling configurations and only checking whether short connections between configurations are collision-free, it can find feasible paths in high-dimensional continuous spaces (robot arm motion planning, car-like robots with complex kinematics) where grids are impractical.
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Path Planni.how_it_works: Starting from the initial configuration as the tree's root, repeatedly: (1) sample a random configuration in the space, (2) find the nearest existing tree node to that sample, (3) extend from that node toward the sample by a small step (checking the new edge for collisions), and (4) add the new configuration as a tree node if valid. The tree grows preferentially into unexplored regions (because random samples are more likely to land in large open areas) -- this is the 'rapidly exploring' property. The algorithm terminates when a sample near the goal is reached (or a node within a goal threshold is added), and the path is the tree path from root to that node.
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Path Planni.use_when: High-dimensional or complex configuration spaces -- robot arm motion planning (used heavily in MoveIt), car-like/non-holonomic robots with complex kinematic constraints, or any planning problem where defining a grid is impractical or the space has continuous obstacles that don't discretize cleanly.
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Path Planni.avoid_when: Don't use plain RRT for 2D mobile robot navigation where grid-based A* works fine and gives more predictable, near-optimal paths -- RRT's paths are typically jagged (random tree edges) and far from optimal, requiring post-processing (shortcutting/smoothing). Also, plain RRT provides no optimality guarantee and no convergence guarantee toward an optimal solution even with more time -- if path quality matters, RRT* is the better choice.
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Path Planni.what_goes_wrong: RRT's paths are highly dependent on random sampling -- running the same query twice can produce noticeably different (and differently-suboptimal) paths, which makes RRT-based planners' output non-deterministic and harder to test/debug ('it worked in my test 9 times but failed the 10th'). Also, in environments with narrow passages (e.g. a doorway), RRT's uniform random sampling has low probability of placing samples precisely within the narrow passage, so the tree can take a very long time (or fail within a time budget) to find a path through it -- the 'narrow passage problem'.
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Path Planni.real_example: A robot arm motion planner using RRT successfully plans around a workbench in most test runs, but occasionally (maybe 1 in 20 runs) times out without finding a plan through a narrow gap between two obstacles -- the random sampling rarely places tree-extension samples that thread through the gap; switching to a planner with goal-biasing (sampling toward the goal more often) or RRT-Connect (bi-directional) substantially reduces this failure rate, though doesn't eliminate the fundamental narrow-passage issue.

8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Path Planni.what_it_is: RRT* is a refinement of RRT that, in addition to extending the tree toward random samples, periodically 'rewires' the tree -- reconnecting nearby nodes through newly-added nodes if doing so reduces their cost-from-root -- so that as sampling continues indefinitely, the tree's paths converge toward the asymptotically optimal path, unlike plain RRT which has no such guarantee.
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Path Planni.why_it_exists: Plain RRT finds A feasible path quickly but that path can be far from optimal and stays that way even with more computation time (the tree doesn't improve already-found paths). For applications where path quality matters (shorter/safer/lower-cost paths) and some additional planning time is acceptable, RRT* trades some speed for a path that keeps improving the longer it runs, approaching the true optimum in the limit.
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Path Planni.how_it_works: Like RRT, RRT* samples random configurations and extends the tree -- but for each new node, instead of connecting only to its nearest neighbor, it considers all nodes within a radius and connects to whichever gives the lowest cost-from-root (not just nearest). It then 'rewires': for each nearby existing node, checks whether routing it through the new node would reduce ITS cost-from-root, and if so, changes its parent to the new node. This rewiring step is what allows previously-suboptimal tree branches to be progressively improved as more samples are added.
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Path Planni.use_when: Motion planning where path quality (length, smoothness, clearance) matters and you can afford more planning time than plain RRT -- offline or semi-offline planning for robot arms, or any scenario where 'good enough quickly' (RRT) isn't sufficient but full grid-based optimal search (A*) is impractical due to dimensionality.
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Path Planni.avoid_when: Don't use RRT* for hard real-time replanning with very tight time budgets -- the rewiring step adds computational overhead per iteration, and 'asymptotically optimal' means the guarantees only materialize with enough samples/time; if you must return a plan within milliseconds, plain RRT (or RRT-Connect) returning a feasible-but-suboptimal path quickly may be preferable, possibly with a separate smoothing pass.
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Path Planni.what_goes_wrong: The 'asymptotic' in 'asymptotically optimal' is doing a lot of work -- in practice, with limited time budgets, RRT*'s path quality improvement over plain RRT can be marginal, while its per-iteration cost (nearest-neighbor searches over a radius, rewiring checks) is notably higher, so naive 'just swap RRT for RRT*' migrations sometimes see WORSE wall-clock performance for similar-quality results within the same time budget -- the benefit really shows up only when given substantially more planning time or for offline planning.
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Path Planni.real_example: A team replaces RRT with RRT* in their robot arm planner expecting smoother, shorter paths 'for free', using the same 1-second planning budget -- the resulting paths are only marginally better than before, while planning sometimes times out where plain RRT would have returned a (worse but valid) plan in time; profiling shows the rewiring step's nearest-neighbor radius searches dominate the budget. Increasing the time budget to 3 seconds (acceptable for their non-real-time pick-and-place task) finally shows the expected quality improvement.

8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Path Planni.what_it_is: Bi-directional RRT (commonly RRT-Connect) grows two trees simultaneously -- one rooted at the start configuration, one rooted at the goal configuration -- and alternates extending each tree toward random samples (or toward each other), terminating when the two trees connect, which is typically much faster than single-tree RRT for long paths since both trees explore toward the middle from opposite ends.
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Path Planni.why_it_exists: Single-tree RRT rooted only at the start has to 'discover' the goal region purely through random sampling, which for long paths (start and goal far apart) means a large fraction of samples are 'wasted' extending the tree in directions that don't help reach the goal. Growing a second tree from the goal means both trees are simultaneously searching toward each other, and a connection between them implies a complete path -- this roughly halves the effective distance each tree needs to cover.
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Path Planni.how_it_works: Maintain two trees, T_start and T_goal. On each iteration, sample a random configuration, extend T_start toward it (as in regular RRT), then attempt to extend T_goal toward the newly-added node (often with a more aggressive 'greedy' extension that takes multiple steps if each is collision-free). Swap the roles of T_start/T_goal each iteration (so both grow at similar rates). When an extension from one tree reaches a node already in the other tree (within a connection threshold), the two trees are joined, and the path is the concatenation of the path from start to the connection point and from the connection point to goal.
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Path Planni.use_when: The default choice for RRT-family planning in practice (e.g. MoveIt's default OMPL planner is often RRT-Connect) -- almost always preferable to single-tree RRT for point-to-point planning since the bi-directional search is strictly more sample-efficient for typical problems.
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Path Planni.avoid_when: Don't use bi-directional RRT if the goal isn't a single configuration but a goal REGION or a goal defined implicitly (e.g. 'any configuration satisfying constraint X') -- rooting a tree at 'the goal' requires a concrete starting configuration for that tree, which is awkward for goal regions; single-tree RRT with goal-region sampling, or other planner variants, handle that case more naturally.
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Path Planni.what_goes_wrong: RRT-Connect's greedy multi-step extension toward the other tree can occasionally 'tunnel' through what should be a forbidden region if the collision-checking resolution (step size for collision checks along an edge) is too coarse -- the greedy extension takes larger steps to connect quickly, and if those steps aren't finely checked, a thin obstacle can be 'skipped over'. This is a collision-checking-resolution issue rather than an algorithmic one, but RRT-Connect's greedier extension makes it more likely to manifest than single-step RRT.
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Path Planni.real_example: A motion plan for a robot arm using RRT-Connect occasionally produces a path that, on execution, has the arm's link briefly intersect a thin obstacle (a sensor mount bracket) -- the planner's collision-checking step size along edges was set assuming the obstacle's minimum dimension, but RRT-Connect's greedy extension occasionally takes a single large step whose endpoints are both collision-free while the middle of that step passes through the thin bracket; reducing the collision-check step size (at some planning-time cost) resolves it.

8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Path Planni.what_it_is: PRM (Probabilistic Roadmap) is a sampling-based motion planning approach that, in a preprocessing phase, randomly samples many configurations, connects nearby collision-free pairs into a graph (the 'roadmap'), and then answers individual start-goal queries by connecting start/goal to the roadmap and running a graph search (e.g. Dijkstra/A*) over it -- unlike RRT, which builds a new tree per query, PRM amortizes the sampling cost across many queries on the same static environment.
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Path Planni.why_it_exists: If an environment is static and many planning queries will be made within it (e.g. a robot arm repeatedly planning between different pick/place poses in the same workcell), rebuilding a search tree from scratch for every query (as RRT does) wastes effort -- PRM builds a reusable roadmap once, and subsequent queries are fast graph searches over that roadmap.
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Path Planni.how_it_works: Construction phase: sample many random configurations, discard those in collision, and for each remaining sample, attempt to connect it to nearby samples with a local planner (straight-line, checked for collision); the result is a graph (roadmap) of collision-free configurations and collision-free edges between nearby ones. Query phase: given a start and goal, connect each to the nearest roadmap nodes (if not already in the roadmap), then run a graph search (Dijkstra/A*) over the roadmap to find a path, concatenated with the start/goal connections.
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Path Planni.use_when: Static (or rarely-changing) environments where MANY planning queries will be performed -- e.g. a fixed robot arm workcell planning repeatedly between known pick/place locations, where the one-time roadmap construction cost is amortized over many fast queries.
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Path Planni.avoid_when: Don't use PRM for environments that change frequently between queries (the roadmap becomes invalid and must be rebuilt or repaired, losing the amortization benefit) or for single-query problems where RRT/RRT-Connect's per-query approach is simpler and the roadmap construction overhead isn't justified.
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Path Planni.what_goes_wrong: PRM roadmaps built with insufficient sample density can have 'disconnected components' -- regions of free space that are reachable but not connected to the rest of the roadmap because no sampled nodes happened to bridge a narrow passage between them, causing queries between those regions to fail even though a path obviously exists. Increasing sample density helps but increases construction time and roadmap size (more nodes/edges to search at query time) -- there's a real tradeoff between roadmap quality/coverage and both construction and query cost.
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Path Planni.real_example: A robot arm workcell's PRM roadmap, built once at deployment, works for most pick/place pairs but consistently fails for queries involving one specific bin in the corner of the workspace -- that bin sits behind a narrow gap between two fixtures that the roadmap's sampled nodes never happened to bridge during construction (low sample density in that region). Rebuilding the roadmap with higher sample density (or adding manually-specified 'milestone' configurations near that bin) connects the previously-isolated region.

8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Path Planni.what_it_is: This is a second occurrence -- the earlier 'Global planner' note covered Hybrid A* as a Nav2 planner PLUGIN choice (Smac Hybrid-A*, vs. NavFn, for car-like robots). This note covers the ALGORITHM itself: a search over the continuous (x, y, theta) state space using a discretized grid for the heuristic/duplicate-pruning but continuous-state motion primitives (often Reeds-Shepp or Dubins curves) for actual expansion, guaranteeing kinematically-feasible (drivable) paths.
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Path Planni.why_it_exists: Plain A* on an (x,y) grid produces paths assuming the robot can move in any of 4/8 grid directions and rotate freely -- physically impossible for car-like (Ackermann-steered) vehicles with a minimum turning radius, which can only follow smooth curves consistent with their steering geometry. Hybrid A* extends A* into the 3D state space (x, y, heading) and restricts expansions to motions the vehicle can actually execute, so the resulting path requires no further 'feasibility fixing'.
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Path Planni.how_it_works: Each search node represents a continuous (x, y, theta) pose (not a grid cell). From a node, successor states are generated by applying a small set of feasible motion primitives -- e.g. 'drive forward at max left steering', 'drive forward straight', 'drive forward at max right steering', and analogous reverse motions -- each producing a new continuous pose along an arc consistent with the vehicle's turning radius. For the heuristic and for pruning duplicate/similar states, the continuous pose is mapped onto an underlying discretized grid (so the standard A* priority-queue/visited-set machinery still applies), but the actual path returned is the sequence of continuous motion primitives, which is inherently drivable. A non-holonomic-aware heuristic (e.g. combining a 2D obstacle-aware distance with a Reeds-Shepp-curve distance ignoring obstacles) guides the search efficiently.
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Path Planni.use_when: Any planning problem where the vehicle has a meaningful minimum turning radius and cannot rotate in place -- cars, trucks, large differential-drive robots where in-place rotation is undesirable, trailers. The output path can be handed directly to a path-following controller without a separate feasibility-correction step.
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Path Planni.avoid_when: Don't use Hybrid A* for robots that genuinely can rotate in place and have no minimum-turning-radius constraint (omnidirectional or small differential-drive robots) -- the extra state-space dimension and motion-primitive machinery add computational cost for no benefit; plain grid A* (optionally with Theta* for any-angle paths) suffices.
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Path Planni.what_goes_wrong: The discretization resolution for the (x, y, theta) state space is a delicate tradeoff -- too coarse, and the search may fail to find a path through tight spaces because no combination of motion primitives from the discretized states happens to thread the gap; too fine, and the state space explodes (especially the theta dimension), making search slow. Analytic expansion (periodically trying a direct Reeds-Shepp curve from the current node straight to the goal, ignoring the grid) is often needed to find paths in open areas efficiently, and tuning how often to attempt this is itself a parameter that affects both success rate and planning time.
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Path Planni.real_example: A car-like robot's Hybrid A* planner reliably finds paths in open areas but frequently fails (times out) for goals requiring a parallel-parking-style maneuver into a tight bay -- the theta discretization (e.g. 5-degree bins) means the specific heading angle needed to enter the bay smoothly falls between bins, and no sequence of motion primitives from nearby discretized states happens to align with the bay's opening; finer theta discretization (e.g. 1-degree bins) finds a path but takes substantially longer, illustrating the resolution/success-rate/time tradeoff directly.

8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Path Planni.what_it_is: D* Lite is an incremental search algorithm for environments where edge costs change over time (new obstacles appear, old ones disappear) -- instead of re-running A*/Dijkstra from scratch after every change, D* Lite efficiently repairs the previous solution by only re-examining the parts of the search affected by the change, typically much faster than full replanning for localized changes.
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Path Planni.why_it_exists: Real robots constantly discover new information -- a sensor reveals an obstacle that wasn't on the map, or a previously-blocked area turns out to be clear. Re-running A* from scratch every time the costmap changes (which can be every sensor update) is wasteful, especially on large maps, when most of the map is unchanged. D* Lite (and its predecessors, D* and Focused D*, used famously on the Mars rovers) exploit the fact that small local changes usually only affect a small region of the previously-computed solution.
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Path Planni.how_it_works: D* Lite searches BACKWARD from the goal (so that when the robot moves forward along the path, the existing search results remain valid for the remaining path -- only the portion ahead of the robot, near the change, needs updating). It maintains two cost estimates per node (g and rhs) and a priority queue of 'inconsistent' nodes (where g != rhs); when an edge cost changes, only the directly-affected nodes are marked inconsistent and added to the queue, and the algorithm propagates these updates outward only as far as needed to restore consistency -- nodes far from the change, or 'behind' the robot, are typically untouched.
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Path Planni.use_when: Robots navigating with frequently-updating costmaps from live sensors, where full A* replanning at sensor-update rate would be too slow on large maps -- D* Lite-style incremental replanning keeps the plan responsive to new obstacle information without the cost of full re-search each cycle.
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Path Planni.avoid_when: Don't use D* Lite if the environment changes so drastically/frequently (e.g. the goal itself moves, or huge swaths of the map invalidate at once) that the 'incremental' savings are minimal -- in the worst case (total map change), D* Lite degenerates to roughly the cost of full replanning anyway, with extra bookkeeping overhead. For largely static environments with rare replans, plain A* per replan is simpler and the incremental machinery isn't worth the complexity.
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Path Planni.what_goes_wrong: D* Lite's incremental updates assume the robot's position relative to the search direction is tracked correctly -- if the robot's actual position diverges significantly from where the planner thinks it is (e.g. due to localisation jumps), the 'only update what's near the robot' assumption can leave stale, inconsistent portions of the search graph that produce a plan inconsistent with the robot's true situation until a full replan catches up. Also, implementations that don't bound how much work an incremental update can do per cycle can occasionally take longer than a full replan for a particularly disruptive (large-area) cost change, defeating the purpose.
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Path Planni.real_example: A warehouse robot using D* Lite-based replanning handles a person walking across its path smoothly (small local cost change, quick incremental update, minor path adjustment) -- but when the robot's localisation experiences a sudden jump (e.g. after passing near reflective surfaces that confuse the LiDAR), the incremental update propagates from the wrong assumed position, producing a path that doesn't actually start from the robot's true location; the system has a fallback that triggers a full replan whenever localisation reports a jump larger than a threshold, specifically to handle this D* Lite edge case.

8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Path Planni.what_it_is: Conflict-Based Search (CBS) is a two-level algorithm for the Multi-Agent Path Finding (MAPF) problem -- finding paths for multiple robots from their individual starts to goals such that no two robots collide -- that finds provably OPTIMAL (minimum total cost) solutions by planning each robot independently at first and only adding constraints to resolve conflicts as they're discovered, rather than searching the full joint configuration space upfront.
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Path Planni.why_it_exists: Planning multiple robots' paths jointly in their combined configuration space is exponential in the number of robots (the joint state space is the product of individual state spaces) -- intractable beyond a handful of robots. CBS avoids this by exploiting the fact that robots usually DON'T conflict with each other most of the time -- it's cheaper to plan each robot independently and resolve the relatively few actual conflicts than to reason about all robots jointly from the start.
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Path Planni.how_it_works: The high-level search maintains a 'constraint tree': the root node has each robot plan its own optimal path independently (ignoring other robots) via single-agent search (e.g. A*). These paths are checked for conflicts (two robots occupying the same cell at the same time, or swapping positions). If a conflict is found between robots A and B at time t, the high-level search branches into two children: one where A is constrained to avoid that cell at time t (and A replans), and one where B is similarly constrained (and B replans). This branch-and-resolve continues until a constraint-tree node is found where all robots' individually-replanned paths have NO conflicts -- this is the optimal joint solution, because each branch only adds the minimum necessary constraint.
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Path Planni.use_when: Centralized multi-robot path planning where a small-to-moderate number of robots (CBS scales reasonably to tens of robots in practice, though worst-case exponential in conflicts) need provably collision-free, cost-optimal paths -- e.g. computing optimal pickup/delivery routes for an AMR fleet in a warehouse during low-traffic periods where optimality matters and there's time budget for the search.
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Path Planni.avoid_when: Don't use vanilla CBS for very large fleets (hundreds of robots) or highly dynamic environments needing real-time replanning at high frequency -- the number of conflicts (and thus branches) can grow large, and CBS's optimality guarantee comes at a computational cost that may not fit real-time budgets; bounded-suboptimal variants (e.g. ECBS) or decentralized/priority-based methods (common in production fleet management) trade optimality for speed and scalability.
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Path Planni.what_goes_wrong: CBS's worst-case behavior occurs in densely-conflicting scenarios (e.g. many robots needing to pass through the same narrow corridor or intersection) where the constraint tree can branch enormously -- a fleet management system relying on plain CBS for a busy intersection during peak traffic might see planning time spike unpredictably, potentially exceeding the time available before the next planning cycle, in stark contrast to its fast performance in low-conflict scenarios (e.g. off-peak hours).
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Path Planni.real_example: A warehouse's fleet planner uses CBS to compute optimal paths for 20 AMRs every planning cycle -- during normal operation, most robots' independent shortest paths don't conflict, and CBS resolves the few conflicts (mostly at aisle intersections) quickly. But during a simulated 'rush' scenario where 8 robots all need to pass through the same central junction within a short window, the number of pairwise conflicts and resulting constraint-tree branches grows sharply, and planning time for that cycle exceeds the 1-second budget -- prompting the team to add a fallback to a faster, suboptimal priority-based planner when CBS doesn't return within the time budget.

8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Fleet Manag.what_it_is: Multi-robot coordination challenges are the set of problems that emerge specifically when multiple autonomous robots share a workspace -- collision avoidance between robots (not just static obstacles), traffic congestion at shared resources (intersections, narrow aisles, elevators, charging stations), task allocation (which robot does which job), deadlocks, and communication/coordination overhead that grows with fleet size.
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Fleet Manag.why_it_exists: A single robot's navigation stack (Nav2) treats other robots as just another dynamic obstacle to avoid -- which works for occasional encounters but breaks down at scale: if every robot independently does local obstacle avoidance with no shared awareness, you get gridlock at intersections, robots blocking each other in narrow aisles with neither able to back up, and inefficient use of shared resources like chargers and elevators. Fleet management exists as a coordination LAYER above individual robot navigation specifically to address these multi-robot-specific failure modes.
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Fleet Manag.how_it_works: Coordination approaches range from fully centralized (a fleet manager computes globally-coordinated paths/schedules for all robots, like CBS) to fully decentralized (robots negotiate locally, e.g. via priority rules or local communication) to hybrid (centralized traffic management for shared 'contested' resources like intersections/elevators, decentralized for general navigation). Common mechanisms include traffic 'lanes' or 'zones' with capacity limits, reservation systems for shared resources (an intersection can only be 'reserved' by one robot at a time), and priority schemes (e.g. robots with passengers or time-critical tasks get right-of-way).
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Fleet Manag.use_when: Any deployment with more than a handful of robots sharing a workspace -- the coordination problems below (traffic, deadlock, task allocation) become significant once robot density and shared-resource contention rise above trivial levels.
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Fleet Manag.avoid_when: Don't over-engineer centralized fleet coordination for very small fleets (2-3 robots) in large spaces where conflicts are rare -- the overhead of a fleet management system may not be justified, and simple per-robot collision avoidance plus occasional manual intervention may suffice until the fleet grows.
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Fleet Manag.what_goes_wrong: Coordination systems that work well at small scale can degrade non-linearly as fleet size grows -- a centralized planner that recomputes a full multi-robot plan every cycle might be fast for 5 robots but become a bottleneck at 50; a decentralized priority scheme that resolves conflicts fine for occasional encounters might produce frequent 'priority inversion' deadlocks (low-priority robot blocks a corridor that a high-priority robot needs, but the low-priority robot also can't move because IT is blocked by a third robot) as encounter frequency rises with density.
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Fleet Manag.real_example: A pilot deployment of 5 AMRs in a large warehouse runs smoothly with simple decentralized collision avoidance and first-come-first-served intersection priority -- but when the fleet scales to 30 robots for full production, the same intersections that rarely saw more than one robot at a time during the pilot now regularly have 3-4 robots arriving simultaneously, and the simple priority scheme causes visible 'standoffs' where robots repeatedly yield to each other in a cycle, none making progress, until a proper reservation-based intersection manager (part of a fleet management layer like Open-RMF) is introduced.

8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Fleet Manag.what_it_is: Task allocation is the problem of assigning incoming jobs (e.g. 'move pallet from A to B', 'deliver item to room 305') to specific robots in a fleet -- the two dominant approaches are auction-based (robots 'bid' on tasks based on their own cost-to-complete, and the lowest bidder wins) and optimisation-based (a central solver computes a globally near-optimal assignment considering all robots and tasks at once, e.g. via a min-cost matching or vehicle-routing formulation).
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Fleet Manag.why_it_exists: With multiple robots and multiple pending tasks, the assignment matters a lot for overall fleet efficiency -- naively assigning 'next available robot to next pending task' (FIFO) ignores that a different robot might be much closer to that task, or that a different assignment overall would minimize total travel distance / maximize throughput. Good task allocation is one of the highest-leverage levers for fleet productivity.
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Fleet Manag.how_it_works: Auction-based: when a task becomes available, each idle (or soon-to-be-idle) robot computes its own 'cost' to perform it (e.g. travel time to the pickup location, considering its current position/battery/queue) and submits a bid; the task is awarded to the lowest bidder. This is decentralized, scales well, and adapts naturally as robots' situations change, but doesn't guarantee a globally optimal assignment when many tasks/robots interact (a greedy sequence of locally-optimal auctions can be globally suboptimal). Optimisation-based: formulate the assignment as an optimization problem (e.g. minimize total travel distance, a min-cost bipartite matching for one task per robot, or a full vehicle-routing-problem formulation for multi-task sequences per robot) and solve it centrally, considering many tasks and robots simultaneously -- can find better global solutions but requires more computation and a central coordinator with full fleet visibility.
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Fleet Manag.use_when: Auction-based for highly dynamic environments with frequent task arrivals where decentralization, low latency, and graceful scaling matter more than perfect optimality -- most real-time warehouse operations. Optimisation-based for batch scenarios (e.g. planning a full shift's worth of deliveries in advance) where computing a near-optimal global assignment upfront yields significant efficiency gains and there's time budget for the computation.
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Fleet Manag.avoid_when: Don't use a heavy optimisation-based global solver for highly dynamic, continuously-arriving tasks where the 'optimal' assignment computed at time T is stale by the time it's computed (robots have moved, new tasks arrived) -- the optimization overhead may not pay off if the world changes faster than you can re-solve. Conversely, don't rely purely on greedy auctions for batch/planned work where a modest amount of upfront global optimization could meaningfully reduce total fleet travel.
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Fleet Manag.what_goes_wrong: Pure greedy auction-based allocation can produce 'clustering' inefficiencies -- e.g. the robot closest to task A also happens to be closest to tasks B and C (all in the same area), wins all three auctions sequentially (each time being the lowest bidder), while a robot on the opposite side of the warehouse sits idle, because the auctions were evaluated independently rather than considering that spreading tasks across robots might reduce overall completion time even if each individual assignment looks locally optimal.
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Fleet Manag.real_example: A warehouse fleet using simple per-task auctions notices that during a delivery surge, one robot ends up with a queue of 8 tasks (all won via sequential auctions because it happened to be centrally located) while two other robots sit idle waiting for their next auction -- switching to a batch optimisation approach that considers the queue depth/workload balance across robots (not just per-task travel cost) when 8+ tasks are pending distributes the surge more evenly and reduces the maximum completion time across the fleet.

8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Fleet Manag.what_it_is: Traffic management in narrow aisles addresses the specific problem that many warehouse aisles are too narrow for two robots to pass each other -- so the fleet system must coordinate which robot enters an aisle, in which direction, and ensure no two robots end up facing each other with no room to pass (or, if they do, has a defined resolution protocol).
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Fleet Manag.why_it_exists: Warehouse aisle widths are often designed around shelving and forklift dimensions, not 'two AMRs side by side' -- so aisles are frequently single-lane from the robots' perspective. Without coordination, two robots entering the same aisle from opposite ends will meet in the middle with neither able to pass, requiring one to reverse the entire aisle length (slow, and risky if it can't see behind it well).
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Fleet Manag.how_it_works: Aisles (or aisle segments) are typically modeled as 'lanes' or 'zones' with a capacity (often 1) in the fleet's traffic graph -- a robot must 'reserve' the aisle before entering, and the reservation system denies entry to a second robot from the other end while the aisle is occupied (the second robot waits at the aisle entrance, which is itself in open space where waiting doesn't block others). Some systems support bidirectional aisles with direction reservations (whoever reserves first gets to go, the other waits) or designate certain aisles as one-way during high-traffic periods.
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Fleet Manag.use_when: Any warehouse/facility layout with single-lane aisles and multiple robots that might need to traverse the same aisle -- essentially any multi-robot warehouse deployment; the aisle reservation/zone-capacity mechanism is a core feature of fleet management systems like Open-RMF.
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Fleet Manag.avoid_when: Don't apply heavyweight aisle-reservation machinery to wide aisles where two robots can safely pass side-by-side -- treating every corridor as single-lane unnecessarily serializes traffic that could flow in parallel, reducing overall throughput. Reserve the narrow-aisle protocol for segments that actually need it.
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Fleet Manag.what_goes_wrong: If aisle reservation zones are defined with boundaries that don't match the robot's actual footprint plus safety margins, a robot can be considered 'still in the aisle' (holding the reservation) for longer than expected after it's visually exited, or conversely can enter before fully clearing the previous occupant, causing near-misses right at aisle entrances/exits. Also, if a robot breaks down INSIDE a reserved aisle, the reservation may never be released (depending on how the system detects this), permanently blocking that aisle for other robots until manual intervention.
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Fleet Manag.real_example: A robot experiences a software fault and stops in the middle of a narrow aisle, but its fleet-management 'aisle reservation' remains held (the robot hasn't explicitly released it, and the fleet manager has no separate 'robot is stuck' detection) -- other robots queue at both ends of the aisle indefinitely, unable to enter, until an operator notices the stalled robot on the monitoring dashboard and manually clears its reservation (or physically moves it) to free the aisle for the waiting robots.

8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Fleet Manag.what_it_is: Deadlock in multi-robot systems occurs when two or more robots are each waiting for a resource (space, aisle, intersection) held by another robot in the group, forming a cycle where none can proceed -- deadlock detection identifies such cycles, and resolution breaks them (typically by forcing one robot to back up or reroute, freeing the resource another robot needs).
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Fleet Manag.why_it_exists: Even with good traffic management (aisle reservations, priorities), deadlocks can still emerge from the INTERACTION of multiple local decisions that are each individually reasonable -- e.g. robot A waits for robot B to clear a cell, B waits for C, and C waits for A, forming a cycle (a classic circular-wait deadlock). Without explicit detection and resolution, such a cycle persists forever (or until a timeout-based, often inefficient, fallback like 'everyone backs up randomly').
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Fleet Manag.how_it_works: Detection: the fleet manager (or a distributed protocol) builds a 'wait-for graph' where an edge from robot X to robot Y means 'X is waiting for a resource Y currently holds'; a CYCLE in this graph indicates deadlock. Resolution: once a cycle is detected, the system picks one robot in the cycle (e.g. the one with the lowest priority, or the one for which backing up is cheapest/safest) and commands it to retreat to a position that doesn't hold any resource needed by the cycle, breaking the circular wait -- the other robots can then proceed, and the retreating robot replans afterward.
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Fleet Manag.use_when: Any multi-robot system dense enough that circular-wait situations can arise -- generally needed once fleets exceed a handful of robots operating in a shared space with bottlenecks (intersections, narrow aisles, doorways).
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Fleet Manag.avoid_when: Don't implement complex graph-cycle-detection machinery for very sparse fleets where deadlocks are theoretically possible but practically vanishingly rare -- a simple timeout-based 'if I've been waiting too long, try backing up' heuristic may be adequate at small scale, with proper deadlock detection reserved for denser deployments where such heuristics start causing visible thrashing.
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Fleet Manag.what_goes_wrong: Resolution strategies that don't account for WHERE a robot can safely retreat to can fail -- 'pick the lowest-priority robot in the cycle and back it up' doesn't help if that robot's only retreat space is itself occupied by another robot (possibly not even part of the original cycle), turning a 3-robot deadlock into a 4-robot one. Also, detection latency matters -- if the wait-for graph is only rebuilt periodically (not event-driven), a deadlock can persist for the full detection interval before resolution even begins, which during peak traffic can mean a meaningful chunk of the fleet sits idle.
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Fleet Manag.real_example: Three robots at a Y-shaped intersection end up in a circular wait -- each is positioned such that it's slightly blocking the cell the next robot in the cycle needs, and standard 'yield to higher priority' rules don't resolve it because the priority ordering itself forms a cycle in this configuration (A yields to B, B yields to C, C yields to A, all 'correctly' per pairwise rules). The fleet manager's deadlock detector identifies the 3-cycle in the wait-for graph after a few seconds and commands the lowest-overall-priority robot to back into a side area, breaking the cycle and letting the other two proceed; without this detection, the standard pairwise yield rules alone would never resolve it.

8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Fleet Manag.what_it_is: Open-RMF (Robotics Middleware Framework) is an open-source framework (originally from Open Robotics) for coordinating fleets of heterogeneous robots -- robots from different vendors, running different software stacks -- across shared infrastructure (lifts, doors, traffic lanes) in a building, providing traffic management, scheduling, and a common coordination layer that individual robots' native fleet managers plug into.
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Fleet Manag.why_it_exists: Large facilities (hospitals, airports, warehouses) increasingly deploy robots from MULTIPLE vendors (a cleaning robot from one company, delivery robots from another, each with their own proprietary fleet manager) that all need to share the same physical infrastructure -- elevators, doors, corridors. Without a common coordination layer, each vendor's fleet manager has no visibility into other vendors' robots, leading to conflicts (two different robots' fleets both think they've 'reserved' an elevator). RMF provides a vendor-neutral coordination layer that all fleets interface with.
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Fleet Manag.how_it_works: RMF maintains a 'traffic schedule' -- a shared map of reserved space-time trajectories across all participating fleets -- and negotiates conflicts (two robots' planned paths overlapping in space and time) by adjusting one or both robots' schedules (delaying, rerouting). It manages shared infrastructure as 'doors' and 'lifts' that any fleet's robot can request to use, queuing/coordinating requests across fleets. Each vendor's fleet connects via a 'Fleet Adapter' (translating between RMF's generic API and that vendor's robot API), so RMF doesn't need to know the internals of any specific robot's navigation stack -- just its current state and how to command it via the adapter.
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Fleet Manag.use_when: Multi-vendor robot deployments in shared facilities (a building with robots from 2+ different manufacturers needing to share elevators, doors, corridors); large facilities wanting a building-level 'robot traffic control' layer independent of any single robot vendor's ecosystem.
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Fleet Manag.avoid_when: Don't adopt Open-RMF for a single-vendor, single-fleet deployment where that vendor's own fleet manager already handles all the coordination needs within their own robots -- RMF's value is specifically in MULTI-fleet/multi-vendor coordination and shared-infrastructure arbitration; for a homogeneous fleet, it's additional complexity without a corresponding benefit.
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Fleet Manag.what_goes_wrong: RMF's traffic schedule and negotiation depend on each fleet's Fleet Adapter accurately reporting robot state (position, planned path, current task) -- a fleet adapter with stale or inaccurate state reporting can cause RMF to make scheduling decisions based on wrong information (e.g. thinking a robot has cleared an intersection when it hasn't), leading to the very conflicts RMF is meant to prevent. Also, integrating a new vendor's fleet requires building/configuring a Fleet Adapter for that vendor's specific API, which can be substantial integration work if the vendor's API doesn't map cleanly onto RMF's abstractions (e.g. if the vendor's robots can't report fine-grained position/path information).
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Fleet Manag.real_example: A hospital deploys delivery robots from Vendor A and cleaning robots from Vendor B, both needing to use the same service elevator -- before RMF, each vendor's fleet manager independently 'reserves' the elevator with no knowledge of the other, occasionally resulting in both fleets dispatching a robot to the elevator simultaneously, with one robot blocking the elevator door while the other's robot waits indefinitely (mutual unawareness). After integrating both fleets' adapters with RMF, RMF's lift coordination ensures only one fleet's robot uses the elevator at a time, queuing the other's request.

8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Fleet Manag.what_it_is: A Fleet Adapter is the integration component that connects a specific robot vendor's fleet (with its own native fleet manager and robot API) to Open-RMF's generic coordination layer -- translating RMF's generic commands (go to this location, wait here, use this lift) into that vendor's specific API calls, and translating the vendor's robot state back into RMF's generic state representation.
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Fleet Manag.why_it_exists: RMF needs to coordinate robots from arbitrary vendors without being rewritten for each one -- the Fleet Adapter is the abstraction boundary that makes this possible. By implementing one adapter per vendor (rather than RMF needing native support for every robot platform), any AMR vendor with a documented API (or ROS2 interface) can participate in RMF-coordinated multi-fleet deployments.
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Fleet Manag.how_it_works: A Fleet Adapter implements a defined interface: it must be able to report each robot's current position/state (mapped onto RMF's shared navigation graph), accept 'go to waypoint X' / 'wait' / 'dock' commands from RMF and relay them to the vendor's fleet manager (via REST API, ROS2 topics/actions, or whatever the vendor exposes), and report task completion/progress back to RMF. RMF's 'free fleet' adapter is a generic reference implementation for ROS2-based robots; vendors with proprietary cloud-based fleet managers typically build a custom adapter that calls the vendor's cloud API.
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Fleet Manag.use_when: Onboarding a new robot vendor/fleet into an RMF-coordinated deployment -- this is the required integration work for each distinct robot platform that needs to participate in shared-infrastructure coordination.
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Fleet Manag.avoid_when: Don't attempt a Fleet Adapter integration if the vendor's robot platform can't report position/state with enough fidelity for RMF's traffic scheduling to be meaningful (e.g. a robot that only reports 'idle' or 'busy' with no location) -- in that case, RMF can't make useful scheduling decisions about that fleet's robots, and the integration effort may not yield real coordination benefit until the vendor's API is improved.
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Fleet Manag.what_goes_wrong: A Fleet Adapter that maps the vendor's robot positions onto RMF's navigation graph using a coordinate transform that's slightly off (different origin/scale between the vendor's map and RMF's building-level map) causes RMF to believe robots are in slightly wrong locations -- which can manifest as RMF granting a lift/door reservation to a robot RMF believes has arrived, when the real robot (per the vendor's own coordinates) is still approaching, or vice versa. Calibrating and validating the coordinate transform between each vendor's map and RMF's shared map is a critical, easy-to-get-subtly-wrong integration step.
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Fleet Manag.real_example: During initial RMF integration of a new AMR vendor, robots occasionally get commanded by RMF to 'wait' for a lift that, from the robot's own perspective, it has already passed -- investigation finds the Fleet Adapter's coordinate transform between the vendor's internal map frame and RMF's shared building graph has a small rotational offset, which is negligible in open areas but accumulates to a meaningful position discrepancy near the lift lobby specifically, causing this class of near-miss-but-not-quite scheduling commands; recalibrating the transform using several more reference points near the lift lobby resolves it.

8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Fleet Manag.what_it_is: RMF task scheduling is the layer that accepts high-level task requests (delivery, loop/patrol, cleaning, docking) and assigns/sequences them across the participating fleets, taking into account each fleet's available robots, the shared traffic schedule, and task priorities/deadlines -- distinct from (and built on top of) RMF's lower-level traffic/lift/door coordination.
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Fleet Manag.why_it_exists: In a multi-fleet building, 'who should do this delivery task' isn't just a question for one fleet's internal task allocator (auction/optimization, as covered earlier) -- it may need to consider which FLEET is even capable of/available for the task (not all robots can use all elevators, reach all areas, or perform all task types), and the resulting robot's movements need to be reflected in RMF's shared traffic schedule so other fleets' coordination accounts for it.
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Fleet Manag.how_it_works: A task request (e.g. 'deliver this cart from location A to location B by time T') is submitted to RMF's task system, which determines which fleet(s) have robots capable of and available for the task (based on registered capabilities and current state), dispatches the task to the chosen fleet's adapter (which in turn uses that fleet's own internal task allocation to pick a specific robot), and incorporates the resulting robot's planned route into the shared traffic schedule so other fleets/robots plan around it. RMF supports task types like 'Delivery', 'Loop' (patrol between two points repeatedly), and 'Clean', with a task management/dispatch dashboard for operators.
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Fleet Manag.use_when: Operators need to dispatch building-level tasks (a delivery request from a hospital ward, a scheduled cleaning route) without caring which specific vendor/fleet/robot fulfills it -- RMF's task layer routes the request appropriately and ensures the resulting robot movement is properly coordinated with everyone else's.
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Fleet Manag.avoid_when: Don't route tasks through RMF's building-level task system if a task is entirely internal to one fleet and never interacts with shared infrastructure (e.g. a robot moving within a zone only that fleet uses) -- that fleet's own native task allocation can handle it directly without the extra coordination layer, though it still needs to report its movements to RMF's traffic schedule if it might cross into shared areas.
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Fleet Manag.what_goes_wrong: If a task is dispatched to a fleet whose robot then takes much longer than expected (e.g. stuck in its own internal traffic, or a hardware issue), RMF's traffic schedule for that robot's REMAINING planned route becomes stale/inaccurate, potentially causing other fleets' robots to be scheduled around a route the delayed robot won't actually traverse on time -- requiring RMF to detect significant deviations from planned schedules and re-negotiate, which adds complexity and potential delay propagation across fleets.
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Fleet Manag.real_example: A delivery task dispatched to Fleet A's robot is delayed because that robot's own internal obstacle-avoidance causes it to wait several minutes for a person to clear a doorway -- meanwhile, RMF had scheduled Fleet B's robot to use a shared corridor segment assuming Fleet A's robot would have cleared it by then. When Fleet A's robot is late, RMF detects the schedule deviation and re-negotiates Fleet B's robot's timing (briefly holding it before the corridor) rather than allowing both robots into the same segment simultaneously -- this re-negotiation is the task-scheduling layer's response to a lower-level traffic deviation.

8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Fleet Manag.what_it_is: A fleet monitoring dashboard is the operator-facing visualization showing the live status of every robot in the fleet -- position on a map, current task, battery level, connectivity/health status, and alerts (stuck, error, low battery) -- typically a web UI consuming the fleet management system's state via a real-time data feed (websockets, ROS2 bridge, or a fleet API).
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Fleet Manag.why_it_exists: Fleet operators (and on-site support staff) need situational awareness without being robotics engineers -- 'is everything running normally, and if not, what needs my attention RIGHT NOW' is the core question. A dashboard aggregates per-robot telemetry into a building-level view, surfacing exceptions (robots stuck, low battery, errors) so operators can intervene before small issues (one robot stuck in an aisle) become big ones (a blocked aisle backing up the whole fleet).
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Fleet Manag.how_it_works: Each robot (or its fleet adapter) streams telemetry -- position, battery, task status, diagnostic codes -- to a central service, often via a pub-sub mechanism (ROS2 topics relayed through a web bridge like rosbridge, or a vendor's cloud telemetry API). The dashboard subscribes to this stream and renders robot positions on a building map (often the same map used for navigation), with color-coded status indicators and drill-down views for individual robots (task history, error logs, battery trend). Alerting rules (e.g. 'robot hasn't moved in N minutes while assigned a task' or 'battery below threshold') trigger visual/audible notifications for operators.
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Fleet Manag.use_when: Any production multi-robot deployment needs this for day-to-day operations -- operators monitoring a fleet of even a handful of robots benefit enormously from a single-pane-of-glass view rather than checking each robot individually.
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Fleet Manag.avoid_when: Don't over-invest in elaborate dashboard features (historical analytics, complex KPI breakdowns) before the basics (live position, status, and stuck/error alerts) are solid and trusted by operators -- a dashboard operators don't trust (because it sometimes shows stale/wrong data) gets ignored regardless of how sophisticated its analytics are.
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Fleet Manag.what_goes_wrong: Telemetry staleness is the most common dashboard trust-killer -- if a robot loses network connectivity, its last-reported position 'freezes' on the dashboard, and without a clear 'last updated N seconds ago' / 'offline' indicator, operators may believe the robot is still at that (stale) position and behaving normally, when it's actually moved or stopped responding entirely. Also, alert fatigue -- if minor/transient conditions (e.g. brief Wi-Fi dropouts causing momentary telemetry gaps) trigger the same alert as a genuinely stuck robot, operators learn to ignore alerts, defeating the dashboard's purpose.
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Fleet Manag.real_example: An operator notices on the dashboard that a robot has been 'at' the same position near a charging station for 45 minutes and assumes it's charging normally -- but the robot actually lost Wi-Fi connectivity 40 minutes ago (after leaving the charging station and resuming its route) and the dashboard is showing its LAST KNOWN position before the dropout, with no 'offline' indicator distinguishing 'stationary and fine' from 'stale data'. Adding a clear staleness indicator (greying out/flagging robots with telemetry older than a threshold) prevents this kind of misread.

8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Fleet Manag.what_it_is: Predictive maintenance uses ongoing robot telemetry (motor currents, battery health metrics, error/fault frequencies, vibration, temperature, wheel odometry vs. actual displacement discrepancies) to forecast component failures BEFORE they happen, scheduling maintenance proactively rather than reactively (fix after breakdown) or on a fixed calendar schedule (which may be too early or too late for a given unit).
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Fleet Manag.why_it_exists: Reactive maintenance (fix it when it breaks) means unplanned downtime -- a robot failing mid-shift in a busy aisle, requiring emergency intervention and potentially blocking other robots. Calendar-based preventive maintenance (replace every N months regardless of actual wear) wastes good components and still doesn't catch failures that occur faster than the schedule assumes. Predictive maintenance uses the actual condition/usage data each robot generates to schedule maintenance individually, ideally right before a component would fail, minimizing both unplanned downtime and unnecessary part replacement.
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Fleet Manag.how_it_works: Robots continuously log operational telemetry (motor current draw, which can indicate increasing friction/wear; battery charge/discharge curves, which degrade characteristically as cells age; frequency of specific error codes; vibration/IMU signatures that change as bearings wear). This telemetry is aggregated centrally and analyzed -- simple approaches use threshold/trend-based rules (e.g. 'flag if motor current for a given motion has increased >15% over baseline'), while more sophisticated approaches train models on historical telemetry-to-failure data to predict remaining-useful-life or failure probability, surfacing robots needing attention on the fleet dashboard before they actually fail.
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Fleet Manag.use_when: Fleets large enough that unplanned downtime has meaningful operational cost, and where enough operating history/telemetry exists (or can be collected) to establish meaningful baselines and trends -- predictive maintenance value scales with fleet size and operating hours.
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Fleet Manag.avoid_when: Don't invest in sophisticated predictive-maintenance ML models before you have reliable telemetry collection and a reasonable volume of historical data (including failure events) to learn from -- without labeled failure history, model-based prediction has nothing to learn from; start with simple threshold/trend-based alerting on key metrics and grow into ML as data accumulates.
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Fleet Manag.what_goes_wrong: Threshold-based alerts calibrated on one robot model/configuration often don't transfer to a different model or even a different unit with different load patterns -- a motor-current threshold tuned for robots in a flat warehouse may trigger false positives for robots on a site with ramps (genuinely higher current draw, not wear), or miss real wear on the flat-warehouse robots if the threshold was set loosely to avoid those false positives. Also, telemetry gaps (a robot offline for a period) can create blind spots in trend analysis that aren't always obviously flagged as 'missing data' vs. 'no issue detected'.
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Fleet Manag.real_example: A fleet's predictive-maintenance system flags a spike in a robot's drive-motor current draw and schedules a maintenance check -- inspection finds a wheel bearing beginning to fail, caught and replaced during a scheduled maintenance window rather than failing mid-shift. Months later, a different robot at a second site (with a ramp section in its route) triggers the SAME current-draw threshold constantly, generating maintenance alerts for a perfectly healthy robot -- the threshold, calibrated at the flat first site, didn't account for the ramp's inherently higher current draw, requiring per-site (or per-route-profile) threshold calibration.

8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Fleet Manag.what_it_is: Battery management and charging coordination covers how a fleet decides WHEN each robot should go charge (based on battery level, current task queue, and predicted task durations), WHERE (which of potentially several charging stations, considering availability and travel distance), and how charging is SEQUENCED across the fleet to avoid all robots needing to charge simultaneously (which would halt operations) or chargers sitting unused while robots run low.
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Fleet Manag.why_it_exists: A robot that runs out of battery mid-task stops wherever it is -- potentially blocking an aisle, an intersection, or a doorway, and requiring manual recovery (push it to a charger or swap its battery). Conversely, a robot that charges too eagerly (going to charge at 70% battery 'just in case') spends time charging instead of working, reducing fleet throughput. Coordinating charging across the fleet -- not just per-robot battery thresholds -- ensures enough robots are always available for tasks while none run critically low.
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Fleet Manag.how_it_works: Each robot reports battery state of charge; the fleet manager tracks this alongside each robot's current task queue and estimates remaining task time vs. remaining battery. When a robot's battery drops below a threshold (often dynamically adjusted based on current workload -- lower threshold during low-demand periods, higher during peak when a robot going offline is costlier), it's scheduled to navigate to an available charging station, chosen based on proximity and current charger occupancy (the fleet manager tracks charger availability as a shared resource, similar to the elevator/door reservation concept). Some fleets stagger charging proactively -- e.g. during low-demand overnight periods, deliberately rotating robots through chargers so that during the next high-demand period, all robots start with high charge.
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Fleet Manag.use_when: Any battery-powered robot fleet -- charging coordination is essentially mandatory once a fleet has more robots than charging stations (the typical case) and needs to maintain continuous operation across shifts.
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Fleet Manag.avoid_when: Don't apply complex predictive charging-scheduling for very small fleets with abundant charging infrastructure (e.g. 3 robots, 3 dedicated chargers, low utilization) -- simple per-robot threshold-based charging ('go charge below 20%') is sufficient when contention for chargers isn't a real constraint.
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Fleet Manag.what_goes_wrong: Static battery thresholds that don't account for a robot's CURRENT location relative to chargers can strand a robot -- a robot at 20% battery on the far side of a large facility from the nearest charger may not make it, especially if its remaining task involves climbing a ramp (higher power draw) or it gets delayed by traffic coordination en route. Also, 'everyone charges at the same threshold' policies can cause clustering -- if demand patterns mean many robots cross the threshold around the same time (e.g. after a busy period), multiple robots converge on a limited number of chargers simultaneously, with some waiting in queues, defeating the purpose of proactive charging.
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Fleet Manag.real_example: During a busy afternoon, several robots that started their shift around the same charge level all cross the 'go charge' threshold within a short window, converging on the facility's 4 charging stations -- 3 robots end up waiting in a queue for a charger while only 1 charges, effectively taking 4 robots out of the active fleet (1 charging + 3 waiting) during a high-demand period. The fix is staggering charging thresholds slightly per-robot (or scheduling proactive charging during the preceding lull) so robots don't all hit the threshold simultaneously.

8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Fleet Manag.what_it_is: Fleet KPI tracking aggregates per-robot and fleet-wide metrics -- uptime/availability (percentage of time a robot is operational and not in error/maintenance), throughput (tasks completed per hour, per robot and fleet-wide), and idle time (time robots spend neither performing a task nor charging, i.e. 'available but unused') -- into reports and dashboards that quantify fleet performance and efficiency over time.
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Fleet Manag.why_it_exists: Operations and business stakeholders need to answer questions like 'is this fleet delivering the ROI we expected', 'are we under- or over-provisioned (too many/few robots for the workload)', and 'is performance degrading over time (more downtime, slower task completion)'. Raw telemetry (individual robot positions/states) doesn't directly answer these -- KPIs are the aggregated, business-relevant summaries computed from that telemetry.
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Fleet Manag.how_it_works: Each robot's state transitions (idle, executing task, charging, error/down) are logged with timestamps; KPIs are computed by aggregating time spent in each state over a period (e.g. 'uptime % = (total time - error/down time) / total time'), counting completed tasks per unit time, and computing idle time as time in 'idle, available' state specifically (distinct from charging, which is 'unavailable but necessary'). Dashboards typically show these per-robot (to spot underperforming units) and fleet-wide (to spot systemic issues -- e.g. fleet-wide idle time rising might indicate task allocation isn't keeping robots busy, not that robots are individually broken).
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Fleet Manag.use_when: Ongoing fleet operations management -- tracking these KPIs over time helps justify fleet sizing decisions, identify degrading robots (declining individual uptime), and identify task-allocation/workflow inefficiencies (high fleet-wide idle time despite a full task queue suggests an allocation problem, not a capacity problem).
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Fleet Manag.avoid_when: Don't treat a single snapshot of these KPIs as meaningful without context -- 'idle time' is expected and healthy during genuinely low-demand periods (overnight), so idle-time KPIs need to be considered relative to demand, not as an absolute target to minimize at all costs (which could push toward overworking the fleet during low-demand periods 'to look busy').
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Fleet Manag.what_goes_wrong: Idle time and uptime can be misleading in opposite directions if 'idle' and 'charging' aren't clearly distinguished -- a robot that spends a lot of time charging might show LOW 'idle' time (looking efficient) while actually being unavailable for tasks a similar fraction of the time as a robot with high 'idle' time but low charging time; without separating these, comparing robots' efficiency on 'idle time' alone can favor the wrong robot. Also, 'tasks per hour' as a sole throughput metric can be gamed/misleading if task complexity varies -- a robot doing many short trips looks more 'productive' by this metric than one doing fewer long trips, even if the long-trip robot is moving more total volume.
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Fleet Manag.real_example: A monthly fleet report shows Robot 7 has the lowest 'idle time' in the fleet and is highlighted as the 'most efficient' unit -- but a deeper look shows Robot 7 also has the highest 'charging time' (its battery degraded faster than other units, requiring more frequent charging), and its actual TASK throughput (tasks per hour) is below fleet average; its low 'idle time' simply reflects that it's either working or charging almost constantly, not that it's particularly productive. The team adds 'tasks per hour' and 'charging time %' alongside 'idle time' in the report to avoid this kind of misleading single-metric ranking.

8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Fleet Manag.what_it_is: WMS (Warehouse Management System) integration connects the robot fleet's task dispatch to the facility's existing inventory/order-management software -- so that when the WMS determines 'pallet X needs to move from location A to location B' (as part of fulfilling an order, replenishing stock, etc.), that requirement is automatically translated into a robot task without manual re-entry.
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Fleet Manag.why_it_exists: The WMS is the system of record for WHAT needs to happen in the warehouse (orders, inventory locations, pick lists) -- it existed before robots and continues to drive overall warehouse operations. The robot fleet is one of potentially several execution mechanisms (alongside human workers) for fulfilling WMS-generated tasks. Without integration, someone would have to manually read WMS tasks and manually dispatch equivalent robot tasks -- error-prone and defeating much of the automation's value.
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Fleet Manag.how_it_works: Integration typically happens via an API (REST, or a message queue) between the WMS and the fleet management system: the WMS sends task requests (pickup location, dropoff location, item/order references, priority/deadline) to the fleet manager's task API, which then handles robot assignment, routing, and execution as covered elsewhere (task allocation, traffic management). Completion (and failure) status flows back to the WMS so it can update order status, trigger the next step in a fulfillment workflow, or flag exceptions for human follow-up. Location references need a shared mapping -- the WMS's location identifiers (e.g. 'Aisle 12, Bay 3, Level 2') must map to the fleet's navigation graph waypoints/coordinates.
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Fleet Manag.use_when: Any robot deployment intended to handle WMS-driven tasks (which is most material-movement automation in warehouses) -- this integration is typically a prerequisite for the robots to be useful for real operational workflows rather than demo/manual-dispatch-only usage.
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Fleet Manag.avoid_when: Don't build a deep, tightly-coupled WMS integration before validating the robot fleet's core navigation/task-execution reliability in a simpler, manually-dispatched mode -- debugging is much harder when issues could originate in either system, and a fragile robot fleet integrated into a production WMS can create operational problems (stuck orders) beyond just 'robot didn't move'.
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Fleet Manag.what_goes_wrong: Location-mapping mismatches between WMS location identifiers and the fleet's navigation graph are a common integration failure point -- if the WMS is updated with a new storage location (e.g. a new shelf added) but the fleet's navigation graph/waypoint mapping isn't updated correspondingly, tasks referencing that location either fail outright or (worse) get mapped to the WRONG nearby waypoint, causing the robot to go to an incorrect (but valid-looking) location. Also, error/failure feedback loops matter -- if a robot task fails (e.g. couldn't reach the location due to a blocked aisle) and this isn't properly communicated back to the WMS, the WMS may consider the task 'in progress' indefinitely, with the corresponding order stuck.
8|⚪ T3 Navigation & Planning|Fleet Manag.real_example: A WMS adds a new pick location during a warehouse reorganization, but the fleet's location-mapping table (translating WMS location codes to navigation waypoints) isn't updated as part of the same change process -- the next order referencing that location either errors out (if the fleet rejects unknown location codes) or, in a worse case discovered later, maps to a similarly-named OLD location that's now used for something else, causing the robot to retrieve the wrong pallet. The fix involves both correcting the immediate mapping and establishing a process (or automated sync) so location changes in the WMS automatically propagate to the fleet's location mapping.

8|⚪ T3 Sensors & ML on Robots|Sensor Int.what_it_is: LiDAR (Light Detection And Ranging) sensors measure distance by emitting laser pulses and timing their return after reflecting off surfaces, producing either a 2D 'scan' (a fan of distance readings at fixed angular increments in a single plane, common on ground robots for obstacle avoidance and 2D SLAM) or a 3D 'point cloud' (a dense set of (x,y,z) points covering a volume, common on autonomous vehicles and robots needing full 3D scene understanding).
8|⚪ T3 Sensors & ML on Robots|Sensor Int.why_it_exists: LiDAR provides direct, accurate metric distance measurements independent of lighting conditions (unlike cameras, which struggle in darkness or glare) and with much higher angular resolution and range than ultrasonic sensors. This makes it the workhorse sensor for obstacle detection, mapping, and localisation in mobile robotics -- the geometric accuracy of LiDAR data is what makes algorithms like AMCL, slam_toolbox, and Nav2 costmaps work reliably.
8|⚪ T3 Sensors & ML on Robots|Sensor Int.how_it_works: 2D LiDAR (e.g. Hokuyo, SICK, RPLidar) spins or sweeps a single laser beam through a plane, publishing a `sensor_msgs/LaserScan` with an array of ranges at known angle increments -- consumed directly by costmaps and 2D SLAM. 3D LiDAR (e.g. Velodyne, Ouyang, Livox) uses multiple laser channels across a vertical field of view, producing `sensor_msgs/PointCloud2` messages; processing typically involves downsampling (voxel grid filters to reduce point count), ground-plane removal (segmenting floor points from obstacle points), and clustering (grouping points into discrete objects) before the data feeds into 3D SLAM, obstacle avoidance, or object detection pipelines.
