8|⚪ T3 Sensors & ML on Robots|Sensor Int.use_when: 2D LiDAR is the standard choice for indoor ground robots operating in a roughly planar environment (warehouses, offices) where 2D costmaps and 2D SLAM are sufficient and cost matters. 3D LiDAR is needed when the environment has 3D structure relevant to navigation (overhanging obstacles, ramps, outdoor terrain, multi-level reasoning) or when feeding perception pipelines that need full 3D geometry.
8|⚪ T3 Sensors & ML on Robots|Sensor Int.avoid_when: Don't reach for 3D LiDAR by default -- it's significantly more expensive, generates much higher data volumes (requiring more compute for processing), and is often unnecessary for robots operating on a single flat level where 2D LiDAR plus a depth camera (for overhangs) covers the need at lower cost and complexity.
8|⚪ T3 Sensors & ML on Robots|Sensor Int.what_goes_wrong: LiDAR can miss certain materials -- glass and highly reflective or very dark/matte black surfaces can absorb or redirect the laser, returning no reading or incorrect ranges, creating 'holes' in scans/point clouds that downstream obstacle-avoidance code may not handle (treating a glass wall as open space). Mounting height matters too -- a 2D LiDAR mounted at a height that happens to be below a table's surface but above the floor will miss table legs or low obstacles entirely, a common real-world surprise when robots are first deployed in a new environment.
8|⚪ T3 Sensors & ML on Robots|Sensor Int.real_example: A warehouse robot using a single 2D LiDAR mounted ~20cm above the floor navigates fine in open aisles but repeatedly bumps into low pallet edges that sit below the LiDAR's scan plane -- the fix involves either adding a second LiDAR at a different height, adding ultrasonic/depth sensors for low obstacles, or accepting the blind spot and relying on slow speeds plus bump sensors as a last-resort safety layer.

8|⚪ T3 Sensors & ML on Robots|Sensor Int.what_it_is: Depth cameras produce an image where each pixel encodes distance from the camera, in addition to (or instead of) standard RGB color -- common consumer/robotics models include Intel RealSense (uses active stereo or structured light, e.g. D435/D455) and Stereolabs ZED (passive stereo using two RGB cameras, computing depth via stereo matching).
8|⚪ T3 Sensors & ML on Robots|Sensor Int.why_it_exists: Depth cameras give dense, per-pixel 3D information over a 2D field of view -- something neither 2D LiDAR (sparse, single plane) nor RGB cameras alone (no direct depth) provide -- at much lower cost than 3D LiDAR. This makes them well suited for close-range 3D perception tasks: detecting objects on a table for manipulation, identifying overhanging obstacles, or building local 3D obstacle representations for navigation.
8|⚪ T3 Sensors & ML on Robots|Sensor Int.how_it_works: Active depth cameras (RealSense) project an infrared pattern (structured light) or use IR stereo with an active IR projector to compute depth even in textureless scenes and low light, publishing both an RGB image and a depth image (often as `sensor_msgs/Image` with depth encoded, plus optionally a `PointCloud2`). Passive stereo cameras (ZED) compute depth purely from matching features between left and right RGB images, similar to human binocular vision -- this works well in textured, well-lit scenes but degrades on blank walls or in darkness (no active illumination). Depth images are commonly converted to point clouds or projected into costmaps for navigation.
8|⚪ T3 Sensors & ML on Robots|Sensor Int.use_when: Useful for short-to-medium range (typically 0.2m-10m) 3D perception where dense depth matters -- detecting and localising objects for manipulation, populating 3D costmap layers with depth-derived obstacles, or providing input to ML perception models (object detection + depth for 3D bounding boxes).
8|⚪ T3 Sensors & ML on Robots|Sensor Int.avoid_when: Don't rely on depth cameras as the primary sensor for long-range navigation obstacle detection (their range is much shorter than LiDAR, and active IR depth cameras can be unreliable outdoors in direct sunlight, which washes out the IR pattern) -- pair them with LiDAR for range-critical navigation and use depth cameras for close-range/manipulation tasks.
8|⚪ T3 Sensors & ML on Robots|Sensor Int.what_goes_wrong: Active IR depth cameras (RealSense) often fail or produce very noisy depth outdoors in bright sunlight because ambient IR overwhelms the projected pattern -- a robot tuned and tested indoors can have its depth-based obstacle detection effectively stop working when taken outside. Passive stereo (ZED) has the opposite issue -- it fails on low-texture surfaces (blank walls, uniform floors) where stereo matching can't find correspondences, producing holes or noisy depth in exactly the large flat regions common in indoor environments.
8|⚪ T3 Sensors & ML on Robots|Sensor Int.real_example: A robot's manipulation pipeline uses a RealSense camera to detect and localise objects on a table, working reliably in the lab -- when deployed near a window with strong sunlight, the depth stream becomes mostly noise during certain times of day, and the manipulation pipeline starts failing to detect objects it could see fine an hour earlier. The team adds a check on depth image quality (validity ratio of returned depth pixels) to detect this degraded-lighting condition and either pause or fall back to RGB-only detection with a fixed working-distance assumption.

8|⚪ T3 Sensors & ML on Robots|Sensor Int.what_it_is: RGB cameras capture standard color images; camera calibration is the process of determining a camera's intrinsic parameters (focal length, principal point, lens distortion coefficients) that describe how 3D points in the world project onto 2D pixels -- without calibration, measurements derived from images (object size, position, distance estimates) are inaccurate, and image distortion (especially from wide-angle lenses) goes uncorrected.
8|⚪ T3 Sensors & ML on Robots|Sensor Int.why_it_exists: Any task that converts pixel coordinates into real-world measurements -- estimating an object's position relative to the robot, projecting LiDAR points onto a camera image for sensor fusion, or computing stereo depth -- requires knowing the camera's intrinsic geometry. Calibration is what turns a raw image into a geometrically meaningful measurement device.
8|⚪ T3 Sensors & ML on Robots|Sensor Int.how_it_works: Calibration is typically done using a known pattern (checkerboard or AprilTag grid) photographed from multiple angles; software (e.g. the ROS `camera_calibration` package, OpenCV's calibration routines) detects the pattern's corners in each image and solves for the intrinsic matrix (focal lengths fx/fy, principal point cx/cy) and distortion coefficients (radial and tangential) that best explain the observed corner positions. The result is published/stored as a `CameraInfo` message (intrinsics + distortion model) alongside the image topic, which downstream nodes use to undistort images or perform accurate 3D projections.
8|⚪ T3 Sensors & ML on Robots|Sensor Int.use_when: Required for any application doing geometric reasoning from images -- visual SLAM (ORB-SLAM3), AprilTag/fiducial-based localisation, stereo depth computation, projecting 3D points (LiDAR, costmap obstacles) onto camera images for visualization or sensor fusion, and any object-distance estimation from a single camera.
8|⚪ T3 Sensors & ML on Robots|Sensor Int.avoid_when: If a camera is used purely for human monitoring/visualization (a video feed an operator watches) with no downstream geometric computation, formal calibration is unnecessary -- though even then, severe lens distortion can make a feed harder to interpret, so light correction may still help.
8|⚪ T3 Sensors & ML on Robots|Sensor Int.what_goes_wrong: Using a camera's `CameraInfo` from a different unit of the 'same model' (assuming all units of a camera model share identical intrinsics) introduces systematic errors -- manufacturing variation means each physical camera has slightly different intrinsics, and small errors compound in downstream geometric calculations (e.g. AprilTag-based pose estimates being consistently off by a few centimeters/degrees). Also, recalibration is needed if a lens is refocused or the camera is physically bumped/disassembled, since this changes the intrinsics -- a calibration done once at setup can silently go stale.
8|⚪ T3 Sensors & ML on Robots|Sensor Int.real_example: A fleet of identical robots ships with a single shared `camera_info.yaml` calibration file copied to all units (calibrated on unit #1) to save setup time -- AprilTag-based docking works fine on unit #1 but other units consistently dock with a small (~2cm) offset, traced back to per-unit intrinsic variation; the fix is calibrating each physical camera individually rather than sharing one calibration file across units.

8|⚪ T3 Sensors & ML on Robots|Sensor Int.what_it_is: An IMU (Inertial Measurement Unit) combines an accelerometer (measures linear acceleration along 3 axes, including gravity) and a gyroscope (measures angular velocity around 3 axes), and often a magnetometer (measures magnetic heading); 'fusion' here refers to the basic sensor-level combination of accelerometer and gyroscope data to estimate orientation (roll/pitch/yaw) -- e.g. via a complementary filter or Madgwick/Mahony filter -- which is distinct from the higher-level multi-sensor fusion (IMU + LiDAR + odometry + GPS) covered in the SLAM & Localisation note.
8|⚪ T3 Sensors & ML on Robots|Sensor Int.why_it_exists: Neither sensor alone gives reliable orientation: gyroscopes are accurate over short timescales but drift (integration error accumulates, so orientation estimates wander over time even when the device is stationary), while accelerometers can determine the gravity-aligned tilt (roll/pitch) at rest but are noisy and corrupted by linear acceleration during motion (can't distinguish 'tilted' from 'accelerating'). Combining them -- gyroscope for short-term accuracy, accelerometer for long-term drift correction toward 'down' -- gives a stable, accurate orientation estimate.
8|⚪ T3 Sensors & ML on Robots|Sensor Int.how_it_works: A complementary filter blends the two estimates in the frequency domain: it trusts the gyroscope-integrated orientation for fast changes (high frequency) and trusts the accelerometer-derived tilt for slow changes (low frequency, since gravity direction is reliable when averaged over time), typically via a simple weighted combination (e.g. `orientation = alpha * gyro_integrated + (1-alpha) * accel_derived`). More sophisticated approaches (Madgwick, Mahony filters) achieve a similar effect with better tuning and lower computational cost, commonly running directly on the IMU's onboard processor, publishing a `sensor_msgs/Imu` message with orientation, angular velocity, and linear acceleration already populated.
8|⚪ T3 Sensors & ML on Robots|Sensor Int.use_when: Any robot needing orientation estimation (roll/pitch for stability monitoring on uneven terrain, yaw/heading as input to localisation) -- IMUs are cheap, high-rate, and provide data even when other sensors (camera, LiDAR) are degraded, making them a near-universal component of mobile robot sensor suites.
8|⚪ T3 Sensors & ML on Robots|Sensor Int.avoid_when: Don't rely on raw IMU yaw (heading) for long-duration absolute heading without correction from another source (magnetometer, GPS heading, or SLAM) -- gyroscope drift means yaw estimates degrade over time even with a good complementary/Madgwick filter; roll/pitch are generally fine long-term (gravity reference doesn't drift) but yaw needs an external reference.
8|⚪ T3 Sensors & ML on Robots|Sensor Int.what_goes_wrong: IMU data quality is highly sensitive to vibration -- a robot with a poorly damped IMU mount on a vibrating chassis (e.g. rough wheels, vibrating motors) gets accelerometer readings dominated by vibration noise, which corrupts both the tilt estimate and any downstream fusion that weights the accelerometer for drift correction. Also, magnetometers (when present) are notoriously sensitive to nearby ferrous metal and electrical currents -- an IMU mounted near a robot's drive motors or battery can report a heading that's consistently off by tens of degrees due to local magnetic interference, a problem that often only appears once the IMU is installed in its final position on the real robot (not on a test bench).
8|⚪ T3 Sensors & ML on Robots|Sensor Int.real_example: A robot's IMU is bench-tested and shows clean, stable orientation -- but after final assembly, its heading estimate drifts erratically whenever the drive motors are under load, traced to magnetic interference from motor current near the IMU's magnetometer. The team either relocates the IMU farther from the motors, shields it, or disables the magnetometer entirely and relies on gyroscope+wheel-odometry for heading instead.

8|⚪ T3 Sensors & ML on Robots|Sensor Int.what_it_is: Wheel odometry estimates a robot's position and orientation change over time by integrating wheel rotation measurements from encoders (sensors that count wheel revolutions/fractions) -- a form of 'dead reckoning' (estimating current position from a known starting point plus measured movement, without external reference).
8|⚪ T3 Sensors & ML on Robots|Sensor Int.why_it_exists: Odometry provides a continuous, high-rate, low-latency estimate of robot motion using sensors the robot already needs for motor control (encoders), without requiring external infrastructure (no need for a map, GPS, or visual features) -- making it the baseline motion estimate that other localisation methods (AMCL, EKF fusion) correct and refine, and the fallback when other sensors temporarily fail.
8|⚪ T3 Sensors & ML on Robots|Sensor Int.how_it_works: Each wheel's encoder reports rotation (ticks per revolution, converted to distance via wheel radius); for a differential-drive robot, left and right wheel distances are combined with the wheelbase (distance between wheels) to compute the robot's linear and angular displacement over a time step, which is integrated over time to produce a continuously updated pose estimate (x, y, theta) published as `nav_msgs/Odometry`. The math is straightforward kinematics, but it assumes wheels roll without slipping.
8|⚪ T3 Sensors & ML on Robots|Sensor Int.use_when: Essentially universal for wheeled mobile robots -- odometry is typically the primary input to the `odom` frame in the tf tree and a key input to EKF-based localisation fusion, providing smooth, high-rate relative motion estimates between the lower-rate corrections from AMCL/SLAM.
8|⚪ T3 Sensors & ML on Robots|Sensor Int.avoid_when: Don't trust raw wheel odometry alone for absolute position over any meaningful duration or distance -- errors accumulate without bound (drift), so odometry-only navigation will have the robot's believed position diverge increasingly from its true position the longer/farther it travels.
8|⚪ T3 Sensors & ML on Robots|Sensor Int.what_goes_wrong: Wheel slip is the dominant error source -- on smooth/wet/loose surfaces, or during sharp turns, wheels can slip or skid, causing the encoders to register rotation that doesn't correspond to actual robot displacement; this error is NOT zero-mean and accumulates systematically (e.g. consistently underestimating distance on a slippery floor). Uneven floor (small bumps, thresholds) and tire deformation/wear also introduce systematic calibration errors in the effective wheel radius, causing odometry to drift consistently in one direction (e.g. always estimating slightly less distance than actual) until recalibrated.
8|⚪ T3 Sensors & ML on Robots|Sensor Int.real_example: A robot's odometry-based position estimate drifts noticeably over a long shift, requiring more frequent AMCL corrections than expected -- investigation finds the facility recently changed flooring (smoother tile replacing carpet in one area), causing more wheel slip during turns on the new surface; the wheel odometry calibration (effective wheel radius/wheelbase) that was tuned on the old flooring no longer matches, and recalibrating against the new surface reduces the drift back to expected levels.

8|⚪ T3 Sensors & ML on Robots|Sensor Int.what_it_is: GPS (Global Positioning System, or more generally GNSS -- Global Navigation Satellite System, including GLONASS, Galileo, BeiDou) provides absolute position estimates (latitude/longitude/altitude) by triangulating signals from orbiting satellites, used for outdoor robot localisation where indoor methods (SLAM-based maps, AMCL) don't apply.
8|⚪ T3 Sensors & ML on Robots|Sensor Int.why_it_exists: Indoor localisation methods (SLAM, AMCL against a pre-built map) don't scale to large outdoor environments -- there's no practical way to pre-map a farm field, a delivery route across a city, or a large outdoor industrial site at the resolution needed, and GPS/GNSS provides a globally-referenced absolute position without needing any pre-existing map, making it the foundation for outdoor robot navigation (delivery robots, agricultural robots, drones).
8|⚪ T3 Sensors & ML on Robots|Sensor Int.how_it_works: A GNSS receiver computes its position from timing signals received from multiple satellites (at least 4 needed for a 3D fix); standard consumer-grade GPS has accuracy of several meters, which is too coarse for precise navigation (e.g. staying within a 1m-wide path). RTK (Real-Time Kinematic) GPS uses a fixed base station with known position to compute and broadcast correction signals, improving accuracy to centimeter-level -- common on agricultural and precision outdoor robots. GPS data is published (often as `sensor_msgs/NavSatFix`) and typically converted to a local Cartesian frame (e.g. via `robot_localization`'s `navsat_transform_node`) before being fused with odometry/IMU in an EKF for a continuous local pose estimate.
8|⚪ T3 Sensors & ML on Robots|Sensor Int.use_when: Outdoor robots operating across areas too large to pre-map with SLAM, or where absolute global positioning (not just relative/local consistency) matters -- agricultural robots following GPS-defined field boundaries, delivery robots navigating city blocks, outdoor security robots patrolling large perimeters.
8|⚪ T3 Sensors & ML on Robots|Sensor Int.avoid_when: Don't rely on GPS for indoor or GPS-denied environments (warehouses, tunnels, urban canyons with tall buildings blocking/reflecting signals, dense forest) -- GPS signals are blocked or severely degraded (multipath reflections off buildings can cause large position errors), and these environments need SLAM/AMCL or other localisation methods instead.
8|⚪ T3 Sensors & ML on Robots|Sensor Int.what_goes_wrong: GPS accuracy degrades significantly near tall structures (urban canyon effect) -- reflected signals (multipath) can cause position jumps of many meters, and a robot navigating near buildings may see its GPS-derived position suddenly jump, causing erratic path-following or the EKF fusion to distrust GPS at exactly the moments it's needed. Also, RTK GPS requires a base station with a clear sky view and a communication link (radio or cellular) to the rover -- if this link drops (out of range, interference), RTK falls back to standard GPS accuracy (meters) without necessarily making this degradation obvious to downstream consumers expecting centimeter accuracy.
8|⚪ T3 Sensors & ML on Robots|Sensor Int.real_example: An outdoor delivery robot using RTK GPS navigates precisely along sidewalks in open areas, but near a row of tall buildings its position estimate jumps by several meters intermittently, causing it to veer toward the street -- the EKF fusion is tuned to trust GPS heavily (since it's normally centimeter-accurate), so it doesn't sufficiently discount these multipath-corrupted readings; the fix involves either detecting GPS quality degradation (e.g. via the receiver's reported fix quality/HDOP) and dynamically reducing GPS trust in the fusion filter near known problem areas, or relying more on odometry+IMU through those segments.

8|⚪ T3 Sensors & ML on Robots|Sensor Int.what_it_is: Ultrasonic sensors measure distance by emitting a high-frequency sound pulse and timing its echo return, providing simple, low-cost proximity detection -- typically short-range (a few cm to a few meters) with a wide, cone-shaped detection beam rather than the narrow, precise beams of LiDAR.
8|⚪ T3 Sensors & ML on Robots|Sensor Int.why_it_exists: Ultrasonic sensors are cheap, simple, and -- critically -- can detect materials that LiDAR struggles with, such as glass (transparent to light but reflects sound) and certain dark/matte surfaces that absorb laser light. This makes them a useful complementary safety sensor, particularly for close-range obstacle detection (bumpers) where LiDAR's minimum range or blind spots leave gaps.
8|⚪ T3 Sensors & ML on Robots|Sensor Int.how_it_works: A transducer emits an ultrasonic pulse (typically 40kHz) and measures the time until the echo returns, computing distance from the speed of sound; the sensor reports a single distance value (or 'object within range / not' for simple versions) for its entire beam cone, which is much wider (often 15-30 degrees or more) than a single LiDAR beam -- meaning an ultrasonic sensor can't distinguish WHERE within its cone an object is, only that something is within range somewhere in that cone.
8|⚪ T3 Sensors & ML on Robots|Sensor Int.use_when: Best as a low-cost, close-range safety/bumper layer -- detecting imminent collisions with glass doors, low obstacles outside a LiDAR's field of view, or as a redundant final safety check before contact, especially on lower-cost robots where a full sensor suite isn't economical.
8|⚪ T3 Sensors & ML on Robots|Sensor Int.avoid_when: Don't use ultrasonic sensors as a primary navigation or mapping sensor -- their wide beam and limited range/resolution make them unsuitable for building maps or precise localisation; they're a coarse proximity/safety sensor, not a geometry sensor.
8|⚪ T3 Sensors & ML on Robots|Sensor Int.what_goes_wrong: Ultrasonic sensors can suffer from cross-talk when multiple units are mounted close together and fire simultaneously or in quick succession -- one sensor's emitted pulse can be picked up by a neighboring sensor's receiver, producing false readings. Also, soft/sound-absorbing materials (foam, fabric, carpet at shallow angles) can absorb the sound pulse and return weak or no echo, causing missed detections -- the opposite failure mode from LiDAR (which struggles with optically transparent/absorptive materials but handles sound-absorptive ones fine).
8|⚪ T3 Sensors & ML on Robots|Sensor Int.real_example: A robot with an array of ultrasonic sensors around its perimeter (for close-range bump avoidance) works fine in testing with sensors firing one at a time, but when the firing rate is increased for faster response, adjacent sensors start producing erratic readings -- diagnosed as cross-talk between neighboring sensors; the fix involves either firing sensors in a staggered/non-adjacent pattern or using sensors with coded/distinguishable pulse signatures.

8|⚪ T3 Sensors & ML on Robots|Sensor Int.what_it_is: Force/torque (F/T) sensors measure the forces and torques (typically along/around all 3 axes -- 6 degrees of freedom total) applied at a point, most commonly mounted at a robot arm's wrist between the arm and the end-effector (gripper/tool), enabling the robot to sense contact forces during manipulation rather than relying purely on position control.
8|⚪ T3 Sensors & ML on Robots|Sensor Int.why_it_exists: Pure position-controlled manipulation (move the arm to exact coordinates) is brittle -- any small error in the target object's actual position/size relative to what the robot expects results in either missing the object or, worse, colliding with it forcefully (since position control will keep 'pushing' toward the commanded position regardless of resistance). F/T sensing lets the robot detect contact and respond -- stopping, adjusting position, or modulating grip force -- enabling robust manipulation despite real-world uncertainty in object pose, size, and compliance.
8|⚪ T3 Sensors & ML on Robots|Sensor Int.how_it_works: An F/T sensor (often using strain gauges arranged to decompose applied loads into 3 force and 3 torque components) sits between the robot's wrist and the end-effector, publishing a `geometry_msgs/WrenchStamped` message (forces in x/y/z, torques about x/y/z) at high rate. Control software uses this feedback for tasks like 'move down until contact is detected' (insertion/placement tasks), 'apply a target grip force' (delicate object handling), or 'comply with external forces' (admittance/impedance control, where the robot yields to applied forces rather than rigidly resisting).
8|⚪ T3 Sensors & ML on Robots|Sensor Int.use_when: Manipulation tasks involving contact with uncertain or variable environments -- peg-in-hole insertion, assembly tasks requiring controlled force application, handling objects of unknown/variable rigidity, or any task where collision detection via force feedback (rather than just vision) improves safety and success rate.
8|⚪ T3 Sensors & ML on Robots|Sensor Int.avoid_when: Don't add F/T sensing for simple pick-and-place of well-characterized rigid objects in well-calibrated positions where pure position control with a basic gripper (open/close, optionally with simple current-based grip-force limiting on the gripper motor itself) is sufficient -- F/T sensors add cost, wiring complexity, and require careful calibration/zeroing (accounting for the end-effector's own weight, which the sensor also measures).
8|⚪ T3 Sensors & ML on Robots|Sensor Int.what_goes_wrong: F/T sensor readings include the weight and inertia of whatever is attached beyond the sensor (gripper, held object) -- if this isn't properly compensated for (a calibration step that subtracts the end-effector's own gravitational and inertial contribution from raw readings), the 'force' signal used for contact detection is contaminated by the end-effector's own weight changing with arm orientation, causing false contact detections or missed real contacts depending on orientation. Also, F/T sensors can saturate or be damaged by forces exceeding their rated range -- a control bug that doesn't stop on an unexpectedly hard collision can drive forces past the sensor's limits.
8|⚪ T3 Sensors & ML on Robots|Sensor Int.real_example: A robot arm's 'move down until contact' insertion task works correctly when the arm is vertical, but fails (triggering false 'contact detected' partway through the motion) when the same task is attempted with the arm at an angle -- the gravity-compensation calibration for the F/T sensor's gravity-load model was done only for the vertical orientation, so at other orientations the gripper's own weight contributes an uncompensated force component that the contact-detection threshold misinterprets as external contact; the fix is a proper full-pose gravity compensation model (accounting for end-effector weight at any arm orientation) rather than a single fixed offset.

8|⚪ T3 Sensors & ML on Robots|Sensor Int.what_it_is: The `sensor_msgs` package defines the standard ROS2 message types for raw sensor data -- `LaserScan` (2D range readings from LiDAR/laser rangefinders), `PointCloud2` (3D point data from 3D LiDAR, depth cameras, or stereo), `Image` (raw or compressed camera images), and `Imu` (orientation, angular velocity, linear acceleration from an IMU) -- providing a common interface that lets sensor drivers and consuming algorithms interoperate regardless of specific hardware.
8|⚪ T3 Sensors & ML on Robots|Sensor Int.why_it_exists: Without standardized message types, every sensor driver would define its own data format, and every algorithm (SLAM, costmaps, perception) would need custom code per sensor model. `sensor_msgs` types let any LiDAR driver publish `LaserScan` and any 2D SLAM algorithm subscribe to `LaserScan`, regardless of whether the underlying hardware is a Hokuyo, SICK, or RPLidar -- this standardization is what makes the ROS ecosystem's plug-and-play composability (swap sensors, reuse algorithms) possible.
8|⚪ T3 Sensors & ML on Robots|Sensor Int.how_it_works: `LaserScan` contains an array of range values plus angle_min/angle_max/angle_increment (defining the scan geometry) and range_min/range_max (valid range bounds), with a header specifying the frame and timestamp. `PointCloud2` is a more complex, flexible binary-encoded format describing an array of points with arbitrary fields (x, y, z, intensity, RGB, etc.) defined by a `PointField` array, allowing it to represent many different point cloud structures efficiently. `Image` contains raw pixel data (with an encoding field specifying format -- rgb8, mono16, etc.) plus width/height/step, or `CompressedImage` for JPEG/PNG-compressed data to save bandwidth. `Imu` contains orientation (as a quaternion), angular velocity, and linear acceleration, each with an associated covariance matrix expressing measurement uncertainty -- used directly by fusion algorithms (EKF/UKF) that need to weight sensor inputs by confidence.
8|⚪ T3 Sensors & ML on Robots|Sensor Int.use_when: Any time you're writing a sensor driver (publish data in the appropriate `sensor_msgs` type so existing tools/algorithms can consume it) or writing an algorithm that consumes raw sensor data (subscribe to the standard type so it works with any compliant sensor driver) -- these are the foundational interchange formats for the entire perception/navigation stack.
8|⚪ T3 Sensors & ML on Robots|Sensor Int.avoid_when: Don't invent custom message types for data that fits an existing `sensor_msgs` type, even if your specific sensor has extra capabilities -- publish the standard type for compatibility with existing tools (RViz2, costmaps, SLAM), and if needed, publish additional sensor-specific data on a SEPARATE topic with a custom message type, rather than replacing the standard one.
8|⚪ T3 Sensors & ML on Robots|Sensor Int.what_goes_wrong: Covariance fields in `Imu` (and other messages) are often left as all-zeros by sensor drivers (meaning 'unknown'), but some fusion algorithms (robot_localization's EKF) interpret all-zero covariance as 'perfect confidence' rather than 'unknown', causing the filter to over-trust that sensor -- a driver that doesn't populate realistic covariance values can silently break fusion tuning that assumes covariances reflect actual sensor noise. Also, frame_id and timestamp consistency matters enormously -- a `PointCloud2` published with an incorrect frame_id (or a frame_id that doesn't have a valid tf transform to the robot's base frame at the message's timestamp) will either fail to transform (dropped silently by some nodes) or be transformed incorrectly, producing points that appear in the wrong place.
8|⚪ T3 Sensors & ML on Robots|Sensor Int.real_example: A team integrates a new IMU whose driver publishes `sensor_msgs/Imu` with all covariance fields zeroed (the driver author didn't bother characterizing the sensor's noise) -- when fed into `robot_localization`'s EKF alongside wheel odometry, the EKF (interpreting zero covariance as 'trust this completely') weights the IMU far more heavily than intended, and the IMU's small heading drift dominates the fused odometry's heading, causing the robot's believed orientation to drift faster than with odometry alone. The fix is populating the IMU driver's covariance fields with realistic values (from the datasheet or empirical characterization) so the EKF weights it appropriately.

8|⚪ T3 Sensors & ML on Robots|ML on Robo.what_it_is: Running real-time object detection models (commonly YOLO -- You Only Look Once -- variants like YOLOv8/YOLOv11) directly on a robot's onboard compute ('edge' hardware -- e.g. NVIDIA Jetson, Intel NUC with iGPU) using the robot's own camera feed, to identify and localise objects (people, pallets, products, obstacles) in real time for navigation, manipulation, or monitoring.
8|⚪ T3 Sensors & ML on Robots|ML on Robo.why_it_exists: Many robot tasks require knowing not just 'is there an obstacle' (which LiDAR/depth handles) but WHAT it is -- a person (requiring more cautious behavior/right-of-way), a specific product (for picking), a docking marker, or a forklift (different traffic rules). Cloud-based inference is too slow (latency) and unreliable (network dependency) for real-time robot control, so detection must run on the robot itself -- 'on the edge'.
8|⚪ T3 Sensors & ML on Robots|ML on Robo.how_it_works: A YOLO model (pretrained on a general dataset like COCO, or fine-tuned on robot-specific imagery) processes camera frames and outputs bounding boxes with class labels and confidence scores in real time (often 15-60+ FPS depending on model size and hardware). On edge devices, models are typically optimized for the target hardware (quantization, TensorRT conversion -- covered separately) to hit real-time frame rates within the device's power/compute budget. Detections feed into downstream logic -- e.g. a 'person detected in path' triggers a navigation behavior change, or a 'product X detected' triggers a manipulation routine.
8|⚪ T3 Sensors & ML on Robots|ML on Robo.use_when: Robots that need semantic understanding of their surroundings beyond geometry -- safety systems that behave differently around people vs. equipment, picking/sorting robots identifying specific items, robots needing to read signage/markers, or any application where 'what is this object' matters for the robot's decision-making.
8|⚪ T3 Sensors & ML on Robots|ML on Robo.avoid_when: Don't add vision-based object detection as a SAFETY-CRITICAL sole input for collision avoidance -- detection models have non-zero miss rates (especially for unusual poses, occlusion, lighting) and should supplement, not replace, geometric obstacle detection (LiDAR/depth-based) for hard safety guarantees; use detection for behavioral decisions (slow down near detected people) layered on top of geometric safety stops.
8|⚪ T3 Sensors & ML on Robots|ML on Robo.what_goes_wrong: Models trained on general datasets (COCO) often underperform on robot-specific viewpoints and conditions -- COCO images are mostly taken at human eye-level with good lighting, while a robot's camera might be mounted low, looking up at people, in a warehouse with very different lighting/occlusion patterns (people partially hidden behind shelving, motion blur from the robot's own movement) -- detection accuracy can be substantially worse than benchmark numbers suggest until fine-tuned on robot-perspective data. Also, real-time constraints can force a tradeoff toward smaller/faster models with lower accuracy, and if frame rate drops below what the control loop expects (e.g. detection runs at 5fps but the safety system expects updates at 10fps), a person could move into a blind window between detections.
8|⚪ T3 Sensors & ML on Robots|ML on Robo.real_example: A robot's person-detection model, trained on standard COCO data, performs well in benchmark testing but in the actual warehouse misses people who are partially occluded by shelving or who are bending down to pick from a low shelf (poses underrepresented in COCO) -- the team collects and labels robot-perspective images from the actual deployment site showing these specific occlusion/pose patterns and fine-tunes the model, substantially improving real-world detection rate for these cases.

8|⚪ T3 Sensors & ML on Robots|ML on Robo.what_it_is: TensorRT is NVIDIA's inference optimization library and runtime that converts trained neural network models into highly optimized engines for NVIDIA GPUs -- including the Jetson family (Orin, Xavier, Nano) of embedded AI computers commonly used on robots -- applying optimizations like layer fusion, precision reduction (FP16/INT8 quantization), and kernel auto-tuning for the specific target GPU.
8|⚪ T3 Sensors & ML on Robots|ML on Robo.why_it_exists: A model trained in PyTorch/TensorFlow and run with the standard framework runtime on a Jetson's embedded GPU is often far too slow for real-time robotics (e.g. running at 3-5 FPS when 15-30 FPS is needed) -- general-purpose framework runtimes aren't optimized for the specific, resource-constrained embedded GPU architecture. TensorRT closes this gap, often providing 2-5x+ speedups (sometimes more with INT8 quantization) by compiling the model specifically for the deployed hardware.
8|⚪ T3 Sensors & ML on Robots|ML on Robo.how_it_works: A trained model (typically exported to ONNX first) is fed to TensorRT's builder, which analyzes the network graph and produces an optimized 'engine' -- a serialized, hardware-specific execution plan with fused operations (combining multiple layers into single GPU kernels), reduced-precision computation (FP16 halves memory/compute vs FP32 with minimal accuracy loss; INT8 quantization can roughly double throughput again but requires calibration data to maintain accuracy), and kernel selections tuned for the specific GPU's capabilities. The resulting engine is loaded at runtime for inference -- but engines are tied to the specific TensorRT version, GPU architecture, and sometimes the specific precision/batch configuration used during the build, so they must be rebuilt if any of these change.
8|⚪ T3 Sensors & ML on Robots|ML on Robo.use_when: Any time a model needs to run at real-time frame rates on Jetson (or other NVIDIA embedded/edge GPUs) and the out-of-the-box framework runtime isn't fast enough -- which is the common case for vision models (detection, segmentation) on robots.
8|⚪ T3 Sensors & ML on Robots|ML on Robo.avoid_when: Don't invest in TensorRT optimization during early model development/iteration -- the conversion process (and especially INT8 calibration) adds friction to the iterate-train-test loop; develop and validate model accuracy with the standard framework runtime first, then convert to TensorRT once the model architecture is finalized for deployment.
8|⚪ T3 Sensors & ML on Robots|ML on Robo.what_goes_wrong: TensorRT engines are NOT portable across different Jetson hardware generations or even different TensorRT/JetPack software versions -- an engine built on a development Jetson Orin with JetPack 5.1 will typically fail to load (or need rebuilding) on a deployed fleet running a slightly different JetPack version, which becomes an operational headache for fleets with hardware/software version drift across units. Also, INT8 quantization can silently degrade accuracy for specific classes or edge cases not well-represented in the calibration dataset -- overall mAP might look fine while a specific important class (e.g. a particular safety-relevant object) sees disproportionate accuracy loss.
8|⚪ T3 Sensors & ML on Robots|ML on Robo.real_example: A team builds and validates a TensorRT-optimized detection model on their development Jetson Orin, then deploys the same `.engine` file to the robot fleet -- some fleet units (running a slightly older JetPack/TensorRT version due to staggered update rollout) fail to load the engine at startup with a version-mismatch error. The fix is either standardizing JetPack versions across the fleet before deployment, or building/shipping per-version engines (or building the engine on first boot on each device from a portable ONNX model) as part of the deployment pipeline.

8|⚪ T3 Sensors & ML on Robots|ML on Robo.what_it_is: ONNX (Open Neural Network Exchange) is an open, framework-agnostic format for representing trained neural network models -- a model trained in PyTorch, TensorFlow, or another framework is exported to ONNX, then run using an ONNX Runtime (which supports various hardware backends -- CPU, various GPUs, NPUs) on the target embedded system, decoupling the training framework from the deployment runtime.
8|⚪ T3 Sensors & ML on Robots|ML on Robo.why_it_exists: Training frameworks (PyTorch, TensorFlow) are optimized for research/training workflows, not necessarily for lean deployment on resource-constrained embedded hardware -- they have large dependencies and aren't always available or efficient on every embedded platform. ONNX provides a portable intermediate representation: train in whatever framework is convenient, export once to ONNX, and deploy using a lightweight runtime appropriate to the target hardware (which might be a Jetson via TensorRT, an Intel-based embedded PC via OpenVINO, or a generic ARM board via ONNX Runtime's CPU execution provider) -- without needing the full training framework on the robot.
8|⚪ T3 Sensors & ML on Robots|ML on Robo.how_it_works: Export functions in PyTorch (`torch.onnx.export`) or TensorFlow trace the model's computation graph and serialize it in the ONNX format (a standardized graph of operators with weights). On the embedded system, ONNX Runtime loads this graph and executes it using an 'execution provider' appropriate to the hardware -- CPU (works everywhere, baseline performance), CUDA/TensorRT (NVIDIA GPUs, for acceleration), OpenVINO (Intel hardware), or others -- allowing the same ONNX file to run (with varying performance) across different hardware via different runtime backends.
8|⚪ T3 Sensors & ML on Robots|ML on Robo.use_when: When deploying models across heterogeneous hardware (different robot platforms with different compute, or as an intermediate step before hardware-specific optimization like TensorRT), or when you want to avoid shipping full training-framework dependencies (PyTorch + CUDA toolkit, often gigabytes) to a lean embedded deployment image.
8|⚪ T3 Sensors & ML on Robots|ML on Robo.avoid_when: Don't treat ONNX export as guaranteed to 'just work' for any model -- some custom operations, dynamic control flow, or framework-specific layers don't have direct ONNX equivalents and either fail to export or require custom operator implementations in the target runtime; complex/novel model architectures should be export-tested early, not assumed exportable late in development.
8|⚪ T3 Sensors & ML on Robots|ML on Robo.what_goes_wrong: ONNX export can silently produce a model that behaves slightly differently from the original -- subtle differences in how operations like batch normalization, padding, or interpolation are implemented between the training framework and ONNX Runtime's execution providers can cause small numerical differences that occasionally matter (e.g. a model with a sharp decision boundary near its threshold). Also, opset version mismatches (ONNX itself has versioned operator sets) between the exporting framework and the target runtime can cause 'unsupported operator' errors that only appear at deployment time on the embedded device, not during export on the development machine if the dev machine happens to have a newer ONNX Runtime that supports the operator.
8|⚪ T3 Sensors & ML on Robots|ML on Robo.real_example: A model exports successfully from PyTorch to ONNX and runs correctly when tested with ONNX Runtime on a development laptop (which has a recent ONNX Runtime version) -- but fails to load on the robot's embedded ONNX Runtime (an older version bundled with the robot's OS image) with an 'unsupported operator' error for an operation that was added to ONNX in a later opset version. The fix involves either exporting with an older target opset version (re-export with `opset_version=` set to match the deployment runtime) or updating the embedded ONNX Runtime version, and adding an export+load test against the ACTUAL deployment runtime version to the CI pipeline.

8|⚪ T3 Sensors & ML on Robots|ML on Robo.what_it_is: Semantic segmentation classifies every pixel in an image into a category (floor, wall, person, shelf, obstacle, drivable-vs-not), producing a dense per-pixel labeling of the scene -- as opposed to object detection's sparse bounding boxes, segmentation gives full scene coverage, useful for understanding traversable space and scene layout.
8|⚪ T3 Sensors & ML on Robots|ML on Robo.why_it_exists: Object detection answers 'where are these specific object instances' but doesn't characterize the rest of the scene -- segmentation answers 'what is every part of what I'm looking at', which is valuable for tasks like determining drivable floor area (vs. walls/clutter), distinguishing different surface types (a robot might behave differently on a ramp vs. flat floor, identifiable via segmentation), or building richer semantic maps that combine geometry (where things are) with meaning (what they are).
8|⚪ T3 Sensors & ML on Robots|ML on Robo.how_it_works: Segmentation models (e.g. architectures like DeepLab, SegFormer, or lighter real-time variants for embedded deployment) take an image and output a same-resolution map where each pixel has a class label, typically via an encoder-decoder architecture that downsamples for feature extraction then upsamples back to full resolution for pixel-level classification. For robotics, segmentation output is often projected into 3D (combined with depth) to create a semantically-labeled point cloud or costmap layer -- e.g. marking floor-classified regions as traversable and everything else as a potential obstacle, independent of whether that obstacle was in any training set's object categories.
8|⚪ T3 Sensors & ML on Robots|ML on Robo.use_when: Scene understanding tasks where 'everything that isn't floor is an obstacle' style reasoning is valuable (handling arbitrary/novel obstacles that a fixed object-detection class list wouldn't recognize), or where surface-type distinction matters for behavior (different speed/caution on different surface types), or for building richer semantic maps for human-robot interaction (a robot describing 'I'm near the kitchen counter').
8|⚪ T3 Sensors & ML on Robots|ML on Robo.avoid_when: Don't use segmentation as the primary geometric obstacle-avoidance signal where simpler depth/LiDAR-based geometric obstacle detection suffices and is more reliable -- segmentation is computationally heavier than basic geometric processing and its 'floor vs not-floor' boundary can be less precise at distance/edges than direct depth measurements; segmentation adds semantic richness on top of, not instead of, geometric safety layers.
8|⚪ T3 Sensors & ML on Robots|ML on Robo.what_goes_wrong: Segmentation models trained on one type of flooring/environment can misclassify novel floor textures or transitions as obstacles (or vice versa) -- a model trained on smooth warehouse concrete might misclassify a textured rubber mat or a floor-level yellow safety stripe as a non-floor obstacle, causing the robot to unnecessarily avoid perfectly traversable areas. Class boundaries at a distance also get blurry -- segmentation accuracy degrades for distant/small regions in the image, so 'floor vs obstacle' classification near the horizon of the camera's view is less reliable than for nearby regions, which matters if the segmentation is used for longer-range planning.
8|⚪ T3 Sensors & ML on Robots|ML on Robo.real_example: A robot's segmentation-based traversability map works well in the area where its training images were collected, but in a newly added section of the warehouse with a different (textured, anti-slip) floor coating, the segmentation model classifies large patches of this new floor as 'not floor', causing the robot to treat traversable area as obstacles and take unnecessarily long detours -- the fix requires collecting and labeling images of the new floor type and fine-tuning/retraining the segmentation model to include it as a recognized 'floor' variant.

8|⚪ T3 Sensors & ML on Robots|ML on Robo.what_it_is: Monocular (single-camera) depth estimation uses ML models to predict per-pixel depth from a single RGB image -- without stereo cameras or active depth sensors -- by learning visual cues (object size, perspective, texture gradients, learned scene priors) that correlate with distance, providing a depth-like signal for obstacle avoidance from cameras that don't have dedicated depth hardware.
8|⚪ T3 Sensors & ML on Robots|ML on Robo.why_it_exists: Dedicated depth sensors (stereo cameras, LiDAR, structured light) add cost, have their own limitations (range limits, lighting sensitivity, sparse data), and aren't present on every camera a robot might have. ML-based monocular depth estimation extracts useful distance information from ordinary RGB cameras that robots often already have for other purposes (object detection), providing a supplementary or fallback obstacle-distance signal without additional hardware.
8|⚪ T3 Sensors & ML on Robots|ML on Robo.how_it_works: A depth estimation model (e.g. architectures derived from MiDaS, DPT, or newer foundation depth models) is trained on datasets with paired RGB images and ground-truth depth (from LiDAR or stereo, used only during training) to predict a depth map from RGB input alone at inference time. The output is typically RELATIVE depth (correct ordering/relative distances) rather than precisely calibrated metric depth unless specifically trained/calibrated for metric output -- relative depth is often sufficient for 'is this getting closer' obstacle-avoidance reasoning even without exact distances.
8|⚪ T3 Sensors & ML on Robots|ML on Robo.use_when: Supplementing obstacle detection on cameras without dedicated depth sensors, providing a depth-like signal for vision-based navigation research, or as a redundant/fallback obstacle cue when primary depth sensors (stereo, active IR) are degraded (e.g. active IR depth failing in bright sunlight, where a monocular RGB-based depth model might still provide useful relative-depth signal).
8|⚪ T3 Sensors & ML on Robots|ML on Robo.avoid_when: Don't rely on monocular depth estimation as a primary, safety-critical obstacle-distance measurement where ACCURATE METRIC distance matters (e.g. 'stop within 0.5m') -- monocular depth is fundamentally ambiguous (the same image could correspond to many different actual 3D scenes) and even good models have meaningful metric error; use it for relative/qualitative obstacle awareness, not precise distance-based safety stops.
8|⚪ T3 Sensors & ML on Robots|ML on Robo.what_goes_wrong: Monocular depth models can be fooled by scenes that violate the visual cues they learned -- a flat image or picture of a scene (e.g. a poster on a wall depicting a hallway) can be estimated as having depth/distance corresponding to the depicted scene rather than the actual flat wall, since the model is reasoning from learned visual patterns, not actual geometry. Similarly, reflective surfaces (mirrors, glass) can produce depth estimates corresponding to the REFLECTED scene rather than the actual surface distance.
8|⚪ T3 Sensors & ML on Robots|ML on Robo.real_example: A robot using monocular depth estimation as a supplementary obstacle cue approaches a wall with a large framed photograph of an outdoor scene -- the depth model, trained on real scenes, estimates significant depth/distance into the 'scene' depicted in the photograph rather than recognizing it as a flat wall a short distance away, briefly causing the supplementary depth signal to disagree sharply with the LiDAR-based geometric reading (which correctly shows a nearby flat surface); since the system weights LiDAR more heavily for actual stopping decisions, this doesn't cause a collision, but it's logged as an anomaly worth being aware of when interpreting monocular depth in environments with flat imagery/displays.

8|⚪ T3 Sensors & ML on Robots|ML on Robo.what_it_is: Human pose estimation uses ML models to detect people in camera images and estimate the positions of their body joints (head, shoulders, hands, etc.), producing a skeleton-like representation -- in robotics, used for safety applications like determining if a person is reaching toward a robot, lying down (fallen), or in a posture that indicates they're working close to/under equipment.
8|⚪ T3 Sensors & ML on Robots|ML on Robo.why_it_exists: Simple person DETECTION (bounding box: 'a person is here') doesn't capture posture/intent -- a person standing well away facing another direction poses a different risk than a person bending down with their hand extended toward the robot's workspace. Pose estimation provides finer-grained information about what a person is DOING, enabling more nuanced safety responses (slow down vs. full stop) than binary presence detection.
8|⚪ T3 Sensors & ML on Robots|ML on Robo.how_it_works: Pose estimation models (e.g. OpenPose-style or newer transformer-based models) detect keypoints (joint locations) for each detected person in an image, often also inferring skeletal connections between them. In robotics safety contexts, this might be combined with depth/3D information to determine not just 'this person has their hand extended' in 2D image space, but whether that hand is within some 3D distance of the robot's workspace -- triggering a safety response (reduced speed, pause, or stop) calibrated to the assessed risk level rather than a uniform response to any detected person.
8|⚪ T3 Sensors & ML on Robots|ML on Robo.use_when: Collaborative robot (cobot) applications where robots and humans share workspace and nuanced, posture-aware safety responses improve both safety and productivity (vs. a uniform 'stop whenever any person is detected nearby', which can make the robot unusably slow in busy human environments) -- or any application where understanding human posture/activity informs robot behavior (e.g. a robot waiting for a person to finish a task before proceeding).
8|⚪ T3 Sensors & ML on Robots|ML on Robo.avoid_when: Don't use pose-estimation-based safety responses as a REPLACEMENT for certified safety systems (light curtains, certified safety-rated LiDAR with defined protective fields, e-stops) in industrial settings with regulatory safety requirements -- vision-based pose estimation is a behavioral/efficiency layer that can make the robot MORE considerate around people, but certified hardware safety systems remain the basis for guaranteed safety stops.
8|⚪ T3 Sensors & ML on Robots|ML on Robo.what_goes_wrong: Pose estimation degrades for partially occluded people (common in cluttered industrial environments -- a person's lower body hidden behind a shelf) and can produce unstable/jittery keypoint estimates frame-to-frame, especially for fast movements or unusual postures (crouching, lying down -- exactly the postures most relevant for 'has someone fallen' safety checks, and which are underrepresented in typical pose-estimation training data which skews toward standing/walking poses). A safety system reacting to jittery pose estimates can produce inconsistent behavior (slowing/speeding repeatedly) that's both inefficient and potentially confusing to nearby humans.
8|⚪ T3 Sensors & ML on Robots|ML on Robo.real_example: A cobot's pose-estimation-based safety system works reliably for standing workers but fails to recognize a worker who has crouched down to pick something up from a low shelf near the robot -- the pose model, trained predominantly on standing/walking poses, produces low-confidence/unstable keypoints for the crouching posture, and the safety logic (which required a minimum confidence to trigger the 'person nearby, slow down' response) doesn't reliably trigger; the team adds crouching/low-posture examples to the training data and also adds a confidence-independent fallback (any detected person-shaped blob within a minimum 3D distance triggers caution, regardless of pose confidence).

8|⚪ T3 Sensors & ML on Robots|ML on Robo.what_it_is: Reinforcement learning (RL) for robot navigation trains a policy (neural network mapping sensor observations to motion commands) through trial-and-error interaction with an environment, using a reward signal (e.g. progress toward goal, penalty for collisions) -- Isaac Lab is NVIDIA's GPU-accelerated robot learning framework (built on Isaac Sim) that enables running thousands of parallel simulated environments simultaneously, dramatically speeding up the RL training process.
8|⚪ T3 Sensors & ML on Robots|ML on Robo.why_it_exists: Classical navigation (Nav2's planners/controllers) relies on explicit geometric models and tuned parameters; RL offers an alternative -- learning navigation behaviors directly from experience, potentially handling situations (dynamic crowds, unusual terrain) that are hard to hand-engineer rules for. RL's notorious sample inefficiency (needing millions of interactions to learn) made it impractical for real robots (can't crash a real robot millions of times) -- Isaac Lab's massively parallel GPU simulation (thousands of simultaneous simulated robot instances) compresses what would be years of real-world experience into hours/days of simulated training.
8|⚪ T3 Sensors & ML on Robots|ML on Robo.how_it_works: A navigation task is defined with an observation space (e.g. LiDAR scan, goal direction/distance, robot velocity), an action space (e.g. linear/angular velocity commands), and a reward function (positive for progress toward goal, negative for collisions/excessive time). Isaac Lab runs many instances of this environment in parallel on GPU, and an RL algorithm (e.g. PPO -- Proximal Policy Optimization, common for continuous control) updates a shared policy network based on experience from all parallel instances simultaneously, converging much faster than single-environment training. The resulting trained policy is then a neural network that can (in principle) be deployed on a real robot, taking sensor observations and outputting velocity commands directly.
8|⚪ T3 Sensors & ML on Robots|ML on Robo.use_when: Research and exploration into learned navigation behaviors, particularly for scenarios where defining good classical-planner parameters is hard (dense dynamic crowds, complex terrain traversal, legged robot locomotion where the action space itself is high-dimensional) -- RL approaches have shown particular promise for legged robot locomotion (learning to walk/run over varied terrain) where classical control is genuinely harder than for wheeled navigation.
8|⚪ T3 Sensors & ML on Robots|ML on Robo.avoid_when: Don't reach for RL-trained navigation policies for standard wheeled-robot navigation in structured environments (warehouses, offices) where Nav2's classical planners (A*/DWB/MPPI) already work reliably, are interpretable/debuggable, and don't require the substantial simulation infrastructure and sim-to-real transfer effort RL demands -- RL navigation is an active research area, not (yet) a drop-in replacement for Nav2 in typical commercial deployments.
8|⚪ T3 Sensors & ML on Robots|ML on Robo.what_goes_wrong: Policies trained purely in simulation often fail to transfer to real robots (the 'sim-to-real gap') -- the simulated dynamics, sensor noise characteristics, and visual appearance differ from reality in ways the policy implicitly relied on during training, so a policy that navigates perfectly in simulation can behave erratically or fail on the real robot. Also, reward function design is notoriously tricky -- a reward that seems reasonable (maximize progress toward goal, penalize collisions) can lead to unintended learned behaviors (e.g. a policy that learns to move very close to walls because the collision penalty wasn't calibrated relative to the progress reward, resulting in 'reward hacking' where the policy optimizes the literal reward function in ways that don't match the designer's actual intent).
8|⚪ T3 Sensors & ML on Robots|ML on Robo.real_example: A navigation policy trained in Isaac Lab achieves excellent results in simulation -- fast, collision-free navigation across thousands of randomized layouts -- but when deployed on the real robot, it oscillates near doorways, a behavior never seen in simulation; investigation finds the simulated LiDAR had perfectly clean readings while the real LiDAR has sensor noise near doorway edges (reflections off door frames), and the policy (never having seen this noise pattern during training) responds to it erratically. This motivates sim-to-real techniques like domain randomisation -- covered in the next note -- where simulated sensor noise is deliberately randomized during training so the policy becomes robust to it.

8|⚪ T3 Sensors & ML on Robots|ML on Robo.what_it_is: Sim-to-real transfer is the broader challenge of making models/policies trained in simulation work on real robots, given that simulation never perfectly matches reality (the 'reality gap'); domain randomisation is a specific technique for narrowing this gap -- during training, randomly varying simulation parameters (textures, lighting, physics properties, sensor noise) across a wide range so the trained model/policy becomes robust to variation rather than overfit to one specific (and inevitably slightly wrong) simulated world.
8|⚪ T3 Sensors & ML on Robots|ML on Robo.why_it_exists: A policy or perception model trained in a single, fixed simulated environment learns to exploit that environment's specific (and unrealistic) regularities -- exact textures, perfectly clean sensor data, precise physics -- regularities that don't hold in reality. Rather than trying to make simulation perfectly match reality (extremely hard, and reality itself varies -- different lighting, different floor textures across deployment sites), domain randomisation instead makes the TRAINING distribution broad enough that reality falls within (or close to) the range of variation the model has already seen, so the model generalizes to real-world conditions as 'just another point in the randomized range'.
8|⚪ T3 Sensors & ML on Robots|ML on Robo.how_it_works: During simulated training, parameters are randomized per-episode or even per-step -- visual domain randomisation varies textures, colors, lighting conditions, camera parameters (for vision-based policies/perception); dynamics randomisation varies physical properties (friction coefficients, mass, motor response characteristics, sensor noise/latency) so control policies become robust to the fact that the real robot's actual physical parameters won't exactly match the simulator's assumed values. The randomization ranges need to be wide enough to plausibly cover real-world variation, but not so wide that the task becomes unlearnable (e.g. randomizing friction from 'ice' to 'glue' might make a walking policy unable to learn anything useful for any single value).
8|⚪ T3 Sensors & ML on Robots|ML on Robo.use_when: Any sim-trained model/policy intended for real-world deployment -- domain randomisation is close to a baseline requirement for sim-to-real RL and is also widely used for vision models (training object detectors on randomized synthetic scenes to generalize to real camera images).
8|⚪ T3 Sensors & ML on Robots|ML on Robo.avoid_when: Don't apply domain randomisation as a substitute for SOME real-world data/validation -- randomisation improves robustness to variation but doesn't guarantee the real world falls within the randomized distribution; sim-to-real transfer should still be validated with real-world testing, and ideally some real data (even a small amount) used for fine-tuning or validation after sim training.
8|⚪ T3 Sensors & ML on Robots|ML on Robo.what_goes_wrong: Overly narrow randomisation ranges (chosen based on what the simulation engineers THOUGHT reality looked like) can miss the actual real-world range -- if real floor friction varies more than the randomized training range assumed, the policy still encounters out-of-distribution conditions at deployment, just a less extreme version of the original sim-to-real gap. Conversely, overly wide randomisation can make training slower/harder to converge, or produce overly conservative policies that sacrifice performance (e.g. a navigation policy trained with very wide sensor-noise randomisation might move unnecessarily slowly even in the clean conditions it actually encounters, having learned to hedge against noise levels rarely seen in practice).
8|⚪ T3 Sensors & ML on Robots|ML on Robo.real_example: A grasping policy trained with visual domain randomisation (random textures/lighting on objects and background) transfers reasonably well to the real robot for most objects, but consistently fails on a specific class of shiny/reflective objects -- the randomized textures used during training, while diverse, didn't include highly specular/reflective surfaces, so the policy's visual understanding has a blind spot for this real-world material property; the team adds reflective material properties to the randomisation range and retrains, improving performance on these objects without degrading performance on the previously-working object types.

8|⚪ T3 Sensors & ML on Robots|ML on Robo.what_it_is: Behaviour cloning (BC) is a learning approach where a robot policy is trained via supervised learning directly on human-demonstrated trajectories -- a human operator performs the task (teleoperating the robot, or via kinesthetic teaching/physically guiding the robot), recording (observation, action) pairs, and the policy is trained to imitate the mapping from observations to the demonstrated actions, without requiring a reward function or trial-and-error exploration.
8|⚪ T3 Sensors & ML on Robots|ML on Robo.why_it_exists: RL requires defining a reward function (often hard to specify well, as discussed in the RL note) and extensive trial-and-error exploration (expensive/risky on real robots). For many manipulation tasks, it's easier for a human to simply DEMONSTRATE the desired behavior (a few dozen to a few hundred demonstrations) than to either hand-engineer a controller or define a reward function and run RL -- BC turns 'show the robot how' into a supervised learning problem, which is generally faster to set up and more sample-efficient for complex manipulation tasks than RL from scratch.
8|⚪ T3 Sensors & ML on Robots|ML on Robo.how_it_works: A human operator controls the robot (via teleoperation interfaces -- joysticks, VR controllers, or physically guiding the arm) to perform the task multiple times, with the robot's sensor observations (camera images, joint positions) and the operator's commands (or resulting robot actions) recorded as training data. A policy network is trained via supervised learning to predict the demonstrated action given the observation -- modern approaches often use architectures like Diffusion Policy or Action Chunking Transformers (ACT) that predict sequences of future actions rather than single-step actions, improving robustness to compounding errors. At deployment, the trained policy runs autonomously, taking the same kinds of observations the demonstrations used and outputting actions.
8|⚪ T3 Sensors & ML on Robots|ML on Robo.use_when: Manipulation tasks that are hard to specify via classical programming or reward functions but are relatively easy for a human to demonstrate -- tasks involving contact-rich manipulation, deformable objects, or tasks with many task-specific nuances that would be tedious to hand-code but natural to demonstrate.
8|⚪ T3 Sensors & ML on Robots|ML on Robo.avoid_when: Don't expect BC policies to generalize well beyond the distribution of demonstrated scenarios -- BC is fundamentally imitation of the specific demonstrations provided, and a policy trained on demonstrations from one set of object positions/types may not handle novel configurations gracefully; for tasks needing broad generalization, either collect much more diverse demonstration data, or combine BC with other techniques (RL fine-tuning, foundation models).
8|⚪ T3 Sensors & ML on Robots|ML on Robo.what_goes_wrong: BC suffers from 'distribution shift' / compounding error -- the policy is trained on observations that result from the DEMONSTRATOR's actions, but at deployment the policy's own (slightly imperfect) actions lead to observations slightly outside the training distribution, and the policy (never having seen these slightly-off states during training) may respond poorly, leading to further drift -- small errors compound over a long task execution. Also, demonstration quality/consistency matters a lot -- if different demonstrations show inconsistent strategies for the same situation (e.g. sometimes approaching an object from the left, sometimes from the right, depending on demonstrator preference), the policy can learn an 'averaged' behavior that's worse than either consistent strategy.
8|⚪ T3 Sensors & ML on Robots|ML on Robo.real_example: A BC policy trained on demonstrations of a pick-and-place task performs well for the first few seconds of execution but increasingly drifts off-trajectory as the task progresses, eventually missing the target placement location -- diagnosed as compounding error from distribution shift: small deviations early in execution put the robot in states slightly different from any demonstration, and the policy's responses to these novel-but-similar states are less accurate, compounding over the task duration. The team addresses this partly by collecting additional demonstrations that include RECOVERY from slightly off-nominal states (not just perfect executions), giving the policy training examples closer to what it actually encounters at deployment.

8|⚪ T3 Sensors & ML on Robots|ML on Robo.what_it_is: Safety constraints in robot ML systems are mechanisms that bound or override ML model outputs (perception detections, learned control policies) to ensure the robot cannot take actions that violate hard safety requirements, regardless of what the ML model outputs -- treating ML components as 'advisory' or 'bounded' rather than having unconstrained authority over robot actions.
8|⚪ T3 Sensors & ML on Robots|ML on Robo.why_it_exists: ML models -- detection models, learned policies, depth estimators -- are statistical and can be WRONG in ways that are hard to fully characterize or test exhaustively (out-of-distribution inputs, adversarial conditions, rare edge cases). For a robot operating around people and valuable equipment, 'the ML model might occasionally be wrong' must not translate into 'the robot might occasionally do something dangerous' -- safety constraints provide a layer that's independent of (and not solely reliant on) the ML components' correctness.
8|⚪ T3 Sensors & ML on Robots|ML on Robo.how_it_works: Common patterns include: velocity/force limits enforced at a lower level (e.g. firmware/hardware limits on maximum speed or joint torque) that a learned policy cannot exceed regardless of its output; geometric safety zones (certified safety-rated LiDAR with defined protective fields that trigger hardware-level stops, independent of any ML-based perception); output filtering/clamping (a learned policy's action output is clamped to a safe range before being sent to actuators); and runtime monitors that check ML outputs for plausibility (e.g. if a depth-estimation model suddenly outputs wildly different values frame-to-frame, a monitor can flag this as likely-erroneous and fall back to a more conservative behavior or a non-ML sensor). The general principle is defense in depth -- safety doesn't depend on any single component (especially not an ML component) being perfect.
8|⚪ T3 Sensors & ML on Robots|ML on Robo.use_when: Any robot system where ML components influence motion/actions and operates in environments where errors have real consequences (near people, expensive equipment, or where failures are costly to recover from) -- which describes essentially all commercially deployed robots with ML components.
8|⚪ T3 Sensors & ML on Robots|ML on Robo.avoid_when: This isn't a 'use when / avoid when' in the sense of being optional for some deployments -- the question is calibrating the STRENGTH of constraints to the risk level; a robot operating in a fully fenced-off area with no human access can have lighter constraints than one sharing space with people, but 'no safety constraints on ML outputs at all' is rarely appropriate for any real deployment.
8|⚪ T3 Sensors & ML on Robots|ML on Robo.what_goes_wrong: Safety constraints that are too conservative can make ML-enabled features practically useless (a learned navigation policy so heavily clamped/overridden by safety layers that it never gets to exhibit the learned behavior that motivated using ML in the first place) -- there's a real tension between safety margins and the value the ML component is supposed to add, requiring careful tuning rather than maximal conservatism by default. Conversely, constraints validated only against the SPECIFIC failure modes the team anticipated can miss novel failure modes -- an ML model can fail in unanticipated ways that existing constraints don't cover, which is why constraints based on FUNDAMENTAL physical/geometric limits (max speed, certified safety zones) are more robust than constraints designed around specific anticipated ML failure patterns.
8|⚪ T3 Sensors & ML on Robots|ML on Robo.real_example: A robot's learned grasping policy occasionally outputs a gripper-closing force command at the extreme high end of its trained range when faced with an object type not well-represented in training data -- without a hardware-level force limit, this could damage fragile objects or the gripper itself. The team adds a hardware/firmware-level maximum gripper force limit that's independent of the policy's output -- when the policy's commanded force exceeds this limit, the firmware clamps it, providing a safety guarantee that holds regardless of what the policy learns or how it behaves on novel inputs, while also serving as a signal (logged clamp events) that the policy is operating outside its comfortable range for that object type.

8|⚪ T3 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Addi.what_it_is: MoveIt 2 is the standard ROS2 framework for robot arm manipulation -- providing motion planning (computing collision-free joint trajectories to reach a target pose), kinematics (forward/inverse kinematics for arbitrary arm configurations), collision checking (against the robot itself and the environment), and integration with perception and execution -- serving as the manipulation-equivalent of what Nav2 is for mobile base navigation.
8|⚪ T3 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Addi.why_it_exists: Computing a collision-free path for a multi-degree-of-freedom arm from its current configuration to a target end-effector pose is a non-trivial motion-planning problem (high-dimensional configuration space, collision constraints against a 3D environment, joint limits) that every manipulation application needs solved -- MoveIt provides this as a reusable, configurable framework rather than requiring each robot/application to implement arm motion planning from scratch.
8|⚪ T3 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Addi.how_it_works: MoveIt is configured per-robot via a 'MoveIt config package' (generated with a setup assistant) that describes the robot's kinematic structure (from URDF), defines 'planning groups' (named sets of joints to plan for, e.g. 'arm' or 'arm_with_gripper'), and specifies which motion planners to use (OMPL's sampling-based planners -- RRT-family algorithms similar in spirit to those covered for mobile navigation -- are the common default, alongside others). At runtime, `move_group` is the central node: it receives planning requests (target pose or joint configuration), checks the current planning scene (robot state + known obstacles, often populated from perception), computes a collision-free trajectory via the configured planner, and sends it to the robot's controllers for execution. The `MoveGroupInterface` (Python/C++) provides a high-level API -- 'move the end effector to this pose' -- abstracting away the underlying planning request/response details.
8|⚪ T3 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Addi.use_when: Any ROS2 robot arm application needing motion planning -- pick-and-place, assembly tasks, any scenario where the arm needs to reach varying target poses while avoiding collisions with itself, the environment, or held objects.
8|⚪ T3 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Addi.avoid_when: Don't use full MoveIt motion planning for very simple, fixed, pre-validated motions where a small set of hand-tuned joint-space waypoints (executed directly via the robot's controller, without per-execution planning) is sufficient and faster -- planning has computational cost and (for sampling-based planners) some run-to-run variability in the resulting trajectory, which isn't always desirable for highly repetitive, validated motions.
8|⚪ T3 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Addi.what_goes_wrong: MoveIt's planning scene (its model of the world for collision checking) is only as accurate as what's fed into it -- if perception doesn't update the planning scene with a newly placed object, MoveIt will happily plan a trajectory THROUGH that object's actual location (it doesn't know it's there). Also, sampling-based planners (OMPL defaults) can produce different trajectories for the same start/goal across runs (since they involve random sampling), which can be surprising if an application expects deterministic, repeatable motions -- and occasionally produce 'valid but awkward' trajectories (collision-free but taking an unnecessarily convoluted path) unless post-processing (path simplification/smoothing) is configured.
8|⚪ T3 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Addi.real_example: A pick-and-place application works correctly in testing (static scene, planning scene matches reality) but in operation, the arm occasionally collides with a tote that was just placed on the table by a previous action -- the perception pipeline updates the planning scene on a periodic cycle, and the new tote's position hadn't been incorporated into the planning scene at the moment the next motion was planned. The fix involves either tightening the perception-to-planning-scene update latency or adding a 'wait for planning scene to reflect latest perception' synchronization step before planning motions immediately after scene-changing actions.

8|⚪ T3 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Addi.what_it_is: Micro-ROS is a ROS2 implementation designed for microcontrollers (MCUs) -- resource-constrained devices (limited RAM/flash, no full operating system, often running real-time operating systems like FreeRTOS or Zephyr) that can't run standard ROS2 (which assumes a full Linux-class OS) -- allowing low-level embedded devices (motor controllers, sensor boards) to participate as first-class ROS2 nodes.
8|⚪ T3 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Addi.why_it_exists: Robots typically have a hierarchy of compute -- a 'main' computer (running full ROS2 on Linux, handling navigation/planning/perception) and various microcontroller-based subsystems (motor drivers, IMU boards, custom sensor interfaces) that traditionally communicated with the main computer via ad-hoc serial protocols, requiring custom bridge code on both ends. Micro-ROS lets these MCU-based subsystems speak ROS2 natively (publish/subscribe to topics, offer services) using the same DDS-based communication as the rest of the system, eliminating custom bridge protocols.
8|⚪ T3 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Addi.how_it_works: Micro-ROS provides a cut-down client library (`rclc`, a C API analogous to `rclcpp`/`rclpy`) plus `micro-xrce-dds`, a lightweight middleware that implements a subset of DDS suitable for constrained devices, communicating with a 'micro-ROS agent' running on the main computer that bridges between the lightweight micro-XRCE-DDS protocol and full DDS -- so from the rest of the ROS2 graph's perspective, the microcontroller's topics/services look like any other ROS2 node's. The agent handles the protocol translation and resource management that the MCU itself can't.
