8|⚪ T3 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Addi.use_when: Embedded subsystems (custom motor controller boards, sensor interface boards, low-level safety controllers) that need to integrate into a ROS2 system's communication graph -- particularly useful when these subsystems are custom-developed (so you control the firmware) and want native ROS2 integration rather than maintaining custom serial protocols and translation nodes.
8|⚪ T3 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Addi.avoid_when: Don't adopt micro-ROS for MCU subsystems that use off-the-shelf protocols (standard motor controller CAN/serial protocols with existing ROS2 driver packages) -- if a mature ROS2 driver already exists for your hardware's native protocol, adding micro-ROS to the MCU firmware itself is extra complexity without clear benefit; micro-ROS is most valuable for CUSTOM firmware where you're already writing the embedded code and want it to speak ROS2 directly.
8|⚪ T3 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Addi.what_goes_wrong: Resource constraints on the MCU (RAM for DDS participant state, message buffers) limit the number of topics/message sizes/QoS configurations that are practical -- a micro-ROS node that tries to publish large messages (e.g. raw sensor arrays) at high rates can exhaust the MCU's limited RAM or saturate the micro-XRCE-DDS link to the agent, in ways that are easy to overlook when designing the ROS2 interface from a 'normal ROS2 node' mindset rather than an embedded-constraints mindset. Also, the micro-ROS agent becomes a single point that must be running and reachable for the MCU's ROS2 participation to work -- if the agent process on the main computer crashes or the transport (often serial/USB) disconnects, the MCU's topics silently disappear from the ROS2 graph without an obvious 'micro-ROS node crashed' signal on the MCU side itself.
8|⚪ T3 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Addi.real_example: A custom sensor board running micro-ROS publishes raw sensor data at a high rate over a USB-serial micro-XRCE-DDS transport -- during integration testing this works fine, but when the main computer's USB hub is under heavy load from other devices, the serial transport occasionally drops bytes, causing intermittent micro-ROS agent disconnects and the sensor topic disappearing for brief periods. The team adds reconnection logic in the agent's supervision and reduces the published message rate/size to leave more margin on the transport.

8|⚪ T3 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Addi.what_it_is: ROS2 Security (SROS2) adds authentication, encryption, and access control to ROS2's DDS-based communication -- using DDS-Security (a standard extension to DDS) to ensure that nodes can verify each other's identity, communication is encrypted, and access to topics/services can be restricted by policy, addressing the fact that ROS2's default configuration has NO security (any node on the network can publish/subscribe to anything).
8|⚪ T3 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Addi.why_it_exists: ROS1 had essentially no security model, and ROS2's default DDS-based discovery/communication is similarly open by default -- fine for a robot isolated on its own network, but a real concern for robots on shared networks, robots with network connectivity to the internet, or multi-tenant/fleet deployments where unauthorized access to robot control topics could be dangerous (someone publishing fake sensor data, or directly commanding robot motion). SROS2 provides the security layer needed for robots operating in less-trusted network environments.
8|⚪ T3 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Addi.how_it_works: SROS2 uses DDS-Security plugins for authentication (X.509 certificates establish node identity), encryption (DDS traffic is encrypted so it can't be read by unauthorized parties on the network), and access control (a 'permissions' policy file specifies which nodes/identities are allowed to publish/subscribe/call services on which topics/services -- implementing least-privilege, e.g. a diagnostic node can READ sensor topics but not WRITE to motor command topics). Setup involves generating a 'keystore' (certificates and keys for each node identity) and permission XML files, then launching nodes with `ROS_SECURITY_ENABLE=true` and pointing them at the keystore -- nodes without valid credentials can't participate in the secured DDS domain.
8|⚪ T3 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Addi.use_when: Robots on shared/untrusted networks, robots with remote/cloud connectivity, multi-robot or multi-tenant deployments where access control between different operators' nodes matters, or any deployment with regulatory/customer security requirements around robot communication.
8|⚪ T3 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Addi.avoid_when: Don't enable SROS2 for early development/prototyping on an isolated development network -- the keystore/certificate/permission-file setup adds operational overhead (every new node needs credentials, every new topic potentially needs permission updates) that's pure friction during rapid iteration; security should be configured for the deployment environment, with development typically running unsecured on isolated networks.
8|⚪ T3 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Addi.what_goes_wrong: Permission policy files that are too restrictive can silently break communication in ways that look like unrelated bugs -- a node that was working fine becomes unable to discover or communicate with another node once security is enabled, because the permission file wasn't updated to grant the needed topic access, and the resulting symptom ('node isn't receiving messages') doesn't obviously point to 'check the security permissions file' as the cause unless you know to look there. Also, certificate expiration is an operational hazard -- certificates generated during setup have expiration dates, and a fleet of robots that's been running for a long time can suddenly experience communication failures across the fleet when certificates expire simultaneously, if certificate lifecycle/renewal wasn't planned for.
8|⚪ T3 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Addi.real_example: A team enables SROS2 for a fleet deployment and tests it thoroughly -- everything works for months, then one day multiple robots simultaneously lose the ability to communicate between certain node pairs, with no corresponding code or config change. After extended debugging, the cause is traced to certificates (all generated in the same batch during initial setup, with a 1-year validity period) expiring simultaneously across the fleet -- the fix involves regenerating certificates with appropriate validity periods and establishing a certificate renewal process well before the next expiration.

8|⚪ T3 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Addi.what_it_is: A digital twin is a virtual representation of a physical robot/system that's kept synchronized with its real-world counterpart's state (position, sensor readings, configuration) -- used for monitoring, simulation-based testing of changes before deploying to the real robot, and visualization, distinct from a generic simulation in that it specifically mirrors a SPECIFIC real instance's current state, not just a generic model.
8|⚪ T3 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Addi.why_it_exists: Testing changes (new navigation parameters, new task sequences, software updates) directly on physical robots is slow, risky, and limited by physical availability -- a digital twin lets engineers test changes against a virtual replica that reflects the real robot's current environment/state, catching issues before deployment. Digital twins also enable remote monitoring/visualization of fleets (an operations dashboard showing where every robot 'really' is, overlaid on a 3D model) and can support predictive analysis (simulating 'what if' scenarios using the twin's current state as a starting point).
8|⚪ T3 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Addi.how_it_works: A digital twin combines a simulation environment (Gazebo, Isaac Sim, or a custom visualization) with real-time data feeds from the physical robot(s) -- the twin's state (robot pose, joint configurations, detected obstacles) is continuously updated from the real robot's telemetry, so the virtual representation tracks reality. For testing, engineers can 'fork' the twin's current state into a simulation, apply proposed changes (new parameters, new code), and observe the simulated outcome without affecting the real robot -- then deploy to the real robot only after the simulated test looks correct.
8|⚪ T3 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Addi.use_when: Fleet operations needing centralized visualization/monitoring of robot state across a facility, or development workflows wanting to validate changes against a realistic, CURRENT representation of the deployment environment before pushing to physical robots -- particularly valuable when physical robot access for testing is limited (production fleet, can't easily pull a robot for testing).
8|⚪ T3 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Addi.avoid_when: Don't invest in building a full digital twin infrastructure for early-stage development with a small number of easily-accessible robots -- the synchronization infrastructure (real-time telemetry pipelines, keeping the virtual model's environment representation current) is significant engineering investment that pays off at fleet scale or when physical access is genuinely constrained, but is overkill for a single robot on a bench.
8|⚪ T3 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Addi.what_goes_wrong: A digital twin is only useful if it stays SYNCHRONIZED with reality -- if the twin's environment model (static map, obstacle layout) drifts from the real facility (new shelving installed, layout changed) without the twin being updated, tests run against the twin can pass while the same change would fail in the real (changed) environment, giving false confidence. This is the digital-twin analog of the general 'simulation doesn't match reality' problem, but specifically dangerous because digital twins are often TRUSTED as 'matching reality' more than generic simulations are.
8|⚪ T3 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Addi.real_example: A team uses a digital twin to validate a new navigation parameter set against the current warehouse layout before deploying fleet-wide -- the simulated test passes cleanly. After fleet deployment, several robots in one section of the warehouse start navigating poorly -- it turns out that section's shelving was rearranged the previous week, but the digital twin's environment model hadn't been updated to reflect the new layout, so the validation test was run against a STALE map that no longer matched reality. The team adds a process step requiring environment-model updates whenever the physical layout changes, with the digital twin's map version tracked alongside the deployment.

8|⚪ T3 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Addi.what_it_is: ros2_control is the ROS2 framework for real-time control of robot hardware -- providing a standardized architecture separating CONTROLLERS (algorithms that compute commands -- e.g. a joint trajectory controller, a differential-drive controller) from HARDWARE INTERFACES (the abstraction layer talking to actual motors/encoders/sensors), coordinated by a central CONTROLLER MANAGER, so the same controller code can run against different hardware (real robot or simulation) without modification.
8|⚪ T3 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Addi.why_it_exists: Without a standard framework, every robot's low-level control software is custom -- tightly coupling control algorithms to specific hardware drivers, making it hard to reuse controllers across robots or to swap between simulation and real hardware. ros2_control's hardware abstraction means a controller written once (e.g. a standard diff-drive controller) works on any robot that provides a conforming hardware interface, whether that's real motor hardware or a Gazebo simulation -- this is the foundational layer that the higher-level Nav2/MoveIt stacks ultimately command through.
8|⚪ T3 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Addi.how_it_works: The CONTROLLER MANAGER runs in a real-time control loop, at each cycle reading hardware state (joint positions/velocities/efforts from the HARDWARE INTERFACE) and writing commands (computed by active CONTROLLERS) back to the hardware interface. HARDWARE INTERFACES are plugins implementing a standard API (`read()`/`write()`) for specific hardware (a real motor controller's driver, or a simulated robot in Gazebo) -- this is the layer covered in more depth by the later 'hardware_interface plugins' note. CONTROLLERS are plugins implementing specific control algorithms (joint position/velocity/effort controllers, diff-drive controllers, trajectory controllers) -- covered in more depth by the later 'ros2_control controllers' note. This note covers the overall ARCHITECTURE: how controller manager, hardware interfaces, and controllers fit together, controller lifecycle (configure/activate/deactivate, similar to node lifecycle), and how the same controller set can target real or simulated hardware via different hardware interface implementations.
8|⚪ T3 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Addi.use_when: Any custom robot hardware needing ROS2-integrated low-level control -- ros2_control is the standard choice for building the control layer of a custom robot (mobile base, arm) that needs to interoperate with the broader ROS2 ecosystem (Nav2, MoveIt expect ros2_control-based interfaces for commanding the robot).
8|⚪ T3 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Addi.avoid_when: Don't build a custom ros2_control hardware interface for hardware that already has a maintained ros2_control driver (many common motor controllers, arms, and mobile bases have existing packages) -- writing a hardware interface from scratch is real-time-sensitive systems code (it runs in the control loop) and is worth avoiding if a working implementation already exists for your hardware.
8|⚪ T3 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Addi.what_goes_wrong: The controller manager's control loop runs at a fixed rate expecting hardware interface `read()`/`write()` calls to complete quickly and deterministically -- a hardware interface implementation that occasionally blocks (e.g. a serial communication call that can stall) can cause the entire control loop to miss its real-time deadline, with effects ranging from jerky motion to triggering safety stops if the deadline miss is severe enough. Also, controller activation/deactivation (switching which controllers are active, e.g. switching from a position controller to a trajectory controller for different phases of operation) needs to handle the transition smoothly -- an abrupt controller switch without proper state handoff can cause a discontinuity in commanded motion (a jerk) at the switch moment.
8|⚪ T3 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Addi.real_example: A custom robot's ros2_control hardware interface, communicating with motor controllers over a serial bus, works fine in testing but occasionally causes the whole control loop to miss its cycle deadline in operation, producing brief jerky motion -- traced to the serial read call occasionally taking longer than expected (USB latency spikes under certain system load). The fix involves moving the serial communication to a separate thread with the hardware interface's `read()`/`write()` operating on the latest available data (non-blocking) rather than blocking on each cycle for fresh serial data.

8|⚪ T3 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Addi.what_it_is: Simultaneous task execution refers to a robot performing multiple distinct tasks/behaviors CONCURRENTLY rather than strictly sequentially -- e.g. a mobile manipulator navigating toward a location while simultaneously running its perception pipeline to identify the target object, or an arm performing a manipulation task while the base continues fine-positioning -- implemented in ROS2 via multi-threaded executors, callback groups, and parallel behavior-tree constructs.
8|⚪ T3 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Addi.why_it_exists: Purely sequential task execution (finish navigating, THEN start perception, THEN start manipulation) wastes time when tasks don't actually depend on strict ordering -- a robot can often be more efficient by overlapping tasks (start perception while still approaching, so the manipulation target is already identified by the time navigation completes). ROS2's concurrency primitives exist so that a single robot's software can genuinely do multiple things at once rather than being limited to one callback/task executing at a time.
8|⚪ T3 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Addi.how_it_works: ROS2 executors process callbacks (subscription callbacks, timers, service handlers) -- a SINGLE-threaded executor processes them one at a time (sequential, even if conceptually 'independent'), while a MULTI-THREADED executor can process multiple callbacks concurrently across threads. CALLBACK GROUPS let you control which callbacks can run concurrently with each other (a 'mutually exclusive' group ensures its callbacks never run concurrently with each other, useful when they share state; a 'reentrant' group allows concurrent execution). At the behavior level, behavior trees (BT.CPP) provide a `Parallel` control node that runs multiple child branches concurrently, succeeding/failing based on configurable thresholds (e.g. 'succeed if at least 1 of 2 children succeeds') -- a common way to express 'do navigation and perception at the same time' at the task-orchestration level.
8|⚪ T3 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Addi.use_when: Tasks that are logically independent (don't need each other's output to start) and where overlapping them reduces total task time -- approach-and-identify patterns (navigate while perceiving), monitoring tasks that need to run continuously alongside a main task (safety monitoring concurrent with any other activity), or multi-actuator robots where different subsystems (arm, base, gripper) can act independently.
8|⚪ T3 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Addi.avoid_when: Don't introduce concurrency for tasks with implicit ordering dependencies that aren't reflected in the explicit task structure -- if task B actually needs a side effect of task A (even if not an obvious data dependency), running them in parallel introduces race conditions; concurrency should be reserved for tasks that are TRULY independent, and dependencies should be made explicit (not just 'usually finishes first in practice').
8|⚪ T3 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Addi.what_goes_wrong: Shared resources (a single arm, a single planning-scene representation, a single set of motor controllers) can't actually be used by multiple concurrent tasks simultaneously -- 'simultaneous task execution' for software callbacks doesn't mean the underlying PHYSICAL resources can be shared; if two concurrently-running behaviors both try to command the arm, one will fail or they'll conflict, regardless of how cleanly the software concurrency is implemented. Also, multi-threaded executors with poorly-chosen callback group assignments can introduce subtle race conditions on shared state (two callbacks in different groups both reading/modifying the same member variable without synchronization) that don't appear in testing (where timing happens to avoid the race) but appear intermittently in production under different timing.
8|⚪ T3 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Addi.real_example: A mobile manipulator's behavior tree uses a `Parallel` node to run 'navigate to table' and 'prepare gripper' concurrently, intending to save time -- but 'prepare gripper' includes a step that also commands the arm into a ready pose, and if navigation hasn't finished (base still moving) when the arm-positioning step runs, the arm's planned trajectory (computed assuming the base is stationary) becomes invalid as the base moves, causing a planning/execution error. The fix is either making 'prepare gripper' wait for navigation to reach a 'close enough' threshold before commanding the arm, or using a `ReactiveSequence` instead of pure `Parallel` so the dependency is explicit.

8|⚪ T3 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Addi.what_it_is: `message_filters` is a ROS2 library providing utilities to combine and synchronize messages from multiple topics -- most commonly `TimeSynchronizer` (exact-timestamp matching) and `ApproximateTimeSynchronizer` (matching messages whose timestamps are close but not identical, within a configurable tolerance) -- so a callback receives a SET of related messages from different topics together, rather than handling each topic's messages independently and trying to manually correlate them by time.
8|⚪ T3 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Addi.why_it_exists: Many tasks need data from multiple sensors that are CORRESPONDING in time -- e.g. an RGB image and a depth image from the same camera frame, or a camera image and a LiDAR scan taken at roughly the same moment for sensor fusion. These topics publish independently at their own rates with their own timestamps, and naively subscribing to both and using 'whatever the latest message is' when either arrives leads to mismatched pairs (e.g. pairing an RGB frame with a depth frame from a slightly different moment, producing visibly misaligned RGB-D data). `message_filters` handles the synchronization logic so callbacks receive genuinely time-corresponding message sets.
8|⚪ T3 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Addi.how_it_works: You wrap subscriptions to each topic in `message_filters::Subscriber` objects, then connect them to a synchronizer (`TimeSynchronizer` for exact match, `ApproximateTimeSynchronizer` with a queue size and time tolerance for near-match) -- the synchronizer buffers incoming messages from each topic and calls your registered callback only when it finds a set of messages (one from each subscribed topic) whose timestamps match within the configured criteria, passing all of them together to the callback. `ApproximateTimeSynchronizer` is far more commonly used in practice since sensors rarely publish at perfectly aligned timestamps -- its queue size parameter controls how many recent messages per topic it retains while searching for matches, trading memory/latency for match tolerance.
8|⚪ T3 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Addi.use_when: Any callback that needs data from 2+ topics that must correspond to (approximately) the same point in time -- RGB+depth fusion, camera+LiDAR fusion for sensor calibration/fusion tasks, or any multi-sensor perception pipeline where temporal alignment matters for correctness.
8|⚪ T3 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Addi.avoid_when: Don't use message filters for topics where temporal alignment doesn't matter (e.g. combining a slow-changing configuration topic with a fast sensor stream, where 'latest available' is fine) -- the synchronization machinery adds latency (waiting for a match) and complexity that's unnecessary if exact timestamp correspondence isn't actually required for correctness.
8|⚪ T3 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Addi.what_goes_wrong: `ApproximateTimeSynchronizer`'s queue size is a common source of subtle bugs -- if one topic publishes much less frequently than another, or if there's a burst of messages on one topic, the queue can fill up with unmatched messages from the faster topic while waiting for a corresponding message from the slower topic, and once full, OLDER messages get dropped -- meaning the synchronizer can silently miss valid matches if its queue isn't sized for the actual rate differences between topics. Also, if one of the subscribed topics stops publishing entirely (sensor failure), the synchronizer will simply never fire (no matches possible without that topic's messages), and a downstream system waiting on the synchronized callback goes silent -- which can look like 'nothing is happening' rather than clearly pointing to 'topic X stopped publishing'.
8|⚪ T3 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Addi.real_example: A perception pipeline uses `ApproximateTimeSynchronizer` to pair RGB images (30Hz) with depth images (15Hz, due to the depth sensor's processing overhead) -- with a small queue size (set to 5), during a brief period of high system load when depth processing falls further behind, the RGB queue fills with unmatched frames and starts dropping old ones, causing the synchronizer to miss matches that would otherwise have occurred once depth catches up. Increasing the queue size (to absorb temporary rate mismatches) and adding a 'last successful sync time' health check (to detect when synchronization has stalled) resolves both the missed-match issue and provides visibility into future stalls.

8|⚪ T3 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Addi.what_it_is: BehaviorTree.CPP is a general-purpose, open-source C++ library for creating and executing behavior trees -- a hierarchical model for designing reactive, modular task/decision logic, used across robotics (Nav2's recovery/navigation logic, MoveIt 2 Task Constructor's task sequencing, custom task orchestration) and beyond. This is the THIRD touchpoint on BT.CPP-related content: the earlier 'Nav2 architecture' note covered WHY Nav2 chose BTs over a state machine, and 'Behaviour trees in Nav2 — BT.cpp' covered Nav2-SPECIFIC tree mechanics (RecoveryNode, PipelineSequence, blackboard usage in navigation); THIS note covers the LIBRARY ITSELF -- its general node-type vocabulary and XML-based tree definition, independent of any specific application like Nav2.
8|⚪ T3 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Addi.why_it_exists: Hand-coding complex reactive task logic (if/else trees handling many combinations of success/failure/retry across subtasks) becomes unmanageable as complexity grows -- behavior trees provide a standard VOCABULARY of node types (Action, Condition, Control, Decorator) that compose into readable, modular, and REUSABLE task logic, and BT.CPP provides a mature, well-tested C++ implementation of this vocabulary plus tooling (Groot editor, logging/monitoring) that many robotics frameworks build on rather than each implementing their own BT engine.
8|⚪ T3 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Addi.how_it_works: A behavior tree is composed of: ACTION nodes (do something, e.g. 'move to pose', return SUCCESS/FAILURE/RUNNING), CONDITION nodes (check something, return SUCCESS/FAILURE without side effects), CONTROL nodes (determine how children are executed -- `Sequence` runs children in order until one fails, `Fallback`/`Selector` tries children in order until one succeeds, `Parallel` runs children concurrently), and DECORATOR nodes (modify a single child's behavior -- `Inverter` flips SUCCESS/FAILURE, `RetryUntilSuccessful` retries on failure, `Timeout` fails if the child takes too long). Trees are typically defined in XML (describing the structure/composition) with the actual node implementations (Action/Condition logic) registered as C++ classes -- the XML can be edited/visualized in the Groot editor (Groot2, covered in the Advanced Navigation group) without recompiling, while the underlying node behaviors are compiled C++.
8|⚪ T3 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Addi.use_when: Any application needing modular, reactive task orchestration -- not just navigation: task sequencing for manipulation (MoveIt 2 Task Constructor builds on similar ideas), high-level mission/task management for any robot, or general game-AI-style decision logic where BT.CPP's mature tooling (visualization, logging, hot-reloadable XML structure) is valuable.
8|⚪ T3 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Addi.avoid_when: Don't reach for a full behavior-tree framework for simple linear sequences with no branching/retry logic -- a straightforward sequential script or simple state machine is more transparent and easier to debug for genuinely linear task flows; BTs earn their complexity when there's real branching, retry, and reactive (interruptible/re-evaluatable) logic to manage.
8|⚪ T3 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Addi.what_goes_wrong: Behavior trees can become difficult to reason about as they grow large -- deeply nested `Sequence`/`Fallback`/`Decorator` combinations can obscure the actual control flow, especially when blackboard variables (shared state read/written by different nodes across the tree) create implicit dependencies between distant parts of the tree that aren't visible just from the tree structure. Also, a common subtle issue is node STATE across tick cycles -- BT.CPP nodes can return RUNNING and be 'ticked' again on the next cycle, and stateful Action nodes need to correctly handle being ticked multiple times while RUNNING (not re-starting their action from scratch each tick) -- a node implementation that doesn't handle this correctly can restart long-running actions repeatedly instead of monitoring an in-progress one.
8|⚪ T3 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Addi.real_example: A custom Action node wrapping a long-running operation (e.g. an external service call) is implemented naively -- each time the node is ticked (which happens repeatedly while the tree is RUNNING), it re-issues the external call instead of checking on a previously-issued call's status, causing the operation to be triggered repeatedly rather than once. The fix follows the standard BT.CPP pattern for asynchronous actions: on first tick, issue the operation and store its handle/future in the node's state; on subsequent ticks (while still RUNNING), check the stored handle's status rather than re-issuing, returning RUNNING/SUCCESS/FAILURE based on that status.

8|⚪ T3 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Addi.what_it_is: Visual-Inertial Odometry (VIO) is a technique that fuses camera-based visual feature tracking with IMU measurements to estimate a sensor's motion (position and orientation over time) -- distinct from the earlier ORB-SLAM3 note (a specific complete SLAM SYSTEM that happens to support visual-inertial input among other modes) and the earlier 'Sensor fusion' note (general multi-sensor EKF fusion architecture); THIS note focuses on VIO as a TECHNIQUE/APPROACH -- the principle of combining vision and IMU specifically, why this combination is particularly powerful, and where it's used as a SLAM front-end.
8|⚪ T3 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Addi.why_it_exists: Vision alone (visual odometry) provides accurate relative motion estimates from feature tracking but can fail during fast motion (motion blur, features moving too far between frames to track) or in feature-poor environments (blank walls, low light). IMU alone drifts (as covered in the IMU note) but provides high-rate motion estimates that are robust to the visual failure modes above (an IMU keeps working during fast motion or in the dark). VIO combines them -- IMU provides high-rate motion prediction between camera frames (and bridges over brief visual tracking failures), while vision provides drift correction that pure IMU integration lacks -- the combination is significantly more robust than either alone, which is why VIO is the dominant approach for SLAM on platforms (drones, AR/VR headsets, handheld scanners) that experience fast motion and can't rely on wheel odometry (no wheels) or external infrastructure (GPS-denied).
8|⚪ T3 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Addi.how_it_works: IMU measurements arrive at high rate (hundreds of Hz) between camera frames (tens of Hz) -- 'IMU preintegration' techniques summarize the IMU measurements between consecutive camera frames into a compact relative motion estimate that's used both to predict where visual features should appear in the next frame (aiding tracking) and as a constraint in the underlying optimization (bundle adjustment / factor graph) that jointly estimates camera poses, 3D feature positions, and IMU bias terms. This tight coupling -- IMU and visual measurements jointly optimized in a single estimation framework, rather than loosely combining separate vision-only and IMU-only estimates -- is what distinguishes VIO from simply running visual odometry and IMU odometry separately and averaging.
8|⚪ T3 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Addi.use_when: Platforms without wheel odometry (drones, legged robots during flight phases, handheld/wearable devices) operating in GPS-denied environments where robust, drift-resistant pose estimation is needed from onboard sensors alone -- VIO is the standard approach for drone state estimation and AR/VR tracking.
8|⚪ T3 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Addi.avoid_when: Don't add VIO complexity for wheeled ground robots that already have reliable wheel odometry + 2D LiDAR SLAM (slam_toolbox/Cartographer) -- for these platforms, wheel odometry already provides a good high-rate motion estimate without the calibration complexity (camera-IMU extrinsic calibration, IMU intrinsic calibration) that VIO requires; VIO earns its complexity specifically for platforms lacking wheel odometry.
8|⚪ T3 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Addi.what_goes_wrong: VIO's accuracy depends heavily on accurate camera-IMU EXTRINSIC calibration (the precise rigid transform between the camera's and IMU's reference frames) -- even small errors in this calibration (a few mm of translation or a fraction of a degree of rotation) can introduce systematic biases that degrade long-term accuracy, and this calibration can be disturbed by physical impacts/vibration over a platform's lifetime without any obvious symptom other than gradually worsening drift. Also, VIO initialization (establishing initial scale and gravity direction, since vision alone has no inherent scale -- a key role the IMU plays at startup) requires sufficient motion during the initialization phase (e.g. the platform needs to actually move/rotate enough for the IMU-vision relationship to be observable) -- a VIO system that starts perfectly still and stationary for too long can fail to initialize or initialize with poor accuracy.
8|⚪ T3 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Addi.real_example: A drone's VIO-based state estimation works well after a fresh calibration, but accuracy gradually degrades over months of operation involving frequent hard landings -- traced to the camera-IMU extrinsic calibration drifting due to repeated mechanical shock gradually shifting the camera's mount relative to the IMU. Recalibrating the extrinsics restores accuracy, and the team adds a periodic recalibration routine (run after a threshold number of flights or detected hard landings) rather than assuming a one-time factory calibration remains valid indefinitely.

8|⚪ T3 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Addi.what_it_is: Multi-robot SLAM extends single-robot SLAM (covered earlier via slam_toolbox, Cartographer, ORB-SLAM3, RTAB-Map) to scenarios where MULTIPLE robots simultaneously build maps -- either of the same shared environment (collaboratively building one map faster, or covering more area than one robot could) or of different areas whose maps later need to be merged into a single consistent global map.
8|⚪ T3 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Addi.why_it_exists: A single robot mapping a large environment takes time proportional to the area (it has to physically visit everywhere). Multiple robots can map different regions in parallel, dramatically reducing total mapping time for large facilities -- but this requires solving problems that don't exist for single-robot SLAM: how do maps built independently by different robots (potentially with different, unknown relative starting positions) get merged into one consistent global map, and how do robots that encounter each other (or overlapping territory) recognize this and use it to improve the combined map.
8|⚪ T3 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Addi.how_it_works: Two broad approaches: CENTRALIZED, where each robot runs its own local SLAM and sends data (maps, or raw sensor data) to a central server that merges them; and DECENTRALIZED, where robots share information more directly (peer-to-peer) and merging happens collaboratively. Map MERGING requires finding the relative transform between two robots' independently-built maps -- if robots start from known relative positions, this transform is known upfront; otherwise, it must be discovered by finding overlapping regions between the maps (similar to loop-closure detection in single-robot SLAM, but ACROSS robots' maps) -- recognizing that 'this part of robot A's map corresponds to this part of robot B's map' and computing the transform that aligns them. Once merged, the combined map can be shared back to all robots for unified localisation.
8|⚪ T3 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Addi.use_when: Large environments where mapping time matters (initial deployment of a fleet into a new large facility -- mapping it with multiple robots in parallel rather than one robot covering the whole space sequentially) or scenarios where robots naturally explore different areas and benefit from a shared map (so a robot entering an area another robot already mapped doesn't need to re-map it).
8|⚪ T3 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Addi.avoid_when: Don't pursue multi-robot collaborative SLAM for environments small/quick enough that single-robot mapping is fast and the coordination overhead (communication, map-merging algorithms, handling the case where merging fails or produces an inconsistent combined map) isn't worth it -- for many warehouse-scale environments, a single robot mapping during an off-hours mapping run is simpler and sufficient, with multi-robot SLAM reserved for genuinely large-scale or time-constrained mapping needs.
8|⚪ T3 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Addi.what_goes_wrong: Map merging can produce a globally INCONSISTENT map if the detected overlap/transform between two robots' maps is wrong (a false-positive overlap match, analogous to a false loop closure in single-robot SLAM, but potentially worse since it's merging two otherwise-independently-consistent maps into one) -- a bad merge can create a combined map with duplicated or distorted regions that's worse than either individual map, and detecting/recovering from a bad merge after the fact (when robots are already relying on the merged map for localisation) is significantly harder than detecting a bad loop closure within a single robot's ongoing SLAM. Also, communication bandwidth/range between robots constrains real-time collaborative approaches -- if robots can't reliably communicate (out of WiFi range in a large facility), real-time map sharing/merging may need to fall back to offline/periodic merging when connectivity is available.
8|⚪ T3 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Addi.real_example: Two robots independently map opposite halves of a large warehouse during an initial deployment, then their maps are merged using a detected overlap region in the middle -- the merge initially looks correct, but a subtle scale/rotation discrepancy in the overlap region (the two robots' odometry had slightly different calibration) produces a combined map where features near the merge boundary are slightly duplicated/offset, causing localisation issues for robots operating near that boundary. The team addresses this by recalibrating both robots' odometry to match before re-mapping, and adds a validation step (checking metric consistency in the overlap region, not just qualitative visual alignment) before accepting a multi-robot map merge as final.

8|⚪ T3 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|ROS2.what_it_is: ROS 2 Jazzy Jalisco is the ROS2 distribution released in May 2024, and -- like Humble Hawksbill (May 2022) before it -- is a Long-Term Support (LTS) release, meaning it receives security/bug-fix support for an extended period (5 years for LTS releases, vs. shorter support windows for non-LTS releases), making it (alongside Humble) one of the recommended choices for production robot deployments that need a stable, long-supported base.
8|⚪ T3 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|ROS2.why_it_exists: ROS2 follows a roughly 6-month release cadence (matching Ubuntu's release cycle, with LTS ROS2 releases aligned to Ubuntu LTS releases -- Jazzy targets Ubuntu 24.04 'Noble Numbat'), with alternating LTS and non-LTS releases. LTS releases exist because production robot deployments need a stable target that won't require frequent OS/ROS upgrades, while the broader release cadence lets newer features and improvements flow into the ecosystem more frequently for those who want them.
8|⚪ T3 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|ROS2.how_it_works: Each ROS2 distribution is tied to a specific Ubuntu LTS version (Jazzy -> Ubuntu 24.04, Humble -> Ubuntu 22.04) and bundles specific versions of core libraries (rclcpp, rclpy, rmw implementations, etc.) plus the broader package ecosystem built/released against that distribution. Jazzy brought improvements like updated RMW (middleware) implementations, refinements to launch system features, and continued evolution of tools like Nav2 and MoveIt 2 that are versioned/released alongside ROS2 distributions. Choosing a distribution means choosing the OS version, the bundled core library versions, and which third-party packages have pre-built binaries available for that distribution (packages need to be released per-distribution).
8|⚪ T3 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|ROS2.use_when: New projects starting development around mid-2024 onward, where Ubuntu 24.04 is an acceptable target OS and the longer support runway of an LTS release (vs. a non-LTS release that will reach end-of-life sooner) is valuable for a project with a multi-year deployment horizon.
8|⚪ T3 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|ROS2.avoid_when: Don't migrate an existing production system from Humble to Jazzy purely 'to be current' without a concrete reason (a needed feature/fix only in Jazzy, or Humble approaching its support end-date) -- distribution migrations require validating that all dependencies (especially third-party packages and custom hardware drivers) have been released for the new distribution, which can be substantial work for systems with many dependencies; migrate when there's a clear need, not preemptively.
8|⚪ T3 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|ROS2.what_goes_wrong: Third-party package availability lags new distributions -- a package that's been stable and widely used on Humble may not yet have an official Jazzy release at the time Jazzy ships, forcing teams to either build it from source (extra maintenance burden) or wait. Also, 'Jazzy supports Ubuntu 24.04' doesn't mean every piece of robot-specific hardware/driver software has been validated on Ubuntu 24.04's newer kernel and library versions -- vendor-provided drivers (for cameras, LiDAR, industrial hardware) sometimes lag OS support, and teams upgrading to Jazzy can hit driver compatibility issues unrelated to ROS2 itself but blocking the upgrade.
8|⚪ T3 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|ROS2.real_example: A team evaluating a migration from Humble to Jazzy finds that ROS2 core packages and Nav2/MoveIt 2 are available for Jazzy, but a specific industrial LiDAR's ROS2 driver package -- maintained by the hardware vendor -- has not yet been released for Jazzy/Ubuntu 24.04 at the time of evaluation. The team either delays the migration until the vendor releases a Jazzy-compatible driver, builds the driver from source against Jazzy themselves (taking on maintenance of that build), or stays on Humble (still within its LTS support window) until the ecosystem catches up.

8|⚪ T3 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|ROS2.what_it_is: Hardware interface plugins are the ros2_control components that implement the actual communication with physical (or simulated) hardware -- this note goes deeper than the earlier general ros2_control architecture overview into the PLUGIN layer specifically: the `SystemInterface`, `ActuatorInterface`, and `SensorInterface` base classes that hardware-specific plugins implement, how they're loaded via `pluginlib`, and how they expose state/command interfaces to the controller manager.
8|⚪ T3 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|ROS2.why_it_exists: The controller manager and controllers need a CONSISTENT API to read hardware state and write commands, regardless of what the underlying hardware actually is (a real motor controller over CAN, a simulated robot in Gazebo, a custom serial-connected board) -- hardware interface plugins are where hardware-SPECIFIC code lives, implementing the standard interface so everything above this layer (controllers, controller manager) is hardware-agnostic.
8|⚪ T3 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|ROS2.how_it_works: A hardware interface plugin implements `on_init()` (parse hardware parameters from the URDF's `<ros2_control>` tag), `on_configure()`/`on_activate()`/`on_deactivate()` (lifecycle transitions), `export_state_interfaces()` and `export_command_interfaces()` (declare what state/command values this hardware exposes -- e.g. 'joint1/position' state interface, 'joint1/velocity' command interface), and `read()`/`write()` (called every control cycle -- `read()` pulls current hardware state into the exposed state interfaces, `write()` pushes commanded values from the command interfaces to the hardware). `SystemInterface` is used for complex multi-joint hardware (most common for robot arms/mobile bases with multiple joints managed together), while `ActuatorInterface`/`SensorInterface` are for simpler single-actuator or sensor-only hardware. Plugins are registered via `pluginlib` (XML plugin description + class export macros) so the controller manager can load them by name from configuration, without compile-time dependencies between the controller manager and specific hardware plugins.
8|⚪ T3 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|ROS2.use_when: Integrating new/custom hardware into ros2_control -- writing a hardware interface plugin is the standard way to make custom motor controllers, sensors, or other actuators available to ros2_control's controllers and the broader ROS2 ecosystem (Nav2, MoveIt 2).
8|⚪ T3 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|ROS2.avoid_when: Don't write a custom `read()`/`write()` implementation that does heavy/blocking work directly in these methods -- they're called in the real-time control loop, and as covered in the general ros2_control note, blocking calls here can cause the controller manager to miss its control-loop deadline; offload slow I/O to separate threads and have `read()`/`write()` operate on the latest buffered values.
8|⚪ T3 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|ROS2.what_goes_wrong: Incorrectly declared state/command interfaces (e.g. a joint's interface name in the hardware plugin not exactly matching what's referenced in the URDF's `<ros2_control>` tag or in controller configuration) cause silent failures -- the controller manager simply won't find the expected interface, and controllers requiring it will fail to configure/activate, often with error messages that point at the CONTROLLER side ('required interface not found') rather than clearly indicating the hardware plugin's interface naming is the actual mismatch. Also, `on_activate()`/`on_deactivate()` need to handle hardware safely -- e.g. `on_activate()` might need to enable motor drivers (energize them), and if this isn't symmetric with `on_deactivate()` (properly disabling), switching controllers or restarting the control stack can leave hardware in an unexpected energized/de-energized state.
8|⚪ T3 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|ROS2.real_example: A new custom hardware interface plugin exports a command interface named `joint1/effort`, but the joint_trajectory_controller configuration (and the URDF's ros2_control tag) was written expecting `joint1/position` -- the controller fails to activate with an error about a missing required command interface. The mismatch is initially confusing because the error references the CONTROLLER's configuration, not obviously pointing at the hardware plugin's interface export -- resolved by carefully cross-referencing the interface names declared in the URDF, the hardware plugin's `export_command_interfaces()`, and the controller's expected `command_interfaces` configuration, which all must agree exactly.

8|⚪ T3 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|ROS2.what_it_is: Controllers are the ros2_control plugins that implement actual control ALGORITHMS -- this note goes deeper than the general ros2_control architecture overview into the CONTROLLER layer specifically: built-in controller types like `joint_trajectory_controller` (executes time-parameterized joint trajectories, used heavily by MoveIt 2), `diff_drive_controller` (converts Twist commands to wheel velocity commands for differential-drive bases), `forward_command_controller` (passes commands through with minimal processing), and `joint_state_broadcaster` (publishes current joint states for the rest of the system to consume).
8|⚪ T3 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|ROS2.why_it_exists: Rather than every robot writing custom control-loop code for common patterns (following a joint trajectory, converting velocity commands to wheel speeds), ros2_control provides a library of well-tested, configurable controller implementations for these common patterns -- a robot's `controller_manager` configuration specifies WHICH controllers to load and how they map to the hardware interface's state/command interfaces, often without needing any custom controller code at all for standard robot types.
8|⚪ T3 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|ROS2.how_it_works: Controllers are loaded by the controller manager (often via the `ros2 control load_controller`/`spawner` CLI tools) and CLAIM specific command interfaces from the hardware interface (e.g. `diff_drive_controller` claims the velocity command interfaces for the left/right wheel joints) -- only one controller can claim a given command interface at a time, which is how the system prevents conflicting commands to the same actuator. `joint_trajectory_controller` takes a trajectory (sequence of joint positions/velocities/accelerations with timestamps, the same format MoveIt 2 outputs) and interpolates/executes it in real-time, claiming position (or velocity/effort) command interfaces for the relevant joints. `joint_state_broadcaster` is a special 'broadcaster' controller that doesn't claim command interfaces at all -- it only reads state interfaces and publishes `sensor_msgs/JointState`, providing the joint-state information that `tf2`, RViz2, and MoveIt 2's planning scene depend on. Controllers can be CHAINED (one controller's output feeds another's input) for layered control architectures.
8|⚪ T3 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|ROS2.use_when: Configuring the control layer for any ros2_control-based robot -- `joint_trajectory_controller` for arms (especially with MoveIt 2), `diff_drive_controller`/similar for wheeled mobile bases, `joint_state_broadcaster` essentially always (since so much of the ecosystem depends on `JointState` being published).
8|⚪ T3 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|ROS2.avoid_when: Don't write a custom controller for functionality a built-in controller already covers well -- `joint_trajectory_controller` and the various drive controllers (diff drive, mecanum, etc.) handle the common cases robustly; custom controllers are for genuinely novel control algorithms (a specialized compliant-control scheme, a non-standard drive kinematics) not covered by existing controllers.
8|⚪ T3 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|ROS2.what_goes_wrong: Controller interface 'claiming' conflicts are a common configuration issue -- if two configured controllers both try to claim the same command interface (e.g. accidentally configuring both `forward_command_controller` and `joint_trajectory_controller` for the same joint's position command), only one can be active at a time, and activating the second while the first is still active fails (or requires explicitly deactivating the first first) -- this is correct behavior (preventing conflicting commands) but can be confusing when first encountered, especially when switching between controllers for different operating modes (e.g. switching from a teleoperation controller to a trajectory-execution controller) without realizing the switch needs to be explicit (deactivate one, activate the other) rather than just 'starting' the new one.
8|⚪ T3 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|ROS2.real_example: A robot configuration includes both a `joint_trajectory_controller` (for MoveIt 2-driven motions) and a separate `forward_command_controller` (used for a direct-teleoperation mode) for the same arm joints -- attempting to activate the teleoperation controller while the trajectory controller is still active fails because both claim the same position command interfaces. The fix is implementing an explicit controller-switching sequence (deactivate `joint_trajectory_controller`, then activate `forward_command_controller` when entering teleop mode, and reverse when returning to MoveIt-driven operation) using the `controller_manager`'s switch_controller service, rather than assuming controllers can simply be 'turned on' independently.

8|⚪ T3 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|ROS2.what_it_is: This note covers the PRACTICAL configuration and tuning of Nav2's MPPI (Model Predictive Path Integral) controller plugin -- specifically its CRITICS framework (the modular cost functions that shape trajectory selection) and key tuning parameters -- building on the earlier 'Local planner — DWB, MPPI' note (which covered WHEN to choose MPPI over DWB as Nav2's local controller plugin) without repeating that plugin-selection framing.
8|⚪ T3 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|ROS2.why_it_exists: MPPI's behavior is determined largely by its CRITICS -- pluggable cost functions evaluated against each sampled trajectory rollout (e.g. `ObstacleCritic` penalizes proximity to obstacles, `PathAlignCritic` rewards staying close to the global path, `GoalCritic`/`GoalAngleCritic` reward progress toward the goal pose, `PreferForwardCritic` penalizes reverse motion) -- and getting good navigation behavior from MPPI is fundamentally about understanding and tuning this critics framework, which is detailed enough to warrant its own deep coverage beyond 'MPPI is an option for the local controller'.
8|⚪ T3 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|ROS2.how_it_works: At each control cycle, MPPI samples a batch of candidate velocity-command sequences (controlled by `batch_size` and `time_steps`/`model_dt` parameters defining how many trajectories and how far into the future each is simulated), simulates the resulting robot trajectory for each using a simple motion model, evaluates each trajectory against ALL configured critics (each critic contributes a weighted cost term), and combines the costs into a final score per trajectory -- the executed command is a weighted average of the sampled commands, weighted by how favorably each trajectory scored (lower cost = higher influence on the final command), which is the 'path integral' aspect (an integral/weighted-average over the sampled trajectory space rather than picking a single 'best' trajectory). Critic WEIGHTS (relative importance of obstacle avoidance vs. path-following vs. goal progress, etc.) are the primary tuning knobs -- e.g. increasing `ObstacleCritic`'s weight makes the robot more conservative around obstacles at the cost of potentially less smooth path-following.
8|⚪ T3 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|ROS2.use_when: After choosing MPPI (per the earlier plugin-selection note) as Nav2's controller -- this note's content applies to actually getting good behavior out of that choice: tuning critic weights for the specific robot/environment, adjusting `batch_size`/`time_steps` to balance computation cost against trajectory-sampling quality.
8|⚪ T3 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|ROS2.avoid_when: Don't tune MPPI critic weights by trial-and-error in the full deployment environment from scratch -- start from Nav2's provided default/example parameter sets (tuned for representative robot types) and adjust incrementally, ideally validating changes in simulation before deploying tuning changes to real robots, since poorly-tuned critic weights can produce navigation behavior that's worse than the defaults in non-obvious ways (e.g. a too-high `PathAlignCritic` weight can make the robot rigidly follow the global path even when a small deviation would avoid an obstacle more smoothly).
8|⚪ T3 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|ROS2.what_goes_wrong: Critic weight interactions are non-obvious -- increasing one critic's weight changes the RELATIVE balance with all others, so tuning is rarely 'adjust one critic in isolation'; a common failure mode is tuning `ObstacleCritic` weight up (to make the robot more cautious) without realizing this makes the robot's behavior near the goal worse (it becomes overly cautious approaching the final goal pose if there's any nearby clutter, since `ObstacleCritic` now dominates `GoalCritic` in that region too). Also, `batch_size`/`time_steps` directly affect computational cost -- increasing them for 'better' trajectory sampling can push MPPI's computation time per cycle close to or over the control loop's period, causing the controller to fall behind real-time, especially on lower-power onboard compute.
8|⚪ T3 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|ROS2.real_example: A robot tuned for cautious obstacle avoidance (high `ObstacleCritic` weight) in a cluttered warehouse aisle navigates obstacles well but then approaches its final goal pose (often near a wall/shelf, by definition of where goals are placed in a warehouse) very slowly and hesitantly, oscillating slightly before settling -- the high `ObstacleCritic` weight that helps in aisles dominates near the goal too, where some proximity to obstacles (the shelf the robot is delivering to) is EXPECTED and shouldn't be heavily penalized. The fix involves either critic weight schedules that change based on distance-to-goal, or accepting a more moderate `ObstacleCritic` weight that's a better overall compromise, validated across both aisle-navigation and goal-approach scenarios rather than tuning against aisle navigation alone.

8|⚪ T3 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|ROS2.what_it_is: The Nav2 Smac planner is actually a FAMILY of global planner plugins (Smac2D, SmacHybrid, SmacLattice) sharing a common search-based planning core -- this note covers the SMAC PLANNER FAMILY's practical configuration within Nav2, building on the earlier 'Global planner — NavFn, Smac (hybrid A*)' note (which covered the high-level choice of Smac-Hybrid vs NavFn as Nav2's global planner) and 'Hybrid A* — kinematic constraints for car-like robots' (which covered the underlying Hybrid-A* algorithm mechanics) -- THIS note focuses on the Smac plugin family's specific variants and configuration within Nav2.
8|⚪ T3 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|ROS2.why_it_exists: Different robot kinematics need different planning approaches even within 'search-based planning with a heuristic' -- SmacHybrid handles car-like/Ackermann kinematics (as covered by the Hybrid-A* note), but SmacLattice extends this further using precomputed MOTION PRIMITIVE LATTICES (libraries of feasible short motion segments for the specific robot's kinematics, generated offline) for even more kinematically-accurate planning for non-circular/non-holonomic robots, while Smac2D provides a simpler grid-based A* for circular/holonomic robots where full kinematic planning is unnecessary. The Smac family exists to give Nav2 users a consistent planner framework across this range of kinematic needs.
8|⚪ T3 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|ROS2.how_it_works: All Smac variants share infrastructure (A*-based search with configurable heuristics, support for the same costmap-based collision checking) but differ in their STATE SPACE and motion model: Smac2D searches over (x,y) grid cells with standard 8-connected (or similar) grid motions, suitable for circular robots that can move in any direction. SmacHybrid searches over (x,y,theta) with Reeds-Shepp/Dubins motion primitives for car-like robots (as detailed in the earlier Hybrid-A* note). SmacLattice uses a MOTION PRIMITIVE LATTICE -- a precomputed set of feasible (x,y,theta) transitions specific to the robot's actual kinematic model, generated by a separate lattice-generation tool offline for the robot's specific turning radius/footprint -- giving more precise kinematic feasibility than SmacHybrid's generic Reeds-Shepp curves, at the cost of needing to generate and maintain this lattice file per robot configuration. All variants support 'analytic expansion' (periodically trying a direct analytic path -- e.g. a straight Reeds-Shepp curve -- to the goal during search, which can find solutions faster when a clear path exists) and configurable smoothers as post-processing.
8|⚪ T3 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|ROS2.use_when: Within the Smac family: Smac2D for circular differential/omnidirectional robots where simple grid-based planning suffices; SmacHybrid for car-like robots where generic Reeds-Shepp-based kinematic feasibility is good enough; SmacLattice when the robot's kinematics are complex/non-standard enough that a generated motion-primitive lattice specific to that robot provides meaningfully better plans than SmacHybrid's generic primitives.
8|⚪ T3 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|ROS2.avoid_when: Don't reach for SmacLattice's added complexity (offline lattice generation, maintaining lattice files per robot configuration) unless SmacHybrid's generic Reeds-Shepp primitives produce demonstrably inadequate plans for your specific robot -- lattice generation is an extra build/maintenance step that's only worth it when the kinematic precision gain matters for your application.
8|⚪ T3 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|ROS2.what_goes_wrong: SmacLattice's motion primitive lattice files are generated for a SPECIFIC robot footprint/turning-radius configuration -- if the robot's physical configuration changes (different wheelbase on a new hardware revision, different footprint due to an added attachment), the lattice file becomes mismatched with the actual robot and needs regeneration; using a stale lattice file can produce plans that are kinematically infeasible for the ACTUAL (changed) robot, defeating the purpose of using a lattice for kinematic precision. Also, analytic expansion, while often a speedup, can occasionally cause the planner to commit to a locally-found analytic path that's globally suboptimal compared to what continued graph search might have found -- usually a minor optimality loss but worth knowing when comparing planner outputs across configurations.
8|⚪ T3 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|ROS2.real_example: A team generates a SmacLattice motion primitive file for their robot's initial wheelbase configuration, and planning works well -- after a hardware revision changes the wheelbase (affecting the minimum turning radius), the team continues using the OLD lattice file (not realizing it needs regeneration), and the planner occasionally produces plans assuming tighter turns than the new (wider-wheelbase) robot can actually execute, causing the controller to struggle to follow certain planned segments. Regenerating the lattice file for the new wheelbase resolves the mismatch -- the team adds lattice regeneration as a checklist item for any hardware change affecting kinematics.

8|⚪ T3 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|ROS2.what_it_is: The Nav2 Collision Monitor is a safety-focused Nav2 component that runs INDEPENDENTLY of the main planning/control pipeline, continuously monitoring sensor data (LiDAR scans, point clouds) against configured safety zones around the robot and triggering immediate velocity limiting or stops when obstacles violate these zones -- providing a fast, dedicated safety layer that doesn't depend on the full costmap/planner/controller pipeline being correct or fast enough.
8|⚪ T3 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|ROS2.why_it_exists: The main Nav2 pipeline (costmaps -> planner -> controller) operates at the rate of the control loop and depends on multiple components working correctly together -- if any part of this pipeline is slow, misconfigured, or temporarily not keeping up (e.g. a costmap update lagging behind), the robot's obstacle-avoidance could be delayed. The Collision Monitor provides an independent, lightweight, fast-reacting safety check directly on raw sensor data -- closer to a dedicated safety system than a navigation feature -- so that even if the main pipeline has issues, immediate collision risks still trigger a response.
8|⚪ T3 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|ROS2.how_it_works: The Collision Monitor is configured with one or more POLYGONS (zones around the robot's footprint, e.g. a 'stop' zone very close to the robot and a 'slowdown' zone further out) and subscribes directly to sensor topics (LaserScan, PointCloud2, or costmap data). On each sensor update, it checks whether any points fall within the configured zones -- if points are detected in a 'stop' zone, it publishes a zero-velocity command (overriding whatever the controller commanded); if points are in a 'slowdown' zone, it can scale down the commanded velocity. This runs as a separate, simple, fast node -- its logic is intentionally much simpler than the full costmap/planning pipeline, trading sophistication for speed and independence.
8|⚪ T3 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|ROS2.use_when: Any Nav2 deployment wanting a dedicated, fast-reacting safety layer for imminent-collision scenarios -- particularly valuable for robots operating near people, where the few-hundred-millisecond difference between 'the full pipeline reacts' and 'a dedicated simple monitor reacts immediately' matters for safety margins.
8|⚪ T3 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|ROS2.avoid_when: Don't treat the Collision Monitor as a certified safety system replacing hardware safety-rated sensors/e-stops for environments with regulatory safety requirements -- it's a software safety layer that significantly improves practical safety margins but runs on the same general-purpose compute as the rest of Nav2 and isn't a certified safety component in the way dedicated safety-rated hardware is.
8|⚪ T3 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|ROS2.what_goes_wrong: Overlapping or conflicting zone configurations between the Collision Monitor and the costmap's inflation/obstacle layers can cause confusing interactions -- e.g. the costmap-based planner/controller might already be avoiding an obstacle smoothly, while the Collision Monitor's independently-configured 'stop' zone triggers an abrupt full stop because the obstacle briefly entered that zone during the smooth avoidance maneuver, producing jerky combined behavior (smooth avoidance interrupted by abrupt stops) if the two systems' zones/thresholds aren't configured with awareness of each other. Also, the Collision Monitor reacting to RAW sensor data means it's subject to sensor noise/spurious readings in a way the (more filtered/processed) costmap might not be -- a single noisy LiDAR point briefly appearing in the 'stop' zone can trigger an unnecessary stop if the monitor doesn't apply any filtering/persistence requirement.
8|⚪ T3 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|ROS2.real_example: A robot configured with both standard costmap-based obstacle avoidance and a Collision Monitor 'slowdown' zone experiences jerky motion when passing close to a wall in a narrow corridor -- the costmap-based controller is already planning a smooth path that maintains a safe (if close) distance from the wall, but the Collision Monitor's slowdown zone, configured independently with a larger margin, repeatedly triggers velocity reduction as the robot's normal (already-safe) path brings wall points into the slowdown zone. The fix involves configuring the Collision Monitor's zones to be consistent with the costmap's inflation radius -- the slowdown zone should be smaller than the margin the controller already maintains, so it only triggers for GENUINELY closer-than-expected obstacles, not for the robot's normal safe operating distance.

8|⚪ T3 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|ROS2.what_it_is: The Nav2 Velocity Smoother is a component that sits between the controller's output (raw velocity commands) and the robot's actual command interface, applying acceleration/deceleration limits and smoothing to produce velocity commands that respect the robot's physical kinematic limits and produce smoother, more comfortable motion -- preventing abrupt velocity changes that the controller might otherwise command.
8|⚪ T3 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|ROS2.why_it_exists: Controllers (DWB, MPPI) select velocity commands based on cost optimization at each cycle, and consecutive commands can sometimes change abruptly (e.g. commanding full speed one cycle and near-zero the next, if the cost landscape changes sharply between cycles) -- sending such abrupt commands directly to motors can cause jerky motion, excessive mechanical stress, wheel slip (sudden acceleration can exceed traction), or simply an uncomfortable ride for any passengers/cargo. The Velocity Smoother enforces SMOOTH transitions between commanded velocities, respecting configured maximum acceleration/deceleration limits.
8|⚪ T3 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|ROS2.how_it_works: The Velocity Smoother subscribes to the controller's output `cmd_vel` and the robot's current velocity (odometry), and at each cycle computes an output velocity that moves toward the COMMANDED velocity but is constrained by maximum acceleration/deceleration parameters (separate limits can be configured for linear x, y, and angular velocities) -- e.g. if the controller suddenly commands a much higher speed than the current speed, the smoother will ramp up toward that speed over multiple cycles rather than jumping immediately, governed by the configured max acceleration. It also handles 'deadband' parameters (commands below a small threshold are treated as zero, avoiding tiny jittery motions) and can apply different smoothing for normal operation vs. emergency stops (where faster deceleration -- up to the deceleration limit -- is appropriate).
8|⚪ T3 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|ROS2.use_when: Essentially all Nav2 deployments benefit from a velocity smoother -- it's a low-cost addition that improves motion quality (less jerky), reduces mechanical wear, and can prevent traction-loss from commanding accelerations the robot's drivetrain/floor friction can't actually achieve.
8|⚪ T3 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|ROS2.avoid_when: Don't configure overly conservative (low) acceleration/deceleration limits in the smoother if the robot needs to respond QUICKLY to safety-relevant velocity commands (e.g. an emergency stop command from the Collision Monitor) -- the smoother sits between the controller and the robot, so overly slow deceleration limits could delay how quickly a 'stop' command actually results in the robot stopping; safety-critical stop commands typically need to bypass or use much higher deceleration limits than normal smoothing.
8|⚪ T3 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|ROS2.what_goes_wrong: If acceleration/deceleration limits configured in the Velocity Smoother don't match the robot's ACTUAL physical capabilities (limits set too high relative to what the motors/drivetrain can really achieve), the smoother's output commands can still exceed what the robot can physically execute -- the smoother smooths the COMMANDED trajectory but doesn't guarantee the robot's actual motion follows it if the limits are unrealistic, so 'smoothed' commands can still result in tracking error if they assume more capability than the hardware has. Conversely, if limits are set too conservatively, the robot's responsiveness suffers across the board -- including for legitimate fast-reaction needs (a tight maneuver that the controller correctly identified as needed gets artificially slowed by the smoother).
8|⚪ T3 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|ROS2.real_example: A robot's velocity smoother is configured with acceleration limits based on the MOTOR's theoretical maximum acceleration, but in practice, on the facility's floor surface, commanding accelerations anywhere near that theoretical maximum causes wheel slip (the floor's friction coefficient is the actual limiting factor, not the motor) -- the smoother dutifully produces smoothly-ramping commands up to the configured limit, but the robot still experiences slip-induced odometry errors during aggressive acceleration phases. The team reduces the configured acceleration limits to match the floor-friction-limited achievable acceleration (determined empirically) rather than the motor's theoretical limit, eliminating the slip.

8|⚪ T3 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|ROS2.what_it_is: MoveIt 2 Servo (`moveit_servo`) is a real-time Cartesian/joint velocity control component for robot arms -- it converts incoming velocity commands (from a joystick, teleoperation interface, or a vision-based servoing algorithm) into safe joint velocity commands at high rate, with built-in collision avoidance and singularity handling, enabling smooth real-time 'jogging' of the arm rather than the discrete plan-and-execute pattern of standard MoveIt 2 motion planning.
8|⚪ T3 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|ROS2.why_it_exists: Standard MoveIt 2 motion planning (the general 'MoveIt 2' note's focus) is plan-then-execute: compute a full trajectory to a target pose, then execute it -- well suited for 'go to this pose' tasks but not for continuous, real-time, operator-driven or vision-feedback-driven motion (teleoperation, visual servoing toward a moving target) where there's no fixed target pose to plan to, just a continuous stream of 'move a bit in this direction' commands. MoveIt Servo fills this gap -- a real-time control loop converting velocity intent into safe joint motion, at rates suitable for responsive teleoperation (tens of Hz).
8|⚪ T3 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|ROS2.how_it_works: MoveIt Servo receives velocity commands (Cartesian twist -- desired end-effector linear/angular velocity -- or joint velocities) at high rate, computes the corresponding joint velocity commands via the robot's Jacobian (mapping Cartesian velocity to joint velocities), and applies several safety layers before sending commands to the robot's controllers: collision checking (using the planning scene, halting/scaling motion that would lead toward a collision), joint limit avoidance (scaling down velocities as joints approach their limits), and singularity avoidance (scaling down velocity near kinematic singularities, where the Jacobian becomes ill-conditioned and small Cartesian velocities would require very large joint velocities). The output feeds the `joint_trajectory_controller` (or similar) at high rate for smooth real-time motion.
8|⚪ T3 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|ROS2.use_when: Teleoperation interfaces (joystick/VR-controller-driven arm control), visual servoing (continuously adjusting arm motion based on real-time vision feedback toward a target that may be moving), or any application needing continuous, reactive arm motion rather than discrete plan-and-execute motions to fixed targets.
8|⚪ T3 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|ROS2.avoid_when: Don't use MoveIt Servo for tasks that ARE naturally 'go to this known target pose' -- standard MoveIt 2 motion planning (with its global collision-free path planning) is more appropriate when the target is known in advance and a planned, validated trajectory (rather than reactive velocity control) is what's needed; Servo is for the continuous/reactive case, not a faster way to do standard pick-and-place motions.
8|⚪ T3 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|ROS2.what_goes_wrong: Near kinematic singularities, small Cartesian velocity commands can require very large joint velocities (the Jacobian's inverse has very large entries) -- MoveIt Servo's singularity avoidance scales down velocity near singularities, but if this scaling is too aggressive or poorly tuned, the arm can become very slow/unresponsive in certain configurations (near-singular regions of its workspace) in ways that feel like the system 'getting stuck' to an operator teleoperating it, without an obvious indication that a singularity is the cause. Also, collision-avoidance scaling in Servo depends on the planning scene being up-to-date (same dependency as standard MoveIt planning) -- if the planning scene doesn't reflect a real obstacle, Servo's collision avoidance won't prevent collision with it, since Servo only knows what the planning scene knows.
8|⚪ T3 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|ROS2.real_example: An operator teleoperating a robot arm via MoveIt Servo finds the arm becomes sluggish and hard to control in a specific region of its reachable workspace, with Cartesian velocity commands producing much less motion than expected -- diagnosed as the arm being near a kinematic singularity in that region (a configuration where the wrist joints align), where Servo's singularity-avoidance scaling significantly reduces velocity to avoid commanding excessive joint speeds. The operator (once aware of this) routes the teleoperation path to avoid that workspace region; for a more permanent fix, the team considers whether the task could be redesigned to avoid requiring the arm to operate near that singular configuration.

8|⚪ T3 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|ROS2.what_it_is: MoveIt 2 Task Constructor (MTC) is a framework for composing complex manipulation TASKS from sequences of smaller, independently-solvable STAGES (e.g. 'move to approach pose', 'open gripper', 'approach object', 'close gripper', 'lift') -- where each stage can have multiple candidate solutions, and MTC searches across combinations of stage solutions to find a complete, feasible task execution, rather than requiring a single monolithic motion plan for the whole task.
8|⚪ T3 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|ROS2.why_it_exists: Real manipulation tasks (pick-and-place, assembly) are naturally composed of distinct phases, each with its own constraints and possibly multiple valid approaches (e.g. an object might be graspable from several different gripper orientations) -- planning the ENTIRE task as one monolithic motion-planning problem is often intractable or produces poor solutions, while planning each phase in complete isolation can produce phase solutions that don't connect well to each other (phase 1 ends in a configuration that phase 2 can't smoothly continue from). MTC addresses this by structuring the problem as a pipeline of stages with explicit connections, where each stage can propose multiple candidate solutions and the framework finds combinations that work end-to-end.
8|⚪ T3 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|ROS2.how_it_works: A task is defined as a sequence of STAGES of different types -- GENERATOR stages produce candidate solutions from scratch (e.g. 'generate grasp poses for this object' might produce several candidate grasps), PROPAGATOR stages take a solution from the previous stage and extend it (e.g. 'given this grasp pose, compute an approach trajectory'), and CONNECT stages bridge between stages that don't directly hand off a single solution (e.g. connecting an 'arm at home position' state to 'arm at pre-grasp position' via motion planning). MTC explores the resulting tree of stage solutions, propagating costs and pruning infeasible branches, ultimately producing one or more complete, executable task solutions ranked by cost -- the highest-ranked complete solution is typically chosen for execution.
8|⚪ T3 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|ROS2.use_when: Multi-stage manipulation tasks where there are genuinely multiple candidate approaches at various stages (multiple grasp options, multiple placement orientations) and you want the planning framework to search across these combinations for a good end-to-end solution, rather than hand-picking a single approach per stage and hoping it composes well with the others.
8|⚪ T3 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|ROS2.avoid_when: Don't use MTC for simple, single-stage motions (a single 'move to pose' with no meaningful alternative approaches) -- standard `MoveGroupInterface` motion planning (covered in the general MoveIt 2 note) is simpler and sufficient when there's no real multi-stage composition or alternative-search problem to solve.
