8|⚪ T3 🔬 Advanced Navigation|Advanced Na.use_when: Multi-site robot deployments where robots need to communicate across WANs (not just a single local network), fog/edge robotics architectures where processing/communication spans robot-local, edge, and cloud tiers with varying network characteristics, or robots with constrained/intermittent connectivity (cellular) where DDS's typical discovery/transport overhead is a poor fit.
8|⚪ T3 🔬 Advanced Navigation|Advanced Na.avoid_when: Don't switch from the default DDS-based `rmw` to `rmw_zenoh` for typical single-site, local-network robot deployments without a concrete WAN/connectivity driver -- DDS implementations are mature, widely used, and well-understood for the standard local-network case; `rmw_zenoh`, while increasingly capable, is a NEWER option in the ROS2 ecosystem with less deployment history, and switching middleware implementations is a significant architectural change to make without a specific problem (WAN communication, constrained links) that DDS genuinely doesn't handle well.
8|⚪ T3 🔬 Advanced Navigation|Advanced Na.what_goes_wrong: As a comparatively newer `rmw` implementation, `rmw_zenoh` may have less mature support for some QoS settings or edge-case behaviors compared to long-established DDS implementations -- an application relying on specific QoS semantics (particular durability/reliability combinations) that work as expected with a mature DDS `rmw` might behave subtly differently (or be less tested) with `rmw_zenoh`, requiring careful validation of QoS-dependent behaviors when switching. Also, mixing `rmw` implementations across a system (some nodes using DDS-based `rmw`, others using `rmw_zenoh`) generally ISN'T directly interoperable without a bridge -- a system can't simply have 'some nodes on Zenoh, some on DDS' and expect them to discover each other; the choice of `rmw` implementation is typically system-wide (or requires explicit bridging).
8|⚪ T3 🔬 Advanced Navigation|Advanced Na.real_example: A team building a multi-site warehouse robot deployment (robots at different physical locations needing to coordinate via a central fleet management system) initially tries running standard DDS-based ROS2 communication across a VPN connecting the sites -- DDS discovery traffic and assumptions about network reachability cause unreliable node discovery across the VPN, with some topics intermittently failing to connect. Switching the cross-site communication layer to `rmw_zenoh` (with Zenoh routers positioned to bridge the sites) resolves the discovery reliability issues, since Zenoh's routing model was designed for exactly this kind of cross-network-segment communication -- though the team validates this primarily for the cross-site fleet-coordination topics, keeping standard DDS for each robot's own local (single-network) internal communication where it continues to work well.

8|⚪ T3 🔬 Advanced Navigation|Advanced Na.what_it_is: PlanSys2 is a ROS2 framework for AUTOMATED TASK PLANNING using PDDL (Planning Domain Definition Language) -- a standard formal language for describing planning problems (available actions with preconditions/effects, the current world state, and a goal state) -- letting a robot AUTOMATICALLY generate a sequence of high-level actions to achieve a goal, rather than having that sequence hand-coded as a fixed behavior tree or state machine.
8|⚪ T3 🔬 Advanced Navigation|Advanced Na.why_it_exists: Behavior trees (BT.CPP, used throughout Nav2) and state machines encode a FIXED structure of how tasks are sequenced/composed, designed by a human developer -- this works well when the task structure is known and relatively stable. PDDL-based task planning instead lets you describe the available ACTIONS (each with preconditions for when it's applicable and effects on the world state) and a GOAL, and a planning ALGORITHM searches for a sequence of actions that achieves the goal from the current state -- useful when the appropriate action sequence depends on the current situation in ways too combinatorially complex to enumerate as a fixed BT, or when goals/available actions change dynamically (new action types can be added without redesigning a whole BT).
8|⚪ T3 🔬 Advanced Navigation|Advanced Na.how_it_works: A PDDL DOMAIN file defines the available action types (parameterized templates -- e.g. 'navigate(robot, from_location, to_location)' with preconditions like 'robot is at from_location' and effects like 'robot is at to_location, robot is not at from_location') and PREDICATES (facts that can be true/false about the world -- 'robot_at(location)', 'object_at(object, location)'). A PROBLEM file describes the current world state (which predicates are currently true) and the GOAL (which predicates should become true). A PDDL PLANNER (search algorithm) finds a sequence of action instances (with specific parameters) that transforms the initial state into one satisfying the goal -- PlanSys2 integrates this planning process into ROS2, executing the resulting plan's actions via ROS2 action servers (each PDDL action type corresponds to a ROS2 action implementation that actually performs that action on the robot), and can REPLAN if execution encounters unexpected states (an action fails, or the world state changes unexpectedly).
8|⚪ T3 🔬 Advanced Navigation|Advanced Na.use_when: Robots performing tasks where the appropriate ACTION SEQUENCE genuinely depends on the current situation in ways that would require an unwieldy number of hand-coded BT branches to cover -- multi-step tasks with many possible orderings/combinations depending on initial conditions (e.g. a robot that might need to pick up objects in different orders depending on which locations currently have which objects), or systems where new capabilities (action types) are added over time and should automatically be incorporated into planning without redesigning existing task logic.
8|⚪ T3 🔬 Advanced Navigation|Advanced Na.avoid_when: Don't reach for PDDL-based planning for tasks with a small, fixed, well-understood set of action sequences -- a behavior tree (or even a simple state machine) directly encoding the known-good sequence(s) is more predictable, easier to debug (the logic IS the BT structure, vs. needing to trace through a planner's search), and avoids the modeling overhead of writing/maintaining PDDL domain definitions that accurately capture action preconditions/effects (an inaccurate PDDL model can lead the planner to generate plans that look valid on paper but fail in execution because the model didn't capture some real-world precondition).
8|⚪ T3 🔬 Advanced Navigation|Advanced Na.what_goes_wrong: PDDL domain modeling is itself a non-trivial task -- if the domain model's preconditions/effects don't accurately capture real-world constraints (e.g. an action's effects description omits a side-effect that matters for later actions' preconditions), the planner can generate plans that are LOGICALLY VALID according to the (incomplete) model but fail when executed on the real robot because the model missed something. Also, PDDL planning can be computationally expensive for large domains (many action types, many objects/locations) -- planning TIME can become significant for complex problems, and a robot needing to replan frequently (due to a dynamic environment) with a complex domain might find planning latency itself becomes an operational bottleneck.
8|⚪ T3 🔬 Advanced Navigation|Advanced Na.real_example: A team models a multi-room delivery task in PDDL, with actions for navigating between rooms and picking up/delivering objects -- the domain model's 'navigate' action effects don't account for the fact that navigating through a room with a closed door requires a separate 'open_door' action first (this constraint wasn't included in the model's preconditions). The planner generates plans assuming direct navigation between any two rooms is always possible, and execution fails when a generated plan requires passing through a closed door with no corresponding open-door action in the plan. The team refines the PDDL domain model to include door-state predicates and appropriate preconditions/effects for navigation actions involving doors, after which generated plans correctly include door-opening actions where needed.

8|⚪ T3 🔬 Advanced Navigation|Advanced Na.what_it_is: This note covers Groot2 -- the visual editor and monitoring tool for BT.CPP-based behavior trees -- as the fourth and final touchpoint on BT.CPP content in this phase (after 'Nav2 architecture' covering WHY BTs, 'Behaviour trees in Nav2 — BT.cpp' covering Nav2-specific tree mechanics, and 'Behaviour Tree.CPP' covering the general library's node-type vocabulary). Groot2 provides a GRAPHICAL interface for CREATING/EDITING behavior tree XML files (without hand-writing XML) and, importantly, for LIVE MONITORING of a running behavior tree -- visualizing which nodes are currently executing, succeeding, or failing in real time.
8|⚪ T3 🔬 Advanced Navigation|Advanced Na.why_it_exists: While behavior trees are defined in XML (as covered in the general BT.CPP note) and can be hand-edited as text, doing so for non-trivial trees is error-prone and hard to visualize -- understanding a complex tree's structure from XML text alone is difficult, and DEBUGGING a running tree (which branch is currently active? why did this subtree fail?) from logs alone is tedious. Groot2 addresses both: a drag-and-drop GRAPHICAL EDITOR for constructing/modifying tree structure (generating the underlying XML), and a LIVE VIEW that connects to a running BT.CPP-based system and visualizes the tree with real-time status (which nodes are RUNNING/SUCCESS/FAILURE/IDLE at each moment) overlaid on the tree structure -- turning 'is my navigation behavior tree doing what I expect' from a logs-archaeology exercise into a visual, real-time display.
8|⚪ T3 🔬 Advanced Navigation|Advanced Na.how_it_works: For EDITING, Groot2 provides a canvas where users drag node types (Sequence, Fallback, Action, Condition, Decorator -- the vocabulary from the general BT.CPP note) and connect them to build the tree structure, with the editor generating/maintaining the corresponding XML -- custom node types (application-specific Actions/Conditions) need to be registered with Groot2 (via a model description) so they appear as available node types in the editor, similar to how they're registered with the BT.CPP runtime. For MONITORING, BT.CPP supports a 'Groot2 publisher' that a running tree can enable -- this exposes the tree's live execution state over a connection Groot2 can attach to, so Groot2 displays the SAME tree structure (loaded from the XML) with each node's current status color-coded in real time as the tree executes -- useful for both development (watching a new tree's behavior) and field debugging (connecting to a deployed robot's running tree to understand current/recent behavior).
8|⚪ T3 🔬 Advanced Navigation|Advanced Na.use_when: Developing or debugging any non-trivial BT.CPP-based behavior tree (Nav2's navigation/recovery trees, custom task trees) -- Groot2's visual editing reduces XML-authoring errors for tree structure, and its live monitoring is valuable for understanding actual runtime behavior, especially for diagnosing 'why did the robot do X' questions by replaying/observing which tree branches were active.
8|⚪ T3 🔬 Advanced Navigation|Advanced Na.avoid_when: Don't rely on Groot2's visual editor as the ONLY way tree XML is managed if the team also needs XML in version control with meaningful diffs -- visual editors can sometimes produce XML diffs that are harder to review (reordering, formatting changes) than hand-edited XML for small changes; teams often use Groot2 for understanding/larger restructuring while making small, targeted changes directly in XML with version-control-friendly diffs, depending on team preference.
8|⚪ T3 🔬 Advanced Navigation|Advanced Na.what_goes_wrong: Groot2's live monitoring requires the running system to have the Groot2 publisher enabled and a network connection from Groot2 to the robot -- in field deployments, this connection (similar to the Foxglove bridge connectivity consideration) is an additional thing that needs to be set up/reachable, and 'I can't see live tree state in Groot2' can be a connectivity issue separate from the tree's actual behavior. Also, for CUSTOM node types, Groot2 needs a model/registration describing each custom node's ports (inputs/outputs) and type -- if this registration is out of sync with the actual C++ node implementation (a port was added/renamed in code but not updated in the Groot2 model), the visual editor may show an outdated/incorrect representation of what a node accepts, potentially leading to edited XML that references ports the actual implementation doesn't have (or vice versa) -- a mismatch that may only surface when the tree is actually run.
8|⚪ T3 🔬 Advanced Navigation|Advanced Na.real_example: A developer adds a new input port to a custom BT.CPP Action node (in C++ code) to support a new configuration option, but doesn't update the corresponding Groot2 node model -- when editing the tree in Groot2, the new port doesn't appear as an option, so the developer can't configure it through the visual editor and either edits the XML by hand to add the port (working around Groot2's outdated model) or updates the Groot2 model registration to match the code change. The team adds 'update Groot2 model' as a checklist item whenever custom BT node ports change, to keep the visual editor's representation in sync with the actual node implementations.

8|⚪ T3 🔬 Advanced Navigation|Advanced Na.what_it_is: This note covers Isaac ROS GEMs -- NVIDIA's collection of GPU-accelerated ROS2 packages for PERCEPTION tasks (visual SLAM, AprilTag detection, stereo depth estimation, object detection, image processing) designed to run efficiently on NVIDIA Jetson hardware -- the third and final touchpoint on the Isaac platform in this phase, distinct from Isaac Sim (the simulator, covered earlier) and Isaac Lab (the RL training framework, covered earlier): Isaac ROS GEMs are for RUNTIME DEPLOYMENT on real robots, not simulation.
8|⚪ T3 🔬 Advanced Navigation|Advanced Na.why_it_exists: Many perception tasks (visual SLAM, stereo depth, object detection -- covered in earlier notes as general capabilities) are computationally demanding, and running them efficiently on embedded Jetson hardware (the common onboard compute for many robots, as covered in the TensorRT note) benefits from GPU-specific optimization beyond what generic ROS2 perception packages provide. Isaac ROS GEMs are NVIDIA-provided, GPU-accelerated implementations of these common perception tasks, packaged as standard ROS2 nodes (subscribing/publishing standard `sensor_msgs` types) -- so robot developers get hardware-accelerated perception 'for free' by using these packages instead of (or alongside) generic CPU-based implementations, without needing to do the GPU optimization work themselves (similar in spirit to how TensorRT accelerates custom models, but for a curated set of common perception PACKAGES rather than arbitrary custom models).
8|⚪ T3 🔬 Advanced Navigation|Advanced Na.how_it_works: Each Isaac ROS GEM is a ROS2 package implementing a specific perception capability using NVIDIA's GPU-accelerated libraries underneath (CUDA, TensorRT, VPI -- Vision Programming Interface) -- e.g. `isaac_ros_visual_slam` provides GPU-accelerated visual SLAM, `isaac_ros_apriltag` provides accelerated AprilTag detection, `isaac_ros_stereo_image_proc` provides accelerated stereo depth computation. From a ROS2 graph perspective, these GEMs look like standard nodes -- they subscribe to standard sensor topics (`Image`, `CameraInfo`) and publish standard outputs (poses, detections, depth images) -- but internally leverage Jetson's GPU for the heavy computation, achieving frame rates not practical with CPU-only implementations on the same hardware. Many GEMs are designed to work together in PIPELINES (e.g. stereo image processing feeding into visual SLAM), with NVIDIA providing example launch configurations for common pipeline combinations.
8|⚪ T3 🔬 Advanced Navigation|Advanced Na.use_when: Robots with NVIDIA Jetson onboard compute needing real-time perception (visual SLAM, depth processing, fiducial detection, object detection) at frame rates that CPU-only implementations on the same hardware can't achieve -- Isaac ROS GEMs let teams get GPU-accelerated perception without building custom CUDA/TensorRT optimization for each capability themselves.
8|⚪ T3 🔬 Advanced Navigation|Advanced Na.avoid_when: Don't adopt Isaac ROS GEMs if your robot's compute isn't NVIDIA/Jetson-based -- these packages are specifically built around NVIDIA's GPU acceleration stack (CUDA, TensorRT, VPI) and aren't portable to non-NVIDIA embedded platforms; for non-NVIDIA hardware, generic CPU-based ROS2 perception packages (or platform-specific acceleration if available for your hardware, e.g. Intel's OpenVINO-based options) are the relevant alternatives, not Isaac ROS GEMs.
8|⚪ T3 🔬 Advanced Navigation|Advanced Na.what_goes_wrong: Isaac ROS GEMs are tied to specific JetPack (Jetson's software stack) versions, similar to the TensorRT engine version-compatibility issue covered earlier -- a GEM built/tested against one JetPack version may not work correctly (or at all) on a Jetson running a different JetPack version, which matters for fleets with version drift across units (the same operational concern raised in the TensorRT note, applying here to a broader set of perception packages rather than just custom model engines). Also, while GEMs handle the GPU-acceleration internals, they still consume GPU resources that are SHARED with other GPU-using components on the robot (a custom ML model also running on the Jetson's GPU, per the object-detection/TensorRT notes) -- running multiple GPU-intensive GEMs alongside custom ML inference can lead to GPU resource contention, where each component individually 'works' but their combined GPU usage exceeds what the Jetson can sustain at the desired frame rates for all of them simultaneously.
8|⚪ T3 🔬 Advanced Navigation|Advanced Na.real_example: A robot uses `isaac_ros_visual_slam` (GPU-accelerated) for localisation alongside a custom YOLO-based object detector (also GPU-accelerated via TensorRT, per the earlier object-detection note) -- individually, both run at their target frame rates in isolation, but when running simultaneously, both frame rates drop noticeably because they're competing for the same Jetson GPU's compute resources. The team profiles GPU utilization with both running and finds neither can run at full target rate simultaneously on this Jetson model -- they either reduce one component's target rate (the object detector, since visual SLAM's rate matters more for localisation stability), or plan for a more capable Jetson variant in the next hardware revision, illustrating that 'each GEM is individually GPU-accelerated and fast' doesn't guarantee multiple GEMs plus custom GPU workloads all fit within one device's GPU budget simultaneously.
